lens: Venue selection and competitive positioning (2026) for a falsification-ladder study of surrogate models for 1-D MOF/COF adsorption columns

papers.citation: Emily Lin, E. Wang, S. Deng, "Neural ordinary differential equations (ODEs) for smooth, high-accuracy isotherm reconstruction, interpolation, and extrapolation", npj Computational Materials 11, 348
papers.what_it_shows: A Neural-ODE surrogate for adsorption isotherms trained entirely on GCMC-simulated data across three MOF databases, benchmarked against IsothermNet/MOFNet/MLP baselines. No experimental measurement anywhere in the paper; data and code on GitHub.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the single most important venue datapoint. It is direct, recent, in-scope proof that npj Computational Materials publishes purely computational adsorption-ML papers with zero experimental validation, provided the code and data are open. It makes npj Comput Mater reachable for us without experiment, and it sets the open-data bar we must meet. It is also the closest npj CM comparator: it is static (isotherms), ours is dynamic (columns) - that gap is our positioning wedge in that venue.

papers.citation: A. Rabeh, E. Herron, A. Balu, S. Sarkar, C. Hegde, A. Krishnamurthy, B. Ganapathysubramanian, "Benchmarking scientific machine-learning approaches for flow prediction around complex geometries", Communications Engineering 4, 182
papers.what_it_shows: Systematic benchmark of 11 SciML models (neural operators, ViT foundation models) on flow prediction. Headline conclusions are negative/cautionary: all models substantially underperform out-of-distribution; larger models trade physical plausibility for global accuracy; geometry encoding is architecture-dependent with no universal solution.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: A Nature-portfolio journal published a paper whose main results are that nothing generalises. This is the strongest precedent that our ladder is publishable at Nature-brand level without experiment, and it names a venue the project has NOT considered (Communications Engineering). It is also a competitor: a referee will ask what our OOD-failure story adds beyond theirs. Our answer must be the mechanism (measured coefficient-map rank), not the observation.

papers.citation: L. Shikhman, "Diagnosing Failure Modes of Neural Operators Across Diverse PDE Families", arXiv:2601.11428
papers.what_it_shows: 750 trained models across FNO, DeepONet-style, and CNO architectures on five PDE families (dispersive, elliptic, multiscale fluid, financial, chaotic). Finds strong in-distribution accuracy does not predict robustness, and failure patterns depend jointly on architecture and PDE family. Uses baseline-normalised degradation factors plus spectral and rollout diagnostics.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is our nearest direct competitor in the 'negative results about neural operators' space, and it is only months old. Our L5 is NOT covered by it: it does not study basis size p, does not measure a POD floor, and does not decompose error into basis vs coefficient-map terms. We must cite it and say so explicitly in the related-work paragraph, or a referee will use it to claim we are late.

papers.citation: J. Westermann, B. Huber, T. O'Leary-Roseberry, J. Zech, "Performance of Neural and Polynomial Operator Surrogates", arXiv:2604.00689
papers.what_it_shows: Head-to-head of reduced-basis neural operators and FNO against polynomial (sparse-grid, tensor-train) surrogates on parametric PDEs. No method is universally superior; polynomial surrogates are substantially more data-efficient for smooth inputs; FNO wins only for rough inputs; derivative-informed training consistently helps.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Directly relevant to L7 ('is learning needed at all?') and to L5. Our L7 compared learning against closed-form adsorption solutions, not against strong classical surrogates. A referee at CMAME/JCP/TMLR will ask why we did not include a polynomial/sparse-grid or Gaussian-process surrogate. This paper both supplies the missing baseline family and gives us the 'match method to problem structure' framing our ladder actually supports.

papers.citation: J. S. Hesthaven, B. Peherstorfer, B. Unger, "Nonlinear model reduction for transport-dominated problems", Acta Numerica 35, 173-272
papers.url_or_id: https://doi.org/10.1017/S0962492926000029 (Cambridge Core, Acta Numerica vol. 35, pp. 173-272)
papers.what_it_shows: Field-defining survey organising nonlinear model reduction into nonlinear parametrisations, reduced dynamics, and online solvers; categorises transformation-based, online-adaptive, and residual-minimisation approaches; frames everything around the Kolmogorov barrier for wave-like phenomena and moving coherent structures.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is now the canonical reference any CMAME/JCP/SISC referee will hold us to. Our two-wave warp is a transformation-based method in their taxonomy. We must cite it, place the warp inside their categorisation, and stop describing the co-moving frame and the two-wave warp as if we invented the idea. Not citing a 2026 Acta Numerica survey on exactly our problem class is a fast-track rejection at any numerical-analysis venue. Note: I verified title, authors, journal, volume and pages by fetching the Cambridge Core article page; the DOI string itself I did not read directly, so treat the DOI as unconfirmed and re-check it before use.

papers.citation: T. Taddei, "A Registration Method for Model Order Reduction: Data Compression and Geometry Reduction", SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing 42(2), A997-A1027
papers.what_it_shows: Constructs a parameter-dependent bijective spatial mapping that makes snapshot data amenable to linear compression, explicitly targeting problems with slowly-decaying Kolmogorov N-widths; combines registration with linear compression for low-dimensional representations.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Our 'two-wave warp' sigma = (t - t_lo(z))/(t_hi(z) - t_lo(z)) is a one-dimensional, physics-chosen registration map. Taddei 2020 is the canonical prior art. The honest novelty claim is not 'we invented a warp' but 'the correct registration for a Type V isotherm column is two-parameter because two waves separate by 40x, and single-front registration provably fails here' - which is a genuine, testable, domain-specific contribution. Framing it any other way is the largest single novelty risk in the paper.

papers.citation: H. Gowrachari, G. Stabile, G. Rozza, "Model Reduction for Transport-Dominated Problems via Cross-Correlation Based Snapshot Registration", arXiv:2501.01299 (also appears as a Springer volume chapter, doi 10.1007/978-3-032-11527-0_10)
papers.what_it_shows: Uses cross-correlation-based snapshot registration to accelerate Kolmogorov n-width decay so that linear (POD-type) ROMs become efficient; tested on 1-D travelling waves and a 2-D isentropic convective vortex.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: A 2025 method that automatically discovers the shift we hand-engineer, on 1-D travelling-wave problems very close to ours. It is both a missing baseline (does automatic cross-correlation registration find our two waves?) and a novelty risk. Running it on our snapshots is a cheap, high-value experiment: if it fails on the two-wave data, that failure is itself a strong result for a ROM venue.

papers.citation: A. S. Krishnapriyan, A. Gholami, S. Zhe, R. M. Kirby, M. W. Mahoney, "Characterizing possible failure modes in physics-informed neural networks", NeurIPS 2021 (arXiv:2109.01050)
papers.what_it_shows: PINNs learn easy problems but fail on slightly harder ones; soft PDE regularisation makes the optimisation landscape harder; curriculum regularisation and sequence-to-sequence training recover 1-2 orders of magnitude of error.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the canonical prior for our L4/L4b result that physics-as-a-soft-loss helps on the time axis but HURTS once hard output bounds exist. Our finding is a sharper, quantified version of theirs (soft penalty vs hard structural constraint, with the crossover located). We must cite it and state the delta precisely; otherwise a referee reads L4 as a 2021 result rediscovered.

papers.citation: V. V. Santana, E. Costa, C. M. Rebello, A. M. Ribeiro, C. Rackauckas, I. B. R. Nogueira, "Efficient hybrid modeling and sorption model discovery for non-linear advection-diffusion-sorption systems: A systematic scientific machine learning approach", arXiv:2303.13555
papers.what_it_shows: Adjoint-sensitivity/JIT-compiled hybrid modelling plus sparse and symbolic regression to recover missing sorption uptake functions from synthetic fixed-bed breakthrough data; reconstructs sorption kinetics and predicts accurately.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The closest published work to our L6 (separate identification of kinetics) and to the original SINDy plan. They report success recovering sorption kinetics from breakthrough curves; we report k_LDF is unrecoverable (R^2 = -0.61). That is a direct apparent contradiction a referee will find. Our defence is the Damkoehler regime: our sampled Da 155-3885 is near local equilibrium where kinetics are structurally unidentifiable. This makes the low-Da re-test (open item 6) not optional but mandatory before submission anywhere in chemical engineering.

papers.citation: Editorial, "What reviewers request the most", Nature Computational Science, published 28 April 2026
papers.what_it_shows: Enumerates the four most common reviewer demands at Nature Computational Science: (1) experimental validation and broader/quantitatively rigorous benchmarking against state-of-the-art; (2) clear justification of why a new tool is needed, no overstated paradigm claims, no selectively reported results, statistical tests present; (3) limitations discussed to prevent misuse, scalability/real-world demonstrations; (4) reproducibility and computational-environment detail.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the journal telling us its bar in its own words. Items (2), (3) and (4) we would pass outstandingly - the retraction ledger, calibrated alpha, 3-seed paired CIs and pre-registered protocol are exactly what is being asked for. Item (1) we fail twice over: no experimental validation and no benchmark against current SOTA operator architectures. Confirms the project's own assessment that Nature Computational Science is not reachable in the present state, and names exactly the two things that would change that.

papers.citation: TMLR Editorial Board, "Acceptance Criteria", Transactions on Machine Learning Research
papers.what_it_shows: Two criteria only: are the claims supported by accurate and convincing evidence, and would some of TMLR's audience be interested. Novelty is explicitly rejected as a necessary criterion; 'significant'/'impactful' are avoided as terms; new state-of-the-art on a benchmark is explicitly not required. Reproducibility and robustness/generalisability studies that lay out actionable lessons are explicitly welcomed. Significance is handled separately via optional Featured/Outstanding certifications.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: TMLR is the only candidate venue whose written policy accepts, verbatim, the paper we actually have: eight rigorous negative results, no SOTA claim, a refuted pre-registered prediction of our own. Every other venue requires us to manufacture a positive headline. This is the highest-probability acceptance in the whole candidate set and the only one where the retractions ledger is an asset rather than a liability.

papers.citation: F. Karl, L. M. Kemeter, G. Dax, P. Sierak, "Position: Embracing Negative Results in Machine Learning", arXiv:2406.03980
papers.what_it_shows: Argues predictive performance alone is a poor indicator of a publication's worth, that the performance-first norm creates perverse incentives and community inefficiency, and proposes concrete measures to normalise publication of negative results.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Cover-letter and framing ammunition. When we submit an eight-negative-result paper, the cover letter needs a citable position statement that this is a recognised methodological contribution rather than a failed project. Note: I confirmed the arXiv preprint only; I did not confirm whether it appeared in the ICML Position track, so do not cite a conference venue for it without checking.

papers.citation: R. A. Coyle, S. C. Pal, P. Walther, S. Park, B. Feng, Z. Zheng, "Sustainable Metal-Organic Framework Water Harvesters in the Artificial Intelligence Era", arXiv:2605.29179
papers.what_it_shows: Perspective on AI/LLMs/data mining for MOF water harvesting, organised around cooperative adsorption, operational RH, uptake capacity, hysteresis and scalability; focused on predictive synthesis, inverse design and synthesis-structure-property relationships.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Maps the AWH+AI conversation as of mid-2026 and shows it is overwhelmingly materials-discovery-facing (which MOF), not device/column-dynamics-facing (how the column behaves). That gap is our opening for a materials venue: we are the transport/dynamics half that this perspective does not cover. It also confirms the field's vocabulary - cooperative adsorption, hysteresis - which our two-wave finding speaks to directly and should be phrased in.

papers.citation: S. Khodakarami, V. Oommen, N. Ahmadi Daryakenari, M. Beekenkamp, G. E. Karniadakis, "Spectral bias in physics-informed and operator learning: Analysis and mitigation guidelines", arXiv:2602.19265
papers.what_it_shows: Analyses how spectral bias - preferential learning of low-frequency over high-frequency content - affects both physics-informed methods and neural operators, and gives mitigation guidelines.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the single most dangerous paper for L5. Our headline mechanism (params->coefficient map scores R^2=0.946 on mode 1, 0.39-0.58 on modes 2-5, median -0.014 beyond mode 24, so DeepONet behaves like a 4-mode oracle at any p) can be attacked as a restatement of spectral bias with a known mitigation. We need a pre-emptive experiment: apply their mitigations (mode-reweighted loss, feature scaling) and show the coefficient-map ceiling does not move. Verified via the arXiv API listing (title, authors, id, date, summary); I did not read the abstract page itself.

papers.citation: S. A. Faroughi, F. Mostajeran, A. H. Mashhadzadeh, S. Faroughi, "Scientific Machine Learning with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks", arXiv:2507.22959
papers.what_it_shows: Comprehensive review of KANs across data-driven learning, physics-informed modelling and deep operator learning, with comparative analysis.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: L3 refuted the KAN premise and L5 found DeepOKAN collapses in 10/45 runs. A 2025 KAN review is the reference frame reviewers will use to judge whether we tuned KANs fairly. Our matched-parameter protocol and the lr-grid audit (defect B22) are the defence, and this review tells us which KAN variants a referee will say we omitted. Verified via arXiv API listing only.

papers.citation: L. Galanti et al., "Towards Surrogate Modeling for Adsorption Processes Using Physics-Informed Neural Networks", Processes 13(9), 2824
papers.what_it_shows: Compares hybrid-PINNs against plain NNs for the adsorption step of a Direct Air Capture process; both are accurate with abundant data, but the physics constraints give hybrid-PINNs a clear advantage in intermediate and low-data regimes.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: A published 2025 result that a referee will read as contradicting L4b's 'physics-as-a-loss hurts once hard bounds exist'. It does not actually contradict us - they vary data volume, we vary whether hard output bounds are present, and our L4b effect appears only after bounds - but we must say so explicitly. It is also the closest chemical-engineering competitor for the physics-informed rung. Confidence limited: the MDPI page returned 403, so citation details come from search snippets and should be re-verified before use.

papers.citation: Perez et al., "Machine learning for optimization of zeolites for boric acid sorption", AIChE Journal 72(2), e70154
papers.what_it_shows: ML models trained on molecular-simulation data (not experiment) predict boric-acid uptake from zeolite structure, Al content, cation species and solution concentration; XGBoost fastest and most accurate.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Evidence that AIChE Journal will publish an ML-on-simulation-data adsorption paper with no experimental validation, and that XGBoost-class models remain the accepted strong baseline in that community - which is exactly our L1 best arm. Makes AIChE J a genuine, if unexciting, fallback. Verified from search snippet only.

papers.citation: "Unified physio-thermodynamic descriptors via learned CO2 adsorption properties in metal-organic frameworks", npj Computational Materials 11, 225
papers.what_it_shows: Learns unified physio-thermodynamic descriptors for CO2 adsorption in MOFs from computed adsorption properties.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Second npj Comput Mater datapoint that descriptor/ML adsorption work without experiment is in scope there. Relevant to L6: our finding that k_LDF is unrecoverable from observable descriptors is a negative descriptor result in a venue that publishes positive descriptor results - a defensible contribution if framed as identifiability rather than as failure. Verified from search snippet only.

state_of_the_art:
As of mid-2026 the venue landscape for this paper is defined by four facts.

(1) Purely computational adsorption-ML is publishable at IF-12 level. npj Computational Materials published IsothermODE (11:348, Nov 2025) with GCMC-only data, no experiment, and full code/data release. Its adsorption-ML output is however almost entirely STATIC - isotherms, uptake capacities, screening descriptors. Nobody in that venue is doing column dynamics.

(2) Negative and benchmark results have crossed into Nature-portfolio journals. Communications Engineering published Rabeh et al. (4:182, Oct 2025), an 11-model SciML benchmark whose headline conclusions are that all models fail out-of-distribution and that accuracy and physical plausibility trade off. Shikhman's failure-mode diagnosis of neural operators (arXiv:2601.11428, 750 models, 5 PDE families) is the 2026 continuation. The "nothing worked, here is why" paper is now an accepted genre - but it is expected at scale (750 models, 11 architectures) and with a mechanism.

(3) The ROM community has consolidated. Hesthaven, Peherstorfer and Unger's Acta Numerica 35 (2026) survey is the reference frame for transport-dominated model reduction; registration/warping (Taddei 2020, SISC 42:A997) is a well-established transformation-based family, with automatic variants appearing (Gowrachari/Stabile/Rozza 2025 cross-correlation registration). A two-parameter warp is a natural, not a startling, member of that family - unless the argument is that the correct registration is dictated by isotherm type, which no one has claimed.

(4) The specific intersection is genuinely empty. The arXiv API returns ZERO papers whose text contains both "breakthrough curve" and "neural operator". The adsorption-breakthrough arXiv corpus is CFD, homogenisation, and hybrid/SINDy sorption discovery - no operator learning, no measured n-width, no basis-size study. And nothing in the operator-learning + Kolmogorov corpus reports the specific L5 signature: a neural operator whose error is flat in basis size while the POD floor it is built on falls 28.7x.

The practical consequence: the project's strongest asset is the DIAGNOSIS (basis error vs coefficient-map error, decomposed and measured), and its strongest venue liabilities are, in order, (a) placeholder material parameters, (b) the Damkoehler regime, (c) absence of experiment, (d) the warp not yet beating the fixed frame by more than 0.0002. (a) and (b) are cheaper to fix than (c) and matter more for the domain venues.
implications: RANK 1 - npj Computational Materials (IF ~11.9; third-party medians ~146 days submission-to-acceptance). REACHABLE WITHOUT EXPERIMENT - proven by IsothermODE. Required framing: NOT a falsification ladder, NOT an architecture comparison. Frame as: 'Static adsorption ML is solved; column dynamics is not, and here is the measured reason.' Lead with the Type V two-wave breakthrough as a materials-physics finding, the 40x separation range, and the novel-material transfer failure (0.0485 nRMSE = 0.42 h error in t_50). Put the coefficient-map bottleneck in as the mechanism. The ladder becomes a methods appendix. Release the 988-run dataset. BLOCKER: the MOF-303 placeholder problem is fatal here - this audience will ask which materials, and 'a synthetic 60-material parametric family' is a weak answer without at least a handful of parameter sets refitted to published water isotherms.

RANK 2 - Communications Engineering (Nature portfolio; NOT on the project's candidate list). REACHABLE WITHOUT EXPERIMENT - proven by Rabeh et al. 2025, an all-negative SciML benchmark. This is the best fit for the paper AS IT ACTUALLY IS: an engineering-relevant, multi-architecture, honestly-negative benchmark with a measured mechanism. It carries Nature branding, does not require a new material, and does not require the warp to win. The framing that works: 'Benchmarking surrogate models for adsorption column dynamics: eight interventions, one binding constraint.' I consider this the single most under-considered option in the candidate set.

RANK 3 - TMLR. HIGHEST PROBABILITY OF ACCEPTANCE OF ANY VENUE, and reachable exactly as-is. Its written criteria explicitly disclaim novelty, significance and SOTA, and explicitly welcome robustness/generalisability studies with actionable lessons. The pre-registered protocol, calibrated alpha=0.005, 3-seed paired CIs, matched training budgets and the 17+23 retraction ledger are not liabilities there - they are the acceptance criteria. Costs: not an IF-ranked journal, and a materials/ChemE readership will not find it. Best used as either (a) the guaranteed home for the full ladder if a domain venue rejects, or (b) the methods paper in a two-paper split.

RANK 4 - CMAME or Journal of Computational Physics. REACHABLE WITHOUT EXPERIMENT, and the correct technical home for the n-width measurement, the basis/coefficient decomposition, and the two-wave warp. BUT: these venues want a method that WORKS. Predicted-warp 0.0508 vs fixed-frame 0.0510 is not a result; it is a tie. Oracle 0.0233 is headroom, not a contribution. Do not submit here until the predicted warp beats the fixed frame by a margin that survives a paired CI. Also mandatory: cite Acta Numerica 35 (2026), Taddei 2020 and Gowrachari 2025, and position the two-wave warp as a problem-specific registration whose novelty is the two-parameter necessity argument (40x separation), not the warp itself.

RANK 5 - Machine Learning: Science and Technology (IOP, IF 4.2, open access). REACHABLE. Explicitly bridges ML applications across physical sciences with methods insight. Will take the whole ladder with minimal reframing and is friendly to negative results in a scientific setting. Modest prestige is the only real cost. This is the low-risk 'publish the whole thing intact' option if TMLR's non-journal status is a concern.

RANK 6 - Digital Discovery (RSC, IF 7.1, 40-46 day first decision, GBP 2200 APC). REACHABLE. Data-first/reproducibility ethos, explicitly welcomes advanced data workflows and databases, and has itself published on the underreporting of negative results in ML-for-chemistry. Excellent home for a paper whose distinguishing feature is process integrity: pre-registration, gates, a public retraction ledger, and an open 988- (or 4080-) run dataset. Out-of-scope list is about low-throughput non-ML work, which does not touch us.

RANK 7 - Computers & Chemical Engineering, then AIChE Journal. Both accept simulation-only work (AIChE J published an ML-on-simulation zeolite sorption paper in 2026). Both are safe, unexciting, and will demand a process-level payoff (optimisation, control, screening throughput) that the ladder does not currently deliver. Also both will immediately notice Da ~ 626 and ask why the kinetic regime was not sampled. Fix Damkoehler before going near either.

NOT REACHABLE WITHOUT EXPERIMENTAL DATA: Nature Communications (its MOF-AWH corpus is device/materials experiment - hydrogel-MOF membranes, fluorophenyl-oligomer MOFs, adaptive harvesting devices - a simulation-only surrogate study has no path), Nature Computational Science (its own April 2026 editorial names experimental validation and SOTA-breadth benchmarking as the top reviewer demands; we fail both), Nature Machine Intelligence (would require a method that wins, not a diagnosis), Nature Chemical Engineering (IF ~29.7, scale-up/process-realisation focus), Advanced Materials and JACS (materials-synthesis venues; a surrogate-modelling paper is out of scope regardless of experiment).

NOT RECOMMENDED AS PRIMARY: Chemical Engineering Journal and Separation and Purification Technology. Their recent adsorption-ML output is dominated by experimentally validated models (e.g. hybrid neural networks validated against measured CO2/N2 breakthrough). More importantly, these audiences will not read eight negative results as a contribution - they will read them as a project that did not work. JMLR is also a poor fit (methodology/theory-oriented); TMLR is its correct sibling for this work.

STRATEGIC RECOMMENDATION - SPLIT INTO TWO PAPERS. Paper A (domain): the dataset, the two-wave physics, the novel-material transfer benchmark, the measured bottleneck -> npj Computational Materials or Communications Engineering. Paper B (methods): the n-width measurement, the basis-vs-coefficient decomposition, single-front refutation, and the two-wave warp -> CMAME/JCP once the warp wins, or TMLR if it does not. One paper carrying all eight rungs plus the warp plus the dataset will be too long for any of these venues and will dilute the one genuinely novel measurement. Additionally consider a NeurIPS Datasets & Benchmarks submission for the 240-material scale-up dataset plus the pre-registered ladder as a benchmark suite - I could not verify the 2026 call before exhausting the search budget, so confirm the track exists and its deadline before planning around it.

TITLE/SCOPE HYGIENE: the title currently claims a COF case that does not exist. Every venue above will catch that. Either add a COF parameter set (cheap - it is the same 1-D solver with different isotherm/kinetic parameters, and COF water isotherms are published) or remove COF from the title and abstract. Leaving it is a correctness problem, not a marketing one.
risks_to_our_claims: NOVELTY OF THE WARP. Taddei (SISC 2020) established parameter-dependent registration for exactly the slow-n-width problem, and Gowrachari et al. (2025) automate the shift discovery on 1-D travelling waves. A CMAME/JCP referee will say the two-wave warp is a low-dimensional registration map and ask why cross-correlation registration was not simply run as a baseline. Mitigation: run it, and make the contribution the NECESSITY argument (two waves, 40x separation range, single-front provably worse: n-width 31 -> 102 modes, 0.0534 vs 0.0510 even with the exact front given free).

L5 REDUCED TO SPECTRAL BIAS. Khodakarami et al. (arXiv:2602.19265, Feb 2026) analyse spectral bias in operator learning and give mitigation guidelines. A referee can claim our flagship result - coefficient-map R^2 collapsing beyond mode ~5 - is textbook spectral bias with a known fix, which would demote the strongest result in the project to a rediscovery. Mitigation: apply their mitigations and show the ~4-mode effective rank does not move. Until that experiment exists this is the largest single risk in the paper.

L6 CONTRADICTED IN PRINT. Santana et al. (arXiv:2303.13555) recover sorption kinetics from synthetic fixed-bed breakthrough curves; we report k_LDF unrecoverable at R^2 = -0.61. A ChemE referee will read this as our identification pipeline being broken rather than the regime being degenerate. Mitigation: the low-Damkoehler re-test is now mandatory, not optional. Reporting identifiability as a function of Da, with their success and our failure both located on that axis, converts the contradiction into the paper's cleanest result.

L7 UNDER-BASELINED. Westermann et al. (arXiv:2604.00689) show polynomial/sparse-grid/tensor-train surrogates beat neural operators on data efficiency for smooth inputs. Our L7 compared learning only against closed-form adsorption solutions (Klinkenberg, constant-pattern, equilibrium-shock). 'Learning wins 3.2x over closed forms' is not the same claim as 'learning is needed', and a referee at a numerics venue will say so. Mitigation: add a polynomial/sparse-grid and a Gaussian-process surrogate to the L7 comparison.

'ALREADY DONE' ON NEGATIVE RESULTS. Rabeh et al. (Commun Eng 2025, 11 models) and Shikhman (arXiv:2601.11428, 750 models) both published broad negative operator-learning studies. Our scale is smaller and our domain narrower. Mitigation: do not compete on breadth. Compete on the mechanism neither of them has - a measured lower bound (the POD floor) that the model provably fails to track, and an error decomposition that localises the failure to the parameter->coefficient map rather than to the basis.

MATERIAL PROVENANCE. Retraction A4 means no result can currently be called MOF-303 and every parameter is an uncited literature-range placeholder. At npj Comput Mater, CEJ, Sep&Pur or AIChE J this is a desk-level problem: the referee's first question is which materials these 60 are. Note this is a SHARPER constraint than the missing experiment, because it is cheap to fix and impossible to argue around.

DAMKOEHLER REGIME. Sampling Da 155-3885 (median 626) is near local equilibrium. Any adsorption specialist will observe that the LDF kinetics are barely active across the entire dataset, and will then question whether L1-L5 conclusions about 'surrogates for adsorption dynamics' generalise at all, since the dataset under-samples the regime where kinetics matter. This threatens the whole ladder's external validity, not just L6.

SPEED CLAIM. The 4.2 s/condition at N_z=2000 reference is our own solver, not COMSOL. The retracted 'orders of magnitude over FEM' claim in 01_INTRODUCTION.md must not resurface. Any ChemE referee will ask for the baseline solver's identity and settings; framing as amortised screening throughput is the only defensible version.

STALE DUPLICATE CODE. kaggle_run/ carries every original defect. Every venue in the recommended set expects a code release (npj Comput Mater's own adsorption precedent ships a GitHub repo). Publishing a repository that contains a superseded, defective copy of the pipeline alongside the corrected one is a reproducibility failure waiting to be found by a referee or a reader.

concrete_actions.action: Replace the placeholder material parameters: refit the Type V Do-Do isotherm to at least 5-6 PUBLISHED water isotherms (MOF-303, MOF-801, Co2Cl2BTDD, CAU-10-H, aluminium fumarate, and one COF), cite each source, and re-anchor the 60-material parametric family so it spans a cited region rather than an invented one. Re-run affected figures.
concrete_actions.rationale: This is the cheapest action that changes the venue tier. It closes retraction A4, lets results be named, kills the 'which materials?' referee question at npj Comput Mater / AIChE J / Digital Discovery, and simultaneously supplies the missing COF case the title already claims. Nothing else on this list is both this cheap and this decisive.

concrete_actions.action: Regenerate a dataset arm with k_LDF extended down so that Damkoehler spans ~1-50 alongside the existing 155-3885, and re-run L6 (and ideally L1/L5 spot checks) on it. Report identifiability of k_LDF as a function of Da.
concrete_actions.rationale: Fixes the single biggest external-validity hole and converts the apparent contradiction with Santana et al. (2303.13555) into a result. It is also the project's own pre-declared re-test of H1: if the separate-vs-joint gap is still absent at low Da, H1 is wrong rather than untested, and either outcome is publishable. Every chemical-engineering referee will find Da=626 unaided.

concrete_actions.action: Run the spectral-bias mitigations from Khodakarami et al. (arXiv:2602.19265) - mode-reweighted loss, output/feature rescaling - against the L5 coefficient map, and report whether the ~4-mode effective rank moves.
concrete_actions.rationale: Pre-empts the most dangerous single objection to the project's strongest result. If the ceiling holds under their mitigations, L5 is a genuinely new obstruction rather than spectral bias with a known fix, and that sentence becomes the paper's central claim. If it moves, we need to know before a referee tells us.

concrete_actions.action: Digitise 1-2 published experimental water/CO2 breakthrough curves for a column whose operating conditions the solver can reproduce, and report a solver-vs-experiment error bar separately from the surrogate-vs-solver error.
concrete_actions.rationale: The project's own handoff says one digitised published breakthrough curve would change the venue tier, and it is right. It does not require a laboratory, it converts 'no experimental validation' into 'validated against published data', and it is the difference between npj Comput Mater being a stretch and being a reasonable target. It does not, on its own, unlock Nature Communications or Nature Computational Science.

concrete_actions.action: Add two missing baseline families: (a) automatic cross-correlation snapshot registration (Gowrachari/Stabile/Rozza, arXiv:2501.01299) applied to our snapshots, and (b) a polynomial/sparse-grid or tensor-train surrogate plus a Gaussian process, added to the L7 comparison per Westermann et al. (arXiv:2604.00689).
concrete_actions.rationale: (a) is the strongest-competitor test for the two-wave warp and, if automatic registration fails on two-wave data, that failure is itself a publishable ROM result. (b) closes the gap between 'learning beats closed forms' and 'learning is needed', which is the claim L7 is currently written as. Both are direct applications of the project's own trap #3 (compare against the strongest competitor).

concrete_actions.action: Push the predicted two-wave warp decisively past the fixed frame. Current 0.0508 vs 0.0510 is a tie; oracle is 0.0233. Improve the warp predictor (more training materials from the scale-up set, better start_logspan features, direct supervision on t_lo/t_hi) until the margin survives a paired CI at alpha=0.005.
concrete_actions.rationale: This is the gate on whether CMAME/JCP are reachable at all. Those venues publish methods that work; a 0.0002 improvement is not a method. It is also the only route to a positive headline that the six negatives would motivate, which every venue except TMLR effectively requires.

concrete_actions.action: Commit to the two-paper split and write two different abstracts now, before drafting: Paper A (domain: dataset + two-wave physics + novel-material benchmark + measured bottleneck) targeting npj Computational Materials with Communications Engineering as the co-primary; Paper B (methods: n-width, basis-vs-coefficient decomposition, single-front refutation, two-wave warp) targeting CMAME/JCP if the warp wins and TMLR if it does not.
concrete_actions.rationale: The single-paper version is too long for every recommended venue and dilutes the one measurement nobody else has. Writing both abstracts first is the cheapest way to discover which results are load-bearing for which audience, and it forces an early decision on whether the warp is ready.

concrete_actions.action: Rewrite the related-work section around the six references a referee will hold us to: Hesthaven/Peherstorfer/Unger (Acta Numerica 35, 2026), Taddei (SISC 42:A997, 2020), Shikhman (arXiv:2601.11428), Rabeh et al. (Commun Eng 4:182, 2025), Krishnapriyan et al. (NeurIPS 2021), Santana et al. (arXiv:2303.13555). For each, state in one sentence what is ours and what is theirs.
concrete_actions.rationale: Every one of these is a live 'this was already done' attack, and four of them are from 2025-2026. A 2026 Acta Numerica survey on precisely our problem class going uncited is a fast rejection at any numerical-analysis venue. The delta sentences are also the paper's novelty argument, so this is drafting, not bookkeeping.

concrete_actions.action: Finish the 240-material scale-up dataset (currently ~1457 of 4080 files, no manifest, generation died), regenerate the manifest, and prepare a versioned public release of it together with the 988-run set, the frozen protocol, the 22 validate.py gates, and the retraction ledger.
concrete_actions.rationale: The learning-curve result (1.82x improvement from 12 -> 48 training materials, not saturated) partially cuts against L1's verdict on the material axis, and that caveat must be resolved before L1 is published as 'eliminated'. The release also meets the open-data bar that the npj Comput Mater adsorption precedent sets, and it is the substrate for a possible Datasets & Benchmarks submission.

concrete_actions.action: Update RESULTS.md with the three findings currently only in logs (warp_predict R^2 +0.895/+0.919 and 0.0508; learning_curve 0.0929 -> 0.0509 over 12->48 materials; l5_fill2 DeepONet ~0.0275 at lr=3e-3, above the previous grid top), and revise the L1 and L5 verdict wording accordingly.
concrete_actions.rationale: The l5_fill2 result means the recorded lr grid did not bracket DeepONet's optimum either - the same defect (B22/trap #3) the project already caught for DeepOKAN. Publishing 0.0296 as DeepONet's best when 0.0275 is on disk is exactly the failure mode the retraction ledger exists to prevent, and a referee who reruns the code will find it.

concrete_actions.action: Resolve the COF claim and the speed claim in the title/abstract: either add the COF parameter set (from the refit in action 1) or remove COF from the title, and reframe the speed claim as amortised screening throughput against the project's own 4.2 s/condition solver rather than against FEM.
concrete_actions.rationale: Both are correctness issues carried over from the superseded framing in 01_INTRODUCTION.md, both are already logged as retractions (A6), and both are the kind of thing a referee finds in the first five minutes. Fixing them costs nothing and removes two easy grounds for rejection.

concrete_actions.action: Remove or clearly quarantine kaggle_run/ before any code release, and add a top-level README stating which directory is authoritative.
concrete_actions.rationale: Every recommended venue expects a code release. Shipping a stale duplicate that carries every original defect alongside the corrected pipeline undermines the reproducibility record that is the project's main credibility asset. The user should make the deletion decision, but it must be made before submission.

lens: How to publish a rigorous negative / falsification result in ML-for-science: precedent papers, venue options, reporting standards, how to present a corrections ledger, and title/abstract framing patterns from real accepted papers.

papers.citation: Nick McGreivy, Ammar Hakim. "Weak baselines and reporting biases lead to overoptimism in machine learning for fluid-related partial differential equations." Nature Machine Intelligence 6(10):1256-1269, 2024. Preprint arXiv:2407.07218.
papers.what_it_shows: Systematic review of 76 ML-for-PDE papers claiming to beat standard numerical methods: 79% (60/76) compare against a weak baseline. Documents outcome-reporting bias and publication bias, i.e. systematic under-reporting of negative results, and attributes it to researcher degrees of freedom plus a positive-results bias. Calls for bottom-up cultural and top-down structural reform.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the single most important citation for the paper. It is the field's own statement, in a Nature-family journal, that negative results in exactly our subfield are under-supplied and valuable. It converts our contribution from 'a project that failed' into 'the missing evidence class the field has been asking for'. It also disciplines us: the mirror-image error is a WEAK TREATMENT (under-tuned ML arm), and our own l5_fill2.log shows the DeepONet learning-rate grid did not bracket the optimum. Fix that before submission or a referee will use this exact paper against us.

papers.citation: Sayash Kapoor, Arvind Narayanan. "Leakage and the reproducibility crisis in machine-learning-based science." Patterns 4(9), 2023. Preprint arXiv:2207.07048.
papers.what_it_shows: Taxonomy of eight kinds of leakage; survey finds leakage in 17 fields affecting 294 papers in the published version (the 2022 preprint states 329 papers / 17 fields — cite the published figure). Case study: civil-war prediction papers claiming complex ML beats logistic regression all fail once leakage is corrected. Proposes 'model info sheets' as a per-claim reporting artefact.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Two uses. (1) It legitimises the whole genre of 'we checked and the claimed gain is not there'. (2) The model info sheet is a concrete precedent for shipping a per-claim provenance artefact — which is essentially what validate.py's 22 gates plus RETRACTIONS.md already are. Frame our infrastructure in their vocabulary and it reads as compliance with an emerging standard rather than as an unusual confession.

papers.citation: Sayash Kapoor, Emily Cantrell, Kenny Peng, ... Arvind Narayanan (19 authors). "REFORMS: Consensus-based Recommendations for Machine-learning-based Science." Science Advances, 2024. Preprint arXiv:2308.07832.
papers.what_it_shows: A 32-question checklist plus paired guidelines for conducting and reporting ML-based science, built by consensus across CS, data science, maths, social science and biomedicine. Explicitly designed to be used by authors, referees AND journals.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the reporting standard we will be held to, and the cheapest large credibility win available: fill in the REFORMS checklist and ship it as Supplementary Item 1. For a paper whose entire claim is 'these interventions do not work', the referee's first instinct is 'you did it wrong'. A completed consensus checklist pre-empts that at essentially zero cost.

papers.citation: Maurizio Ferrari Dacrema, Paolo Cremonesi, Dietmar Jannach. "Are We Really Making Much Progress? A Worrying Analysis of Recent Neural Recommendation Approaches." RecSys 2019 (Best Full Paper). arXiv:1907.06902.
papers.what_it_shows: Of 18 neural recommenders from top venues, only 7 were reproducible with reasonable effort; 6 of those 7 were beaten by simple nearest-neighbour or graph heuristics, and the last did not consistently beat a well-tuned non-neural linear ranker. Won the conference's best-paper award.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The canonical proof that a purely negative benchmark paper can win the top award at a major venue. It is also the template for tone: worried, systematic, exhaustively reproducible, with all code released. Our L3 (MLP beats both KAN families at matched parameters, 8/9 significant) and L7 (learning beats closed forms 3.2x) are structurally identical claims — a refutation and a fair-comparison verdict in the same paper.

papers.citation: Michael Roberts, Derek Driggs, ... Carola-Bibiane Schönlieb (AIX-COVNET). "Common pitfalls and recommendations for using machine learning to detect and prognosticate for COVID-19 using chest radiographs and CT scans." Nature Machine Intelligence 3:199-217, 2021. arXiv:2008.06388.
papers.what_it_shows: From 2212 studies screened, 61 reviewed: NONE of the 61 models is of potential clinical use, due to methodological flaws and/or bias. Delivers recommendations in five areas: data, evaluation, reproducibility, manuscript documentation, and the peer-review process.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Proof that a categorical zero-positive result publishes in a Nature-family ML journal — provided it is paired with prescriptive recommendations. This is the structural lesson for us: a negative result lands at a higher venue when it ships a method others can adopt. Our falsification-ladder protocol plus the calibrated-alpha cluster bootstrap plus the retraction ledger IS that transferable method. Sell the methodology as a co-equal contribution, not as housekeeping.

papers.citation: Kevin Musgrave, Serge Belongie, Ser-Nam Lim. "A Metric Learning Reality Check." ECCV 2020. arXiv:2003.08505.
papers.what_it_shows: Four years of claimed deep-metric-learning gains — often 'more than doubling' decade-old baselines — evaporate under a corrected experimental protocol; real improvement is 'marginal at best'. The paper's positive deliverable is a new evaluation protocol and an open benchmarking library.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The 'reality check' title/abstract pattern, and the strongest precedent for the structure we should use: debunk + supply the corrected protocol + release the harness. Their positive deliverable was a benchmarking library; ours is the verified solver, the frozen protocol and the 988-run dataset.

papers.citation: Léo Grinsztajn, Edouard Oyallon, Gaël Varoquaux. "Why do tree-based models still outperform deep learning on typical tabular data?" NeurIPS 2022 Datasets & Benchmarks track. arXiv:2207.08815.
papers.what_it_shows: A 45-dataset benchmark with matched hyperparameter search shows tree ensembles remain state of the art on medium-sized tabular data, then identifies three concrete inductive-bias mechanisms (uninformative features, rotation non-invariance, irregular target functions) that explain why.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The best available model for our paper's shape: a negative headline whose value comes from a MEASURED MECHANISM, not from the negative alone. Our L5 bottleneck decomposition (basis error falls 28.7x while coefficient-map error is flat at 0.051; median R^2 = -0.014 beyond mode 24) is the direct analogue. Frame the mechanism as the contribution and the six eliminations as the evidence that it is the binding one.

papers.citation: Aditi S. Krishnapriyan, Amir Gholami, Shandian Zhe, Robert M. Kirby, Michael W. Mahoney. "Characterizing possible failure modes in physics-informed neural networks." NeurIPS 2021. arXiv:2109.01050.
papers.what_it_shows: PINNs fail on convection/reaction/diffusion problems that are only slightly beyond trivial. The cause is measured, not asserted: the soft PDE regularisation makes the optimisation problem ill-conditioned, and the failure is in the loss landscape, not the architecture. Two remedies (curriculum regularisation, seq2seq) recover 1-2 orders of magnitude.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The exact precedent for our L4/L4b result: physics as a soft penalty helps on one axis (0.1425 -> 0.0639) and HURTS once hard bounds exist (0.0124 -> 0.0194). Cite this to establish that 'soft physics penalties are regime-dependent and can be actively harmful' is an accepted, mechanism-backed finding, not our idiosyncratic failure. It also legitimises our 'hard constraints beat soft penalties' framing (hard bounds = best single intervention, 11.5x on time).

papers.citation: Patrick Chatain, Michael Rizvi-Martel, Guillaume Rabusseau, Adam Oberman. "Numerical PDE solvers outperform neural PDE solvers." arXiv:2507.21269, 2025.
papers.what_it_shows: A differentiable finite-difference model (DeepFDM) with embedded forward-Euler discretisation and stability constraints beats FNO, U-Net and ResNet baselines by one to two orders of magnitude in error, with far fewer parameters and epochs, on parametric PDEs with spatially varying coefficients.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: A 2025 title that is a flat declarative reversal — the most aggressive framing pattern currently in circulation in our subfield, and evidence that it is now publishable. Also directly relevant to L7: it is the strongest current statement that structure-embedding beats generic operator learning, which is precisely our 'hard structure pays, soft penalties do not' thesis. Cite it as concurrent independent support, and note it is a preprint (check for a journal version before submission).

papers.citation: Florian Karl, Lukas Malte Kemeter, Gabriel Dax, Paulina Sierak. "Position: Embracing Negative Results in Machine Learning." arXiv:2406.03980, 2024. (OpenReview id 3RXAiU7sss suggests the ICML 2024 Position Paper track; I could not load OpenReview to confirm the venue.)
papers.what_it_shows: Argues that predictive performance alone is a poor indicator of a publication's worth, that the current incentive system creates inefficiency and misaligned incentives, and proposes concrete measures to normalise publishing negative results.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: A short, citable position statement to put in our first paragraph justifying the paper's existence. Useful rhetorical cover, low scientific weight. VENUE CLAIM UNCONFIRMED — verify whether this is ICML 2024 Position track before citing it as a peer-reviewed venue; cite as arXiv otherwise.

papers.citation: Julia M. Rohrer, Warren Tierney, Eric L. Uhlmann, ... Tal Yarkoni. "Putting the Self in Self-Correction: Findings From the Loss-of-Confidence Project." Perspectives on Psychological Science, 2021. DOI 10.1177/1745691620964106.
papers.what_it_shows: 13 researchers publicly stated they no longer believe one of their own published findings (5 methodological errors, 4 invalid inference, 7 p-hacking). A survey of 316 researchers found 44% had lost confidence in at least one of their own findings but only 17% made it public; the top barriers were insufficient certainty (68%), belief the finding was unnoticed (46%), coauthors' feelings (33%), and — critically — NO APPROPRIATE VENUE (25%).
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the precedent that answers 'is a public corrections ledger a strength or a liability?'. The published, peer-reviewed answer is that self-correction is rare because there is no venue, not because it is discreditable, and that the community response to high-profile self-corrections (Carney) was predominantly POSITIVE. Cite this in the Methods paragraph that introduces RETRACTIONS.md. It reframes 17 withdrawn claims from 'this pipeline is unreliable' to 'this is the disclosure norm the field says it wants and almost never gets'.

papers.citation: TMLR (Transactions on Machine Learning Research) — official Acceptance Criteria page, JMLR.
papers.what_it_shows: Two criteria only: (1) are the claims supported by accurate and convincing evidence, (2) would some of TMLR's audience be interested. Explicitly states a paper must not be rejected for not achieving state of the art on a benchmark, and that 'novelty of the studied method is not a necessary criterion for acceptance'.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The one venue whose WRITTEN criteria are a perfect fit for this manuscript: our claims are unusually well evidenced and our headline is explicitly not a state-of-the-art number. TMLR is the correct safety net and, given a fast turnaround and a Featured Certification, a respectable primary target for the methods framing. It is also the venue where the retraction ledger is an asset rather than a risk.

papers.citation: Machine Learning: Science and Technology (IOP) — About / scope and article types.
papers.what_it_shows: Scope covers both ML-driven applications in the sciences and methodological advances motivated by scientific problems. Accepted article types explicitly include BENCHMARKS, CHALLENGES, dataset articles, perspectives, technical notes, and comments/replies. Authors are required to provide all technical details ensuring reproducibility (code, workflows, datasets). No explicit negative-results article type.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: MLST's 'Benchmark' article type is the closest formal container for a falsification ladder: it lets us submit the ladder AS a benchmark of interventions rather than as a failed method paper, and its mandatory-reproducibility policy rewards the validate.py harness. Strong realistic target alongside TMLR. Note there is no negative-results article type, so the framing burden stays on us.

papers.citation: NeurIPS Paper Checklist (official guide), NeurIPS.
papers.what_it_shows: 16 mandatory items. Item 2 requires a separate Limitations section and warns explicitly that 'a worse outcome might be if reviewers discover limitations that aren't acknowledged in the paper'. Item 7 requires error bars or significance information with the factors of variability and the calculation method stated, and warns against intervals that extend outside the achievable range. Items 4/5/8 cover reproducibility, code/data, and compute.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Item 7's 'do not report intervals outside the achievable range' is literally our retraction A15 (nRMSE 26,000 for a bounded model). Item 2's warning is the argument for the corrections ledger in one sentence. Adopt the checklist verbatim even for a journal submission: it gives us a neutral, external authority for every disclosure choice we make, so the ledger reads as compliance rather than confession.

papers.citation: I Can't Believe It's Not Better (ICBINB) workshop series, NeurIPS 2020-2023 / ICLR 2025 — Call for Papers and review criteria.
papers.url_or_id: https://i-cant-believe-its-not-better.github.io/neurips2020/cfp/ ; neurips.cc/virtual/2022/workshop/49960 (2022 edition: 'Understanding Deep Learning Through Empirical Falsification')
papers.what_it_shows: Two tracks: (1) unexpected failures of new methods with rigorous ablation showing WHY the approach performs poorly; (2) undesired effects in widespread taken-for-granted practice — flawed metrics, outdated baselines, unsuitable datasets. Reviewed on clarity, rigour and transparency, 'vulnerability and honesty in discussion', quality of limitations discussion, and significance of new insight — explicitly prioritising understanding over performance. The 2022 edition's subtitle is 'Understanding Deep Learning Through Empirical Falsification'.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the only venue whose stated review rubric rewards exactly what we have, including the ledger ('vulnerability and honesty'). Its 2022 subtitle is almost our paper's subtitle. Two concrete uses: (a) submit a 4-page version to the current edition for early referee signal at near-zero cost, and (b) borrow its two-track framing — our L1/L2/L3/L5 are Track 1 (methods fail, mechanism measured), our L7 and the weak-baseline audit are Track 2 (practice critique).

papers.citation: Andreas Bender, Nadine Schneider, Marwin H. S. Segler, W. Patrick Walters, Ola Engkvist, Tiago Rodrigues. "Evaluation guidelines for machine learning tools in the chemical sciences." Nature Reviews Chemistry 6:428-442, 2022. DOI 10.1038/s41570-022-00391-9.
papers.what_it_shows: Perspective arguing that heterogeneity in evaluation design and metrics across chemistry ML makes new algorithms impossible to compare, and laying out method-development and evaluation guidelines by publication type, with worked examples.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The chemistry-side counterpart to REFORMS. If we target a chemistry or materials venue (Digital Discovery, npj Comput. Mater., MLST), this is the evaluation standard a domain referee will invoke. Our novel-material split, calibrated alpha and matched-parameter comparisons are already above this bar — say so explicitly in Methods rather than leaving the referee to notice.

papers.citation: Nongnuch Artrith, Keith T. Butler, François-Xavier Coudert, Seungwu Han, Olexandr Isayev, Anubhav Jain, Aron Walsh. "Best practices in machine learning for chemistry." Nature Chemistry 13(6):505-508, 2021. DOI 10.1038/s41557-021-00716-z.
papers.what_it_shows: A short comment with an explicit 'Checklist for reporting and evaluating machine learning models', covering data provenance and multi-source combination, feature/descriptor definition with comparison against standard feature sets, and release of a trainable software implementation.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The item 'comparisons against standard feature sets are provided' is directly relevant to our L6 observable-descriptor redesign (54 features, 12 RH x 3 T isotherm fingerprint). Cite it as the standard we followed when justifying descriptor choice, which is otherwise the softest point in L6.

papers.citation: Jan S. Hesthaven, Benjamin Peherstorfer, Benjamin Unger. "Nonlinear model reduction for transport-dominated problems." arXiv:2602.01397, 2026 (survey).
papers.what_it_shows: A 2026 survey of nonlinear model reduction for regimes where linear reduced spaces are intrinsically inefficient — transport-dominated problems with wave-like phenomena and moving coherent structures. Organised around nonlinear parametrisations, reduced dynamics and online solvers; categorises transformation-based methods, online adaptive techniques, and residual-minimisation formulations. Explicitly framed around the Kolmogorov barrier.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: THIS IS OUR BIGGEST NOVELTY RISK AND ALSO OUR BEST POSITIONING TOOL. A referee will ask why our two-wave warp is not just a transformation-based nonlinear model reduction method that this literature already contains. Read this survey and position the two-wave warp inside its taxonomy explicitly. Our genuinely new claims are then narrow and defensible: (a) the warp is driven by a MEASURED two-wave structure from a Type V isotherm with a 40x separation range, (b) single-front alignment is measurably WORSE (31 -> 102 modes), and (c) the residual obstruction is front LOCATION, not the frame — none of which the survey supplies for adsorption.

papers.citation: Philipp Krah, Arthur Marmin, Beata Zorawski, Julius Reiss, Kai Schneider. "A robust shifted proper orthogonal decomposition: Proximal methods for decomposing flows with multiple transports." arXiv:2403.04313, 2024 (rev. 2025).
papers.what_it_shows: Extends shifted POD to flows with MULTIPLE simultaneous transports by writing the field as a sum of co-moving data fields, optimising the co-moving fields directly and penalising their nuclear norm to promote low rank, with a robustness term for interpolation error and noise.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The direct prior-art threat to the two-wave warp: 'multiple transports, one frame each' already exists and is state of the art. Our construction differs (we normalise the interval between two fronts, sigma = (t - t_lo)/(t_hi - t_lo), rather than summing co-moving fields), and our binding constraint is front prediction rather than decomposition. But we MUST cite it, state the difference precisely, and ideally run sPOD as a baseline on our data. If we do not, a reviewer from the model-reduction community will.

papers.citation: Ravid Shwartz-Ziv, Amitai Armon. "Tabular data: Deep learning is not all you need." Information Fusion 81:84-90, 2022. DOI 10.1016/j.inffus.2021.11.011.
papers.what_it_shows: Deep tabular models proposed at top venues do not generalise to datasets other than those used in their own papers; XGBoost outperforms them, and deep models are harder to optimise.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Mainly a TITLE PATTERN ('X is not all you need') and a citation for why our XGBoost/RF arms beating MLPs in L1 is an expected, publishable finding rather than an implementation failure. Verified through search metadata and the ScienceDirect/ACM listings, not by reading the full text.

papers.citation: Zachary C. Lipton, Jacob Steinhardt. "Troubling Trends in Machine Learning Scholarship." arXiv:1807.03341, 2018; ICML 2018 Debates workshop; reprinted in ACM Queue 17(1), 2019.
papers.what_it_shows: Four failure patterns in ML writing: failure to distinguish explanation from speculation; failure to identify the true source of empirical gains (e.g. crediting architecture when the gain came from hyperparameter tuning); mathiness; and misuse of language. Root cause diagnosed as 'complacency in the face of progress'.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The 'identify the source of the gain' trend is our paper's spine: L2 (capacity), L3 (edge basis), L5 (basis size) are all attributions of a non-gain to its true cause. Quote this standard in the introduction to explain WHY a ladder is the right instrument. Verified through search metadata only; I did not fetch the full text.

papers.citation: D. Sculley, Jasper Snoek, Alexander B. Wiltschko, Ali Rahimi. "Winner's Curse? On Pace, Progress, and Empirical Rigor." ICLR 2018 Workshop track.
papers.what_it_shows: Argues the rate of empirical advance in ML has outpaced the growth of empirical rigour, gives examples where progress was slowed as a result, and proposes incentive-structure changes.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Short, highly citable framing for why matched-budget, multi-seed, calibrated-alpha comparisons (our working agreement) are the actual contribution. Verified through search metadata and dblp only; I did not fetch the paper.

papers.citation: John R. Platt. "Strong Inference: Certain systematic methods of scientific thinking may produce much more rapid progress than others." Science 146(3642):347-353, 1964.
papers.what_it_shows: Prescribes an explicit four-step loop applied to every problem: devise alternative hypotheses; devise a crucial experiment that will exclude one or more; carry it out cleanly; recycle. Describes the result as a 'conditional inductive tree' or logical tree, and argues fields that do this systematically advance much faster.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The intellectual charter for the eight-rung ladder, and a genuinely useful framing device: our L0-L7 IS Platt's conditional inductive tree, pre-registered. Opening the paper by naming the method 'strong inference' — with the 1964 citation — instantly reclassifies eight negative rungs from 'a sequence of failures' to 'a designed exclusion procedure'. Cheapest single framing improvement available. Verified through search metadata (PubMed record and multiple secondary sources); I did not fetch the original PDF.

papers.citation: Julius Adebayo, Justin Gilmer, Michael Muelly, Ian Goodfellow, Moritz Hardt, Been Kim. "Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps." NeurIPS 2018. arXiv:1810.03292.
papers.what_it_shows: Introduces model-parameter-randomisation and data-randomisation tests; several popular saliency methods are insensitive to the model they claim to explain, and so should not be used for explanation. A later 2021 paper ('Revisiting Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps', arXiv:2110.14297) argues some conclusions are artefacts of the tasks used.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The best precedent for 'a cheap invariance test that a whole method family fails' becoming a highly cited contribution. Our direct analogue already exists and is under-sold: the DeepOKAN SEED-INVARIANCE detector that caught 10/45 collapsed runs agreeing to 2.7e-7 across different p, learning rates AND seeds. Promote that from an anecdote to a named, reusable diagnostic with its own subsection. The 2021 rebuttal is also a useful caution: state the scope of our invariance test precisely. Verified through search metadata; arXiv id 1810.03292 is from memory and should be double-checked before citing.

papers.citation: Shereen Elsayed, Daniela Thyssens, Ahmed Rashed, Hadi Samer Jomaa, Lars Schmidt-Thieme. "Do We Really Need Deep Learning Models for Time Series Forecasting?" arXiv:2101.02118, 2021.
papers.what_it_shows: A windowed multi-output gradient-boosted regression tree outperforms eight state-of-the-art deep forecasting models from top conferences across nine datasets.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The interrogative 'Do we really need X?' title pattern, plus support for our L7 framing question ('is learning needed at all'). Note our L7 answered YES (learning wins 3.2x over the best closed form) — this citation lets us present that as a non-obvious, non-foregone outcome, which is exactly what makes L7 credible rather than self-serving. Verified through search metadata only.

papers.citation: Weiheng Zhong, Qibang Liu, Diab Abueidda, Seid Koric, Hadi Meidani. "A comprehensive comparison of neural operators for 3D industry-scale engineering designs." arXiv:2510.05995, 2025.
papers.what_it_shows: Standardised benchmark of four neural-operator families (branch-trunk/DeepONet, graph, grid/FNO, point-based) across six datasets and multiple physics, scored on accuracy, compute, memory and deployment complexity. Reports trade-offs rather than a winner.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Establishes the 2025 norm that neural-operator comparisons must be matched and multi-criterion, which our L5 (90 configurations, each family at ITS OWN best learning rate, matched ~200k parameters and 8000 steps) already satisfies. Cite it to show our L5 protocol meets current community standards, and to justify reporting cost alongside accuracy.

papers.citation: "Want for nothing, need for null, useful output from negative results" — Matter (Cell Press), 2024.
papers.what_it_shows: Appears from the search listing to be a Matter editorial/commentary arguing for the value of negative results in materials science.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: If it is what it appears to be, it is a materials-journal editorial explicitly inviting negative results — the single most useful thing to cite in a cover letter to a materials venue. UNVERIFIED: cell.com returned HTTP 403 and I could not read it or confirm its authors, exact title, article type, or whether Matter actually invites such submissions. Do not cite until fetched.

state_of_the_art:
As of 2026, the rigorous negative result is an established and rewarded genre in ML, but it is only rewarded when it satisfies four conditions that have hardened into de facto standards.

(1) It must be systematic rather than anecdotal. The exemplars are systematic reviews with counts (McGreivy & Hakim: 79%, 60/76 papers use a weak baseline; Roberts et al.: 0 of 61 COVID models clinically usable; Ferrari Dacrema et al.: 7 of 18 reproducible, 6 of those beaten by heuristics; Kapoor & Narayanan: 17 fields, 294 papers) or exhaustive matched-budget benchmarks (Grinsztajn et al.: 45 datasets with matched hyperparameter search; Musgrave et al.: a corrected protocol re-running four years of claimed gains).

(2) It must supply a measured MECHANISM, not just a null. The negative results that became highly cited all name a cause: Grinsztajn names three inductive biases; Krishnapriyan names loss-landscape ill-conditioning from soft regularisation; Kapoor & Narayanan name a leakage taxonomy. A bare null is a workshop paper; a null with a measured binding constraint is a journal paper.

(3) It must ship a positive, reusable artefact. Every high-impact example pairs the negative with something others can adopt: a protocol and library (Musgrave), a benchmark suite (Grinsztajn), recommendations in five areas plus a peer-review prescription (Roberts), model info sheets (Kapoor & Narayanan), a 32-question consensus checklist (REFORMS), or a corrected method (Krishnapriyan's curriculum regularisation, Chatain's DeepFDM).

(4) It must pre-empt the "you did it wrong" reflex with an auditable protocol. The reporting standards that referees now reach for are REFORMS (Science Advances 2024, 32 questions, explicitly aimed at journals and referees), the NeurIPS Paper Checklist (mandatory Limitations section; error bars with stated variability factors and achievable ranges), and, in chemistry, Bender et al. 2022 and Artrith et al. 2021.

On venues: there is no top-tier journal in this space with a formal "negative results" article type. What exists instead is (a) TMLR, whose written criteria explicitly forbid rejecting for lack of SOTA or novelty and demand only that claims match evidence — the best structural fit; (b) MLST (IOP), which has a formal "Benchmark" article type and mandatory reproducibility, letting a falsification ladder be submitted as a benchmark; (c) Nature Machine Intelligence, which has published the two flagship negative/systematic-review papers in this genre (McGreivy & Hakim 2024, Roberts et al. 2021) but only when paired with field-wide prescriptions; (d) the ICBINB workshop series (NeurIPS 2020-2023, ICLR 2025+), whose review rubric explicitly scores "vulnerability and honesty in discussion" and whose 2022 subtitle was "Understanding Deep Learning Through Empirical Falsification"; and (e) pre-registration as a publication model, with two archival PMLR volumes (v148, 2020; v181, 2021) but no journal adoption in ML.

On self-correction: the empirical answer to "is a public corrections ledger a liability?" comes from the Loss-of-Confidence Project (Rohrer et al., Perspectives on Psychological Science 2021). 44% of 316 surveyed researchers had lost confidence in one of their own findings; only 17% made it public; 25% cited the absence of an appropriate venue as the barrier; and community reaction to prominent self-corrections was predominantly positive. There is no published evidence that disclosed self-correction damages reception — the documented problem is the opposite, that it almost never happens. The NeurIPS checklist makes the argument operational: undisclosed limitations that a reviewer discovers are worse than disclosed ones.
implications: Your paper's genre already exists and is award-winning; the question is only execution. 'Are We Really Making Much Progress?' won Best Full Paper at RecSys 2019 with a strictly negative result, and Nature Machine Intelligence has published two purely negative/critical papers in this exact space. Stop treating the negative framing as a fallback from the plan in 00_MASTER_PLAN_DYNAMICS.md; it is the stronger paper.

The single differentiator between a cited negative result and an ignored one is a MEASURED MECHANISM. You have the best-in-class version of this: l5_bottleneck.py splits the error into basis error (falls 28.7x) and coefficient-map error (flat at 0.051), with per-mode R^2 = 0.946 on mode 1 and median -0.014 beyond mode 24, calibrated against an oracle to yield 'DeepONet at any p performs like a 4-mode reconstruction'. That decomposition, not the list of eliminations, is the paper. Restructure so it appears in the abstract and in Figure 1.

Six negatives plus one positive is the ideal shape, and you have the positive: the two-wave warp collapses the n-width from 31 to 13-17 modes and reaches oracle nRMSE 0.0203, beating DeepONet's 0.0281 with only POD + a gradient-boosted regressor. Every high-impact negative-result paper pairs the null with a constructive deliverable. Lead the abstract with the mechanism, close it with the coordinate change.

The mirror image of McGreivy & Hakim's 'weak baseline' critique is a WEAK TREATMENT, and a referee who has read that paper will apply it to you symmetrically. Your own logs already contain the ammunition: l5_fill2.log shows DeepONet reaching ~0.0275 at lr=3e-3, ABOVE the top of the recorded grid, meaning the L5 grid did not bracket DeepONet's optimum either. Any elimination whose grid did not bracket the arm's optimum is not yet an elimination.

The L1 headline 'more data is eliminated' is currently contradicted by your own unpublished learning_curve.log: 1.82x improvement (0.0929 -> 0.0509) as training materials go 12 -> 48, not saturated. If this reaches a referee as a supplementary file while the abstract says data is eliminated, the paper is dead. L1 must be re-scoped in the abstract to the axis it actually tested: more OPERATING CONDITIONS per material does not help; MATERIAL DIVERSITY does, and has not saturated.

'Not supported' is not 'no effect', and your L6 CI is wide enough that a statistician referee will say so. CI [-0.0137, +0.0454] on a mean around 0.057 admits effects up to ~80% of the signal in the beneficial direction. Report the minimum detectable effect at 12 held-out materials explicitly, exactly as you already did for the DeepONet-vs-DeepOKAN null ('cannot resolve a 21% difference'). Do this for every null in the ladder or referees will assume the ones without it are the ones that would look bad.

The pre-registration is your strongest and most under-used asset, because the protocol was frozen 2026-08-20 before any model was trained and it recorded predictions that then FAILED — the n-width prediction called 'the load-bearing result of the ladder' was refuted (A17), and the primary hypothesis H1 was not supported with a pre-declared failure condition quoted verbatim. A pre-registration that only ever confirms is worthless; one that killed its own headline is proof the design was real. Say this in the abstract.

Name the method. Platt's 'strong inference' (Science 1964) gives the eight-rung ladder a 60-year-old pedigree and a one-word handle: a conditional inductive tree of alternative hypotheses, each excluded by a crucial experiment. That single reframing converts 'a sequence of things that did not work' into 'a designed exclusion procedure', at the cost of one citation.

Your corrections ledger is defensible but not self-explanatory, and the difference is presentation. Two moves make it a strength: (a) cite Rohrer et al. 2021 to establish that self-correction is rare because there is no venue, not because it is discrediting, and that reaction to it is predominantly positive; (b) keep Part A (17 withdrawn claims) and Part B (23 pre-contamination defects) rigorously separate in the manuscript, because Part B defects corrupted nothing and belong in a Methods appendix, not a retraction list. Presenting 40 items undifferentiated invites the reading you fear.

The two-wave warp has real prior art in the transport-dominated model-reduction literature (shifted POD with multiple transports, Krah et al. 2024; the 2026 Hesthaven-Peherstorfer-Unger survey), and that community will referee this paper if it goes to CMAME or JCP. Your defensible novelty is narrow and must be stated narrowly: the two-wave structure is MEASURED from a Type V isotherm with a 40x separation range, single-front alignment is measurably worse (31 -> 102 modes), and the residual obstruction is front LOCATION rather than the frame. Claim those three and nothing broader.

Venue strategy should be two-track, not single-shot. TMLR's written criteria are a near-perfect fit (claims-match-evidence, explicitly no SOTA or novelty requirement) and its Featured Certification carries real weight; MLST's 'Benchmark' article type is the best domain-facing container. npj Computational Materials remains a stretch without experimental validation, and the six open items in CONTINUE_HERE.md (uncited MOF-303 parameters, no COF, no experiment) are the binding constraint on venue tier, not the negativity of the result.

Ship the checklists. REFORMS (32 questions), the NeurIPS Paper Checklist, and — for a chemistry venue — Bender et al. 2022 and Artrith et al. 2021 all exist as external, neutral authorities. Completing them as supplementary items costs a day and converts every disclosure in the paper from an idiosyncratic confession into standards compliance. For a manuscript with 17 retractions, this is the highest return-on-effort action available.
risks_to_our_claims: WEAK TREATMENT, the mirror of the weak baseline. l5_fill2.log shows DeepONet hits ~0.0275 at lr=3e-3, above the top of the recorded learning-rate grid. A referee citing McGreivy & Hakim will argue that if your grid did not bracket the arm's optimum, your elimination measures your grid, not the method. This is currently true of at least L5 and possibly L2/L3, and it is documented in your own logs.

SELF-CONTRADICTION ON L1. learning_curve.log records a 1.82x improvement (0.0929 -> 0.0509) as training materials go 12 -> 48, unsaturated, while RESULTS.md's headline table says 'more data -> eliminated'. This is a direct internal contradiction between an unpublished log and the abstract-level verdict, on the very first rung. If a referee or a post-publication reader finds it, every other verdict becomes suspect.

L6 CI MIS-REPORTED IN RESULTS.md. The protocol log (03_LADDER_PROTOCOL.md line 1120) records joint-minus-separate = -0.01554, CI [-0.04540, +0.01372]. RESULTS.md line 394-395 reports separate-minus-joint = +0.0147 with CI [-0.0155, +0.0450]. The sign-flipped CI should be [-0.01372, +0.04540]; the reported lower bound (-0.0155) is the point estimate, not a CI endpoint, and the point estimates disagree (0.0147 vs 0.01554). CONTINUE_HERE.md line 62 reports a third variant. For a paper whose credibility rests on statistical care, a garbled CI on the PRIMARY pre-registered hypothesis is the worst possible defect.

UNDERPOWERED NULLS PRESENTED AS ELIMINATIONS. With 12 held-out materials, several 'no difference' verdicts cannot resolve effects of practical size — you already concede this for DeepONet vs DeepOKAN ('cannot resolve a 21% difference'). A referee will ask why that caveat appears once and not at L2, L4 (material axis) and L6. Absence of the caveat elsewhere reads as selective reporting, which is precisely the sin McGreivy & Hakim document.

EXTERNAL VALIDITY. All eight rungs run on one synthetic dataset from one solver, 60 materials, one isotherm form, with a Damkohler range (155-3885, median 626) that you yourself say under-samples the informative regime (Da ~ 1-50). A referee can dismiss the entire ladder as 'negative results on a near-equilibrium synthetic corpus'. The pre-declared low-Da re-test of H1 is not done, so H1 is arguably untested rather than unsupported.

PRIOR ART ON THE ONE POSITIVE RESULT. Shifted POD with multiple transports (Krah et al. 2024) and the broader transformation-based nonlinear model-reduction literature (Hesthaven, Peherstorfer & Unger survey, 2026) already handle multi-front transport. Without an sPOD baseline on your data and an explicit positioning paragraph, the two-wave warp reads as a rediscovery, which would strip the paper of its only positive contribution.

THE POSITIVE RESULT DOES NOT ACTUALLY WIN YET. Predicted-warp nRMSE is 0.0508 against fixed-frame 0.0510 (warp_predict.log) — a 0.4% difference with no CI reported. Presenting this as a win without a paired interval, after eight rungs of insisting on calibrated alpha and paired CIs, is a double standard a referee will catch immediately. Either report it as a tie with 2.17x measured headroom, or supply the CI.

THE LEDGER READ UNCHARITABLY. Forty disclosed items (17 Part A + 23 Part B) with no external framing can be read as 'this pipeline produced wrong answers forty times; why should we believe the forty-first?'. The specific items that look worst out of context are A1 (a figure with two fully synthesised model curves) and A15 (nRMSE 26,000 for a bounded model). These need a one-line explanation each at first mention, or they become the reviewer's headline.

TITLE/SCOPE MISMATCH. The project title claims a COF case that does not exist, and every MOF-303 parameter is an uncited literature-range placeholder (A4). A domain referee checks this in the first five minutes. Either produce a COF case and cited parameters, or retitle before submission — this is a desk-reject risk independent of everything else.

NO EXPERIMENTAL VALIDATION, ANYWHERE. The error budget cannot currently separate solver-vs-experiment from surrogate-vs-solver. This caps the venue and gives any reviewer a clean, unanswerable objection: 'you have shown that ML cannot match YOUR SOLVER, which has itself not been shown to match reality'. One digitised published breakthrough curve materially changes this.
