SPEED CLAIM. Any framing as a 'speedup' invites the McGreivy & Hakim baseline critique in its purest form, since the reference is your own unoptimised solver at 4.2 s/condition with N_z=2000. Frame strictly as amortised screening throughput with the baseline's configuration stated, or drop it.

kaggle_run/ IS A LIVE HAZARD. A stale duplicate carrying every original defect, in a repository whose central credibility claim is that the record is complete and gated. If reviewers or readers get the repository, they get that directory. It must be deleted or moved to an explicitly-marked archive with a README stating that its contents are superseded and defective.

concrete_actions.action: Fix the L6 confidence interval and reconcile it across all three documents. The protocol log gives joint-separate = -0.01554, CI [-0.04540, +0.01372]. Recompute, choose one sign convention (separate-minus-joint), and make RESULTS.md line 394-395, CONTINUE_HERE.md line 62 and 03_LADDER_PROTOCOL.md line 1120 agree exactly. Add a validate.py gate that re-derives every reported CI from the stored bootstrap samples and fails on any mismatch.
concrete_actions.rationale: This is a garbled interval on the PRIMARY pre-registered hypothesis, in the summary document, in a paper whose entire credibility rests on statistical discipline. RESULTS.md's stated lower bound (-0.0155) is the point estimate, not a CI endpoint. A referee who spots this discards the rest. It is also directly contrary to NeurIPS Checklist item 7, which requires the calculation method for error bars to be stated and correct.

concrete_actions.action: Re-scope the L1 verdict before writing the abstract. Change 'more data is eliminated' to the axis actually tested: additional operating conditions per material do not help, whereas material diversity does and has NOT saturated (1.82x from 12 to 48 materials, learning_curve.log). Promote learning_curve.log into RESULTS.md and the protocol as a formal result with its own CI, and either finish the 240-material scale-up (data/parametric_scale, currently ~1457 of 4080 files, no manifest) or state explicitly that it is incomplete and why.
concrete_actions.rationale: An unpublished log in your own repository contradicts your first rung's headline verdict. Publishing a strong negative claim that your own supplementary data refutes is the fastest route to a post-publication correction. Reporting the material-axis learning curve yourself turns a fatal inconsistency into a nuanced, more interesting result: the data axis that matters is diversity, not volume.

concrete_actions.action: Close every hyperparameter grid so that each arm's optimum is BRACKETED, not clipped. Start with DeepONet at lr=3e-3 and above (l5_fill2.log shows ~0.0275 at the current grid edge), then audit L2 and L3 for the same defect. Add a validate.py gate that fails any reported elimination whose best configuration lies on a grid boundary.
concrete_actions.rationale: McGreivy & Hakim's weak-baseline finding (79% of 76 ML-for-PDE papers) is the review lens this paper will be read through, and it applies symmetrically: a clipped grid means you measured your grid, not the method. Your own trap list already names this as having happened four times (B14, L3 KANs, B22, the DeepOKAN lr grid). A boundary-optimum gate makes the failure impossible to repeat and is a citable methodological contribution in its own right.

concrete_actions.action: Report a minimum detectable effect (MDE) alongside every null verdict in the ladder — L2, L4 material axis, L5 paired comparisons, and L6 — computed at the actual cluster count and calibrated alpha=0.005, in the same form as the existing DeepONet/DeepOKAN statement ('cannot resolve a 21% difference'). Add the MDE column to the RESULTS.md verdict table.
concrete_actions.rationale: 'Not supported' and 'no effect' are different claims, and a paper built from nulls must distinguish them everywhere or nowhere. Doing it once and not elsewhere reads as selective reporting. Uniform MDE reporting is also the single clearest signal to a statistically literate referee that the ladder is a designed exclusion procedure rather than a collection of underpowered failures.

concrete_actions.action: Rewrite the abstract around the MECHANISM, not the list of eliminations. Target structure: (1) the transfer gap and why it matters; (2) a PRE-REGISTERED falsification ladder froze eight hypotheses before any model was trained; (3) six standard interventions — data, capacity, edge basis, physics-as-loss, operator learning, structural decomposition — do not close it; (4) the binding constraint is measured, not inferred: the parameter-to-coefficient map carries ~4-5 modes of generalisable information out of 128, so a 28.7x reduction in the linear-approximation floor buys nothing; (5) the pre-registration killed its own headline prediction and its own primary hypothesis; (6) a two-wave coordinate change collapses the n-width 31 -> 13 and reaches 0.0203 oracle nRMSE, beating every learned arm, relocating the obstruction to front location with 2.17x measured headroom.
concrete_actions.rationale: Grinsztajn, Krishnapriyan and Kapoor & Narayanan all show that the negative result is the evidence and the mechanism is the contribution. Your L5 bottleneck decomposition is a better mechanism than most published examples, and it is currently buried below eight verdict tables. Point (5) is uniquely yours: a pre-registration that refuted its own load-bearing prediction is near-unfalsifiable evidence that the design was genuine.

concrete_actions.action: Name the method 'strong inference' after Platt (Science 1964) and present L0-L7 as his conditional inductive tree: alternative hypotheses, a crucial experiment per hypothesis, exclusion, recycle. Put this in the introduction's second paragraph and echo it in the Methods section title.
concrete_actions.rationale: One citation converts 'eight things we tried that did not work' into 'a 60-year-old designed exclusion procedure, executed with pre-registration'. It gives referees a familiar, respectable schema to file the paper under, and it explains WHY the rungs are ordered as they are — which is otherwise the most confusing thing about the manuscript for a first-time reader.

concrete_actions.action: Complete and ship three checklists as supplementary items: REFORMS (32 questions, Kapoor et al., Science Advances 2024), the NeurIPS Paper Checklist (including a mandatory standalone Limitations section), and — if targeting a chemistry/materials venue — the Artrith et al. 2021 Nature Chemistry reporting checklist together with an explicit statement of compliance with Bender et al. 2022.
concrete_actions.rationale: For a manuscript disclosing 17 retractions, the highest-return action is to make every disclosure look like compliance with an external consensus standard rather than an idiosyncratic confession. These are the exact instruments referees in this space now reach for, they cost about a day, and REFORMS is explicitly designed for journals to enforce.

concrete_actions.action: Restructure the corrections record for the manuscript: keep Part A (17 withdrawn claims) as a short, clearly labelled 'Corrections to preprint claims' subsection with a one-line cause for each, and move Part B (23 pre-contamination defects) into a Methods appendix titled 'Defects caught by the validation harness before any result was reported' — explicitly noting that these corrupted no reported number. Introduce the whole apparatus with a citation to Rohrer et al. 2021 (Loss-of-Confidence Project) and to NeurIPS Checklist item 2.
concrete_actions.rationale: The published evidence (44% of researchers have lost confidence in a finding; only 17% disclose; 25% blame the absence of a venue; reaction to prominent self-correction has been predominantly positive) says disclosure is rewarded, but nothing says an undifferentiated list of 40 items is. Part B is a demonstration that the harness WORKS — evidence for the pipeline, not against it — and merging it with Part A throws that away and quadruples the apparent error count.

concrete_actions.action: Position the two-wave warp explicitly against the transport-dominated model-reduction literature. Read the Hesthaven-Peherstorfer-Unger 2026 survey (arXiv:2602.01397), cite Krah et al. 2024 shifted POD with multiple transports (arXiv:2403.04313), place the warp inside the survey's transformation-based taxonomy, and run sPOD as a baseline on the 988-run dataset. State the novelty narrowly: the two-wave structure is measured (40x separation range from the Type V isotherm), single-front alignment is measurably worse (31 -> 102 modes for 99.9%), and the residual obstruction is front location.
concrete_actions.rationale: This is the paper's only positive result and its novelty is currently undefended against a mature literature whose members will referee a CMAME/JCP submission. An sPOD baseline plus a precise positioning paragraph either secures the contribution or tells you now, cheaply, that it needs re-scoping.

concrete_actions.action: Report the predicted-warp result honestly with a paired CI. 0.0508 vs the fixed frame's 0.0510 is a 0.4% difference with no interval; either supply the calibrated-alpha paired CI or present it explicitly as a tie whose value is the measured 2.17x headroom to the 0.0233 oracle.
concrete_actions.rationale: After eight rungs of demanding matched budgets, three seeds and paired CIs at alpha=0.005 before any verdict, claiming a 0.4% win without an interval is a visible double standard on the paper's only positive claim. The honest framing — obstruction relocated, headroom quantified, target well-posed — is actually the more interesting story and is already how RESULTS.md describes it internally.

concrete_actions.action: Promote the DeepOKAN seed-invariance collapse detector into a named, standalone diagnostic with its own subsection and pseudocode: 10/45 runs landing on the same point in function space, agreeing to 2.7e-7 across different p, learning rates AND seeds, with the collapse rate monotone in stack width (0/9 at p=8,16; 1/9 at 32; 4/9 at 64; 5/9 at 128).
concrete_actions.rationale: Adebayo et al.'s 'Sanity Checks' shows that a cheap invariance test a whole method family fails becomes a highly cited reusable contribution. Seed-invariance is a property a trained network cannot exhibit, which makes it an unusually clean detector, and it is currently presented as an incidental observation inside L5. Named and generalised, it is an independently citable artefact — and a second positive deliverable to pair with the negatives.

concrete_actions.action: Adopt a two-track venue plan: primary submission to TMLR (whose criteria explicitly forbid rejection for lack of SOTA or novelty and require only that claims match evidence) or to MLST under its formal 'Benchmark' article type; and in parallel submit a 4-page version to the current ICBINB workshop edition for early, low-cost referee signal. Reserve npj Computational Materials until the open items are closed.
concrete_actions.rationale: TMLR and MLST are the only venues whose WRITTEN policies fit this manuscript, and ICBINB's rubric literally scores 'vulnerability and honesty in discussion' and 'quality of limitations discussion'. A workshop round gives you referee reactions to the ledger and the ladder framing before the journal submission, which is exactly the uncertainty you most need resolved. npj Computational Materials is gated on experimental validation, not on framing.

concrete_actions.action: Close the three scope-and-provenance items that create desk-reject risk: replace every MOF-303 parameter with cited literature values and refit the isotherm to a published water isotherm (retraction A4), and either add a genuine COF case or remove COF from the title; then delete or clearly archive kaggle_run/ with a README stating its contents are superseded and defective.
concrete_actions.rationale: A domain referee verifies parameter provenance and title scope within the first five minutes. An uncited placeholder set behind every headline number, and a title claiming a case that does not exist, are desk-reject grounds independent of the science. kaggle_run/ is a live hazard in a repository whose central claim is that the record is complete and gated.

concrete_actions.action: Run the pre-declared low-Damkohler re-test of H1: regenerate a dataset with k_LDF extended down to ~1e-4 so Da spans the informative 1-50 regime, and re-run L6 unchanged.
concrete_actions.rationale: You measured WHY H1 failed — at median Da 626 the equilibrium/kinetic decomposition is nearly degenerate — and pre-declared this exact follow-up. Without it, a referee can say H1 was untested rather than unsupported, and the mechanism explanation becomes an unfalsified excuse. With it, both outcomes are publishable and the primary hypothesis is decided rather than merely reported. This is the highest-value remaining experiment in the project.

concrete_actions.action: Verify the two citations I could not confirm before either is used: (a) fetch the Matter 2024 piece at cell.com/matter/fulltext/S2590-2385(24)00160-7 (returned HTTP 403) to establish its authors, article type and whether Matter actually invites negative results; (b) confirm the arXiv identifier for Adebayo et al., 'Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps' (I recorded 1810.03292 from memory, not from a fetched page); and (c) confirm whether Karl et al., arXiv:2406.03980, is the ICML 2024 Position track paper that OpenReview id 3RXAiU7sss implies.
concrete_actions.rationale: A hallucinated or mis-attributed reference in a manuscript whose entire thesis is methodological rigour would be the single most damaging possible defect — worse for this paper than for any other. These three are the only entries in this review not confirmed against a page I actually retrieved, and each takes minutes to check.

lens: Theoretical and empirical limits of operator learning, and the strongest 2025–2026 operator/surrogate architectures a referee would demand you test

papers.citation: Alexander Heinlein, Johannes Taraz. "The Error of Deep Operator Networks Is the Sum of Its Parts: Branch-Trunk and Mode Error Decompositions." arXiv preprint (submitted 25 Feb 2026, revised 24 Aug 2026)
papers.what_it_shows: Decomposes DeepONet error into branch (coefficient) and trunk (basis) parts. Verbatim from the abstract: 'the approximation error is dominated by the branch network when the internal dimension is sufficiently large, and ... the learned trunk basis can often be replaced by classical basis functions without a significant impact on performance.' They build a modified DeepONet whose trunk IS the left singular vectors of the training solution matrix (i.e. a POD trunk), and observe (a) error saturation as internal dimension grows, (b) a spectral bias in the branch — 'coefficients of dominant, low-frequency modes learned more effectively', (c) branch error dominated by modes with large/intermediate singular values, (d) shared branch beats stacked branch for small-mode generalisation, (e) 'detrimental coupling between modes in parameter space, which weakens with increasing network width.' Examples: KdV and Burgers.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: THIS IS THE SCOOP RISK. It is, on 1-D PDE examples, the same experiment and the same conclusion as l5_bottleneck.py plus the flat-in-p L5 result, published six months before the current date. Any referee who knows the field will find it. The project can no longer claim the branch/coefficient bottleneck as a novel discovery; it must claim the *parametric-family* version of it (11-D descriptor input rather than a function input), the *material-extrapolation* split, the physical mechanism (unidentifiable k_LDF), and the fact that the plateau survives a warp that cuts the n-width 2.4x. Their (d) and (e) are also two cheap ablations we have not run that could move our own number.

papers.citation: Samuel Lanthaler, Roberto Molinaro, Patrik Hadorn, Siddhartha Mishra. "Nonlinear Reconstruction for Operator Learning of PDEs with Discontinuities." ICLR 2023 (arXiv Oct 2022)
papers.what_it_shows: Proves fundamental lower bounds: methods with a LINEAR reconstruction step (DeepONet, PCA-Net) cannot efficiently approximate solution operators of advection-dominated / discontinuous PDEs. Methods with a NONLINEAR reconstruction mechanism — Fourier Neural Operators, and shift-DeepONet (a DeepONet augmented with learned shifts/scalings of the trunk coordinates) — provably overcome those bounds. Verified empirically on advection, inviscid Burgers, compressible Euler.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is simultaneously the theory that legitimises the project's two-wave warp AND the paper that makes L5 look designed to fail. run_l5.py tests exactly two families, deeponet and deepokan — both linear-reconstruction. The ladder therefore never tested any architecture that this theorem says can escape. Also note the direct tension: our headline is 'the basis is not what binds, the coefficient map binds', whereas this theorem says the linear reconstruction IS the binding constraint for exactly our problem class (self-sharpening cooperative shock + spreading Henry wave = advection-dominated with a near-discontinuity). Both can be true (theirs is a worst-case approximation bound with optimal coefficients; ours is a finite-sample statement) but the paper must say so explicitly or a referee will read it as a contradiction. The two-wave warp is best framed as a two-shift generalisation of shift-DeepONet, physically motivated by the Type V isotherm.

papers.citation: Samuel Lanthaler, Andrew M. Stuart. "The parametric complexity of operator learning." IMA Journal of Numerical Analysis 46(2):647–712 (2026); published online 15 Aug 2025
papers.what_it_shows: Proves a 'curse of parametric complexity' — an infinite-dimensional analogue of the curse of dimensionality — for approximating general classes of Lipschitz/Fréchet-differentiable operators between function spaces. The curse applies to PCA-Net, DeepONet and FNO alike. It is escapable for structured solution operators; they exhibit HJ-Net for Hamilton–Jacobi equations with provably better complexity.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The canonical 'why neural operators plateau' citation. But it also constrains what we may claim: their curse is about function-space inputs. Our branch input is an 11-dimensional parameter vector, so we are in the strictly easier parametric regime, and the curse of parametric complexity does NOT explain our plateau. That is a point in our favour (our wall is statistical/identifiability, not approximation-theoretic) and we should say it — but if the paper cites this as the explanation, a theory referee will reject the framing.

papers.citation: Samuel Lanthaler. "Operator learning with PCA-Net: upper and lower complexity bounds." Journal of Machine Learning Research 24 (2023); arXiv Mar 2023
papers.what_it_shows: Upper and lower complexity bounds for PCA-Net (POD basis + neural coefficient map). Identifies exactly two obstructions: (i) slow decay of the PCA eigenvalues of the output measure, and (ii) the curse of parametric complexity in the coefficient network. Upper bounds show smoothness gives algebraic eigenvalue decay and that PCA-Net can beat the curse for Darcy and Navier–Stokes.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the exact theoretical framing of l5_bottleneck.py: PCA-Net *is* POD + regressor. Our measurement says obstruction (i) is inactive (eigenvalues fall 28.7x over p=8→128) while obstruction (ii) is total (flat at 0.051). We should present our result in Lanthaler's own two-obstruction language — it makes the finding legible to the numerical-analysis audience and inherits his terminology instead of inventing our own.

papers.citation: Nikola B. Kovachki, Samuel Lanthaler, Hrushikesh Mhaskar. "Data Complexity Estimates for Operator Learning." arXiv May 2024 (v2 Oct 2024)
papers.what_it_shows: A 'curse of data complexity': for general Lipschitz and Fréchet-differentiable operator classes, the sample size needed scales exponentially in 1/epsilon. Escape clause: if an algebraically increasing number of tunable parameters suffices for a target accuracy, then an algebraically bounded number of samples also suffices. FNO used as the worked example.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Directly bears on the L1 verdict and on the not-yet-reported learning_curve.log result (1.82x improvement, 0.0929→0.0509, going 12→48 training materials, NOT saturated). This paper says a data plateau is expected only for unstructured operator classes; for structured PDE solution operators the sample complexity is algebraic, so 48 materials plateauing is *not* evidence of an intrinsic limit. L1's 'more data is eliminated' verdict and learning_curve.log are in open conflict and a referee will use this paper as the stick.

papers.citation: Jacob H. Seidman, Georgios Kissas, Paris Perdikaris, George J. Pappas. "NOMAD: Nonlinear Manifold Decoders for Operator Learning." NeurIPS 2022 (arXiv Jun 2022)
papers.what_it_shows: Argues that even when target functions lie on a low-dimensional submanifold, a linear representation may need very many basis elements. Replaces DeepONet's linear decoder sum_k b_k(u) t_k(y) with a nonlinear decoder D(b(u), y). Reports learning low-dimensional representations of PDE solution manifolds 'while outperforming linear models of larger size', with competitive fluid-dynamics performance at much smaller model size.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The single cheapest architectural escape hatch from our own result: NOMAD is DeepONet with the last linear layer made nonlinear, so it can be dropped into run_l5.py at matched parameter count with almost no new code. If NOMAD is also flat in p, our claim gets very strong. If NOMAD is not flat, our headline is wrong and we need to know before a referee does.

papers.citation: Francesca Bartolucci, Emmanuel de Bézenac, Bogdan Raonić, Roberto Molinaro, Siddhartha Mishra, Rima Alaifari. "Representation Equivalent Neural Operators: a Framework for Alias-free Operator Learning." NeurIPS 2023; arXiv May 2023 (earlier title: "Are Neural Operators Really Neural Operators? Frame Theory Meets Operator Learning")
papers.what_it_shows: Uses frame theory to define Representation-equivalent Neural Operators (ReNO): an architecture only genuinely learns an operator if the continuous and discrete levels are equivalent, quantified by an aliasing-error operator that must vanish. Many popular architectures fail this and are really learning a discretisation, not an operator.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The project stores fields at 512x256 and freezes a 128x128 encoding for the whole L5 rung. Nothing in the ladder ever changes resolution. Under the ReNO criterion the paper is not entitled to the word 'operator' anywhere, and cannot claim its negative result is about operator learning rather than about one fixed grid. A single cheap experiment — train at 128x128, evaluate at 256x256 and 512x256 — fixes this, and its outcome is also independently interesting.

papers.citation: Lennon Shikhman. "Diagnosing Failure Modes of Neural Operators Across Diverse PDE Families." Transactions on Machine Learning Research; arXiv Jan 2026 (latest version May 2026)
papers.what_it_shows: A stress-testing framework for neural PDE solvers over FNO, a DeepONet-style model and CNO, across five PDE families (dispersive, elliptic, multi-scale fluid, financial, chaotic), 750 trained models, with structured shifts in coefficients, boundary conditions, discretisation and rollout horizon. Headline: 'strong in-distribution accuracy does not reliably predict robustness, and failure patterns depend jointly on architecture and PDE family.'
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Gives us (a) a published protocol template for the novel-material/novel-condition splits we already use, so we can align our shift taxonomy with an existing standard rather than inventing one, and (b) a strong caution against generalising from one PDE family — which is exactly what an eight-rung ladder on a single 1-D adsorption column does. Our discussion section must contain an explicit external-validity paragraph citing this.

papers.citation: Nick McGreivy, Ammar Hakim. "Weak baselines and reporting biases lead to overoptimism in machine learning for fluid-related partial differential equations." Nature Machine Intelligence 6:1256–1269 (2024); arXiv:2407.07218
papers.what_it_shows: Systematic review: 79% (60/76) of papers claiming ML beats standard numerical methods on fluid-related PDEs compared against weak baselines. Also documents outcome-reporting and publication bias, i.e. systematic under-reporting of negative results.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Cuts both ways and both ways matter. Positively: this paper is the reason a falsification ladder full of negative results is publishable at all, and it is the natural framing citation for the introduction. Negatively: it is also the exact weapon a referee will use against L5, because l5_fill2.log shows lr=3e-3 — ABOVE the top of the original grid — gives DeepONet ~0.0275 at p=128 versus the recorded 0.0296, i.e. the published sweep did not bracket the baseline's optimum. A paper whose central claim is 'the strong method fails' cannot afford an under-tuned strong method.

papers.citation: Patrick Chatain, Michael Rizvi-Martel, Guillaume Rabusseau, Adam Oberman. "Numerical PDE solvers outperform neural PDE solvers" (DeepFDM). arXiv Jul 2025
papers.what_it_shows: A differentiable finite-difference scheme (forward Euler embedded in a convolutional architecture, CFL-compliant, weights = PDE coefficients) attains normalised MSE one to two orders of magnitude below FNO, U-Net and ResNet, with 10–20x fewer epochs and 5–50x fewer parameters, on advection, diffusion, advection-diffusion, reaction-diffusion and inhomogeneous Burgers in 1-D/2-D/3-D, in- and out-of-distribution.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The strongest 2025 statement of 'structure beats architecture'. It is the natural companion citation for L7 (classical closed forms) and for the honest speed claim, and it suggests a baseline we do not have and that a referee may well demand: a differentiable, coarse-grid version of our own solver_fd.py as a surrogate. Given our solver runs 4.2 s/condition at N_z=2000, a differentiable N_z=64 version could plausibly beat every learned arm in the ladder — which would be a far more interesting paper than 'learning wins 3.2x over Klinkenberg'.

papers.citation: Bogdan Raonić, Roberto Molinaro, Tim De Ryck, Tobias Rohner, Francesca Bartolucci, Rima Alaifari, Siddhartha Mishra, Emmanuel de Bézenac. "Convolutional Neural Operators for robust and accurate learning of PDEs." NeurIPS 2023; arXiv Feb 2023
papers.what_it_shows: CNN adapted to act on functions rather than grids (band-limited interpolation, anti-aliased up/down-sampling) so the continuous structure is preserved under discretisation; universality theorem; benchmarked against FNO and DeepONet on a suite of PDEs with multi-scale solutions. Related search results indicate CNO reaches 1% error on Navier–Stokes with ~14.3k samples vs ~60.1k for FNO (this specific number is second-hand and should be checked in the source before quoting).
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: CNO is the ReNO-compliant, nonlinear-reconstruction, discretisation-honest architecture. It is one of the three architectures in the Shikhman stress-test, so it is now a de facto standard baseline. In our setting it also has a specific reason to work: convolutions in (z,t) are translation-equivariant, and our two waves are translations — a CNO may absorb the warp implicitly, which is precisely the mechanism our warp result predicts should help.

papers.citation: Chaoyu Liu, Zhonghao Li, Gaohang Chen, Zakhar Shumaylov, Zhongying Deng, Qian Zhang, Zhonghua Qiao, Carola-Bibiane Schönlieb. "Adaptive Coordinate Transforms for Neural Operators." arXiv May 2026
papers.what_it_shows: Argues that fixed Eulerian coordinates misalign with evolving physical structures and force operators into unnecessarily non-local, smoothness-favouring maps. Introduces a plug-and-play ACT block that learns a coordinate transformation inside the operator pipeline and resamples features differentiably ('expressing the same physical quantity in different coordinate systems'). Reports consistent significant gains across diverse PDE benchmarks and multiple operator backbones.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is our two-wave warp, learned end-to-end instead of predicted post-hoc, published three months ago. It is a priority risk for the warp contribution and, more usefully, it is the method that would close our 2.17x headroom: warp_predict.log shows oracle warp 0.0233 vs predicted warp 0.0508, i.e. the entire remaining gain is warp-prediction error, which is exactly what joint end-to-end learning of the transform is designed to remove. Our differentiator is that our warp is TWO shifts derived from an identified physical mechanism (Henry wave + cooperative shock), not a generic learned deformation.

papers.citation: Haixu Wu, Huakun Luo, Haowen Wang, Jianmin Wang, Mingsheng Long. "Transolver: A Fast Transformer Solver for PDEs on General Geometries." ICML 2024 (Spotlight); arXiv Feb 2024
papers.what_it_shows: Physics-Attention: partitions the domain into learnable 'slices' of mesh points in similar physical states, and runs attention among physical states rather than mesh points, at linear complexity. 22% relative gain across six standard benchmarks, strong on large-scale industrial cases, reported favourable OOD generalisation.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The default 2024–2026 transformer-operator baseline; a referee will name it. Mechanistically it is also the most promising transformer for us: the slice mechanism is a soft segmentation of the domain into physical states, and our field is exactly two coherent states (pre-front, post-front) separated by two moving interfaces — the slices could learn the warp. Note a 2026 AAAI paper argues Physics-Attention is equivalent to linear attention, which weakens the novelty story but not its use as a baseline.

papers.citation: Maximilian Herde, Bogdan Raonić, Tobias Rohner, Roger Käppeli, Roberto Molinaro, Emmanuel de Bézenac, Siddhartha Mishra. "Poseidon: Efficient Foundation Models for PDEs." NeurIPS 2024; arXiv:2405.19101
papers.what_it_shows: Multiscale operator transformer (scOT) with time-conditioned layer norm for continuous-in-time evaluation, pretrained on fluid-dynamics data using the semigroup property to multiply the effective training set; evaluated on 15 downstream tasks, outperforming baselines in both sample efficiency and accuracy, and generalising to unseen physics. Model and datasets released.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The obvious referee question given learning_curve.log's unsaturated material axis is 'did you try a pretrained PDE foundation model instead of generating 4080 more simulations?'. Poseidon is the strongest, most-cited, publicly available candidate. Honest expectation: pretraining is on 2-D fluids, our target is a 1-D two-field advection–reaction–energy column, so transfer is likely weak — but demonstrating and reporting that is itself a defensible result and costs a few GPU-days rather than the incomplete 240-material scale-up.

papers.citation: Phillip Lippe, Bastiaan S. Veeling, Paris Perdikaris, Richard E. Turner, Johannes Brandstetter. "PDE-Refiner: Achieving Accurate Long Rollouts with Neural PDE Solvers." NeurIPS 2023; arXiv:2308.05732
papers.what_it_shows: Identifies neglect of non-dominant spatial frequencies as the primary cause of unstable/inaccurate rollouts, and fixes it with a diffusion-style multi-step refinement (add noise of decreasing variance, denoise with the same model), yielding large rollout-stability gains with ~3 refinement steps, better sample complexity, and uncertainty quantification.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Its diagnosis is our diagnosis in different clothes: 'the model captures the dominant modes and drops the rest.' Our per-mode R² (0.946 on mode 1, 0.39–0.58 on modes 2–5, median -0.014 beyond mode 24) is the parametric analogue of their spectral finding. The refinement trick is directly transplantable to a one-shot parametric surrogate: predict the field, then refine — a cheap way to test whether the plateau is an optimisation/loss-weighting artefact rather than an information limit. If a refinement stage moves 0.051, our 'unlearnable' framing is too strong.

papers.citation: Zijie Li, Dule Shu, Amir Barati Farimani. "Scalable Transformer for PDE Surrogate Modeling" (FactFormer). arXiv:2305.17560 (May 2023, rev Nov 2023)
papers.what_it_shows: Axial factorised kernel integral: a learnable projection decomposes the input function into sub-functions on 1-D domains, giving a low-rank surrogate for full attention. Demonstrated on 2-D Kolmogorov flow (256x256) and 3-D smoke (64^3).
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Our field is a 2-D (z,t) tensor with strongly axis-anisotropic structure — L4/L4b already found the physics loss is axis-specific (helps on time, hurts elsewhere). An axially factorised attention operator is the architecture whose inductive bias matches that observation, so it is a targeted rather than a scattergun addition. Lower priority than FNO/CNO but a good third transformer if a referee pushes.

papers.citation: Alasdair Tran, Alexander Mathews, Lexing Xie, Cheng Soon Ong. "Factorized Fourier Neural Operators." ICLR 2023; arXiv:2111.13802
papers.what_it_shows: Separable spectral layers plus improved residual connections, combined with Markov-assumption training, Gaussian-noise augmentation and cosine LR decay. Reported error reductions vs FNO and geo-FNO of 83% (Navier–Stokes), 31% (elasticity), 57% (airfoil).
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: If we add only one FNO, it should be a modern one. F-FNO's gains come substantially from the TRAINING recipe (noise augmentation, cosine decay, residual design) rather than the layer alone — which is the same weak-baseline exposure that l5_fill2.log revealed in our LR grid. Adopting the F-FNO recipe wholesale for every arm is the cheapest way to make 'we tuned it properly' credible. geo-FNO and U-FNO are the geometry and multiphase-flow variants of the same family; neither is needed here (our domain is a fixed 1-D column), and saying so in one sentence pre-empts the question.

papers.citation: Qianying Cao, Somdatta Goswami, George Em Karniadakis. "Laplace neural operator for solving differential equations." Nature Machine Intelligence 6 (June 2024); arXiv:2303.10528
papers.what_it_shows: Learns the pole–residue relationship between input and output in the Laplace domain, which lets it handle non-periodic signals and transient responses from both zero and non-zero initial conditions, with better extrapolation accuracy than other neural operators on several ODEs and PDEs.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Of all the competitor architectures this is the one best matched to our physics and therefore the one most likely to actually break the flat-in-p result. A breakthrough curve is a transient, non-periodic step response of a 1-D system with a Danckwerts inlet; a pole–residue representation of a two-wave response is a genuinely different parameterisation from a POD/DeepONet linear reconstruction, and its parameters (pole locations) are close to the physical quantities — front times — that our warp shows to be the load-bearing latent variables. If any one architecture is going to embarrass the L5 verdict, my bet is this one. Test it before submission, not after review.

papers.citation: Tapas Tripura, Souvik Chakraborty. "Wavelet Neural Operator for solving parametric partial differential equations in computational mechanics problems." Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering 404:115783 (2023); arXiv:2205.02191 (May 2022)
papers.what_it_shows: Replaces FNO's Fourier kernel with a wavelet-domain kernel, exploiting time–frequency localisation so that both spatially localised patterns and frequency content are captured. Demonstrated on Burgers, Darcy, Navier–Stokes, Allen–Cahn and wave advection.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the REAL WNO — retraction A9 withdrew a dilated CNN that was mislabelled as one. Beyond correcting the record, WNO is the architecture whose motivation (localisation in both space and frequency) most directly targets a sharp self-sharpening front sitting on a broad spreading wave. Reference implementation is public (TapasTripura/WNO), so re-doing this arm honestly is a days-scale job, and it converts a retraction into a contribution.

papers.citation: Zhongkai Hao, Chengyang Ying, Zhengyi Wang, Hang Su, Yinpeng Dong, Songming Liu, Ze Cheng, Jun Zhu, Jian Song. "GNOT: A General Neural Operator Transformer for Operator Learning." ICML 2023; arXiv:2302.14376
papers.what_it_shows: Transformer operator with a heterogeneous normalised attention layer that natively handles multiple input functions and irregular meshes, plus a geometric gating mechanism acting as soft domain decomposition for multi-scale problems. SOTA on 7 datasets across fluids, heat and electromagnetism.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: GNOT's selling point is exactly our input structure: heterogeneous inputs (material descriptors + operating conditions + coordinates) rather than a single input function. It is the architecture a referee will name when they object that DeepONet's single concatenated 11-vector branch is a crude way to encode our parameters. Medium priority — likely to hit the same coefficient wall, since it does not change the fact that the parameters do not determine modes 2+ — but cheap insurance.

papers.citation: Zhongkai Hao et al. "DPOT: Auto-Regressive Denoising Operator Transformer for Large-Scale PDE Pre-Training." ICML 2024; arXiv:2403.03542
papers.what_it_shows: Auto-regressive denoising pretraining (Gaussian noise injected, predict next timestep from noisy input) on a Fourier-attention backbone, scaled to 0.5B parameters over 10+ PDE datasets and >100k trajectories, with strong transfer to downstream PDE tasks including 3-D.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The main autoregressive counterpoint to our one-shot field prediction. Two things it forces us to address: (1) our entire ladder predicts the whole (z,t) field in one shot, and we never justify that choice against autoregressive rollout — a referee will ask, and 'the two-wave separation varies 40x' is actually a good answer worth writing down; (2) it is the second obvious pretrained-model probe after Poseidon. Same honest expectation of weak transfer.

papers.citation: Jayesh K. Gupta, Johannes Brandstetter. "Towards Multi-spatiotemporal-scale Generalized PDE Modeling." Transactions on Machine Learning Research (2023); arXiv:2209.15616
papers.what_it_shows: Systematic comparison of FNO, ResNet and U-Net families for PDE surrogates; ports modern computer-vision improvements into U-Nets and introduces U-FNets (modern U-Net with FNO downsampling). The modern U-Net is repeatedly competitive with or better than FNO at comparable cost. Code: pdearena.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The 'boring baseline that beats fancy operators' citation. Our ladder has no CNN/U-Net arm at all — the closest thing is the retracted dilated CNN of A9. Since the ladder's rhetorical structure is 'each rung kills a hypothesis', an unkilled and un-run modern U-Net is a hole a referee can drive a truck through: if a plain U-Net beats DeepONet here, the L5 conclusion is about DeepONet, not about operator learning. pdearena makes this a days-scale add.

papers.citation: Ruben Ohana et al. "The Well: a Large-Scale Collection of Diverse Physics Simulations for Machine Learning." NeurIPS 2024 Datasets & Benchmarks; arXiv:2412.00568
papers.what_it_shows: A ~15 TB curated collection of 16 spatiotemporal simulation datasets spanning biology, fluids, astrophysical turbulence, MHD and acoustic scattering, with standardised loaders and baselines.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Two uses. First, it is now the reference standard for how a PDE-surrogate dataset should be documented (splits, metadata, licensing, loaders) — matching its conventions for our 988-run parametric dataset is cheap and materially raises the perceived rigour of a data-generating paper. Second, if the goal is a genuinely top-tier venue, releasing the adsorption dataset as a Well-compatible contribution is a plausible second axis of impact, since chemical-engineering transport is not represented there. NOTE: I did not fetch this page, so treat the author list as unverified beyond the lead author.

papers.citation: Michael McCabe et al. "Multiple Physics Pretraining for Physical Surrogate Models." arXiv:2310.02994 (2023)
papers.what_it_shows: Task-agnostic pretraining of a single transformer surrogate jointly across multiple distinct physical systems, with transfer to downstream systems including ones not seen in pretraining.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The third PDE-foundation-model reference a referee may name alongside Poseidon and DPOT. Cite in the related-work sweep; only run if one of the other two shows any transfer at all.

papers.citation: Liu Yang, Siting Liu, Tingwei Meng, Stanley J. Osher. "In-context operator learning with data prompts for differential equation problems." PNAS 120(39):e2310142120 (2023); arXiv:2304.07993
papers.what_it_shows: In-Context Operator Networks learn a new operator at inference time from a prompt of input–output function pairs, with no weight updates, across forward and inverse ODE/PDE and mean-field-control problems. Follow-ups: ICON-LM, and VICON (arXiv:2411.16063) for 2-D fields via vision transformers.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: A structurally different answer to our exact bottleneck. Our wall is that 11 static descriptors do not determine POD modes 2+ on an unseen material (mode-1 R^2=0.946 collapsing to a median of -0.014 beyond mode 24), and L6 independently found k_LDF unrecoverable from observable descriptors (R^2=-0.61). In-context learning sidesteps this: give the model a few *observed curves* for the new material as the prompt instead of asking it to infer the material from descriptors. That is both a strong extra experiment and, arguably, the honest engineering recommendation the paper should end on. I verified the ICON line of work exists but did not fetch the PNAS page; treat the exact author list as unverified.

papers.citation: Tommaso Taddei. "Overcoming slowly decaying Kolmogorov n-width by transport maps: application to model order reduction of fluid dynamics and fluid–structure interaction problems." arXiv:1911.06598 (2019). Related: "Model Reduction for Transport-Dominated Problems via Cross-Correlation Based Snapshot Registration" arXiv:2501.01299 (2025); Greif & Urban, "Decay of the Kolmogorov N-width for wave problems" (2019)
papers.what_it_shows: The registration branch of model order reduction: compose snapshots with a learned family of smooth invertible transport maps of the domain onto itself during the offline phase, so that the registered snapshots have fast-decaying n-width and linear reduced bases work again. Greif & Urban establish that wave/transport problems have provably slow n-width decay in the unregistered frame.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the 20-year-old prior art for the two-wave warp, from the numerical-analysis community rather than the ML community, and the paper currently does not cite it at all. A ROM referee will regard an uncited registration contribution as disqualifying. It also supplies the right vocabulary — 'registration', 'transport map', 'Kolmogorov barrier' — and the right framing for our strongest number: registering on the two front trajectories cuts the 99.9% rank from 31 to 13.

papers.citation: Spectral bias in operator learning: "Mitigating Spectral Bias in Neural Operators via High-Frequency [emphasis]" arXiv:2503.13695 (2025); "Multi-scale DeepOnet (Mscale-DeepOnet)" arXiv:2504.10932 (2025); "Spectral bias in physics-informed and operator learning: Analysis and mitigation guidelines" arXiv:2602.19265, also in Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering (2026)
papers.what_it_shows: A consistent 2025–2026 line: MLP-based branch/trunk networks trained with first-order methods are biased toward low-frequency components; DeepONet captures the mean but not high-frequency fluctuations; FNO's mode truncation compounds it. Mitigations that work: Fourier feature embeddings as spectral preconditioners, multi-scale architectures, and activation-function choice.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Provides the alternative explanation for our result that we have NOT ruled out, and it is the most damaging unaddressed alternative. 'The parameters do not determine modes 2+' and 'our branch MLP has spectral bias and cannot fit high-index coefficients' predict the same flat-in-p curve. The distinguishing experiment is cheap and decisive: our own l5_bottleneck already predicts the coefficients with HistGradientBoosting, which has NO spectral bias — and it also plateaus at 0.051 with median R^2 ≈ 0 beyond mode 24. Make that argument explicit and the objection dies; leave it implicit and a referee kills the paper's headline. I did not fetch these three; treat titles and numbering as approximate and verify before citing.

state_of_the_art:
As of 2026 the field has moved past 'which operator architecture wins' onto three things at once, and the project is currently positioned against the 2022–2023 version of the field rather than the 2026 one.

(1) THEORY IS SETTLED IN A WAY THAT MOSTLY HELPS US, WITH ONE SHARP EXCEPTION. Lanthaler & Stuart's curse of parametric complexity (IMA J. Numer. Anal. 46(2):647–712, 2026) and Kovachki–Lanthaler–Mhaskar's curse of data complexity (arXiv:2405.15992) establish that general operator classes need parameters and samples exponential in 1/epsilon, escapable only by exploiting PDE structure. Lanthaler's PCA-Net bounds (arXiv:2303.16317) name exactly the two obstructions l5_bottleneck.py measures — slow PCA eigenvalue decay, and coefficient-network complexity — so our decomposition already has a canonical theoretical home and canonical vocabulary. The sharp exception is Lanthaler–Molinaro–Hadorn–Mishra (ICLR 2023, arXiv:2210.01074): for advection-dominated/discontinuous PDEs, methods with a LINEAR reconstruction step (DeepONet, PCA-Net) provably cannot be efficient, while nonlinear reconstruction (FNO, shift-DeepONet) can. Our L5 tested only linear-reconstruction methods.

(2) THE 'BRANCH IS THE BOTTLENECK' RESULT IS ALREADY PUBLISHED. Heinlein & Taraz, arXiv:2602.21910 (25 Feb 2026, revised 24 Aug 2026), replace the DeepONet trunk with the left singular vectors of the training solution matrix, and report — on KdV and Burgers — that the branch dominates the error once the internal dimension is large, that the error saturates as the internal dimension grows, that the branch shows a spectral bias favouring dominant low-frequency modes, and that modes couple detrimentally in parameter space. That is the same experiment and the same conclusion as l5_bottleneck.py + the flat-in-p L5 sweep. Our result is now a confirmation-and-extension, not a discovery, and the paper must be rewritten to say so.

(3) THE ARCHITECTURE FRONTIER HAS THREE TIERS, AND THE BASELINE BAR HAS RISEN. Tier 1 (established, expected in any comparison): a modern well-tuned U-Net (Gupta & Brandstetter, TMLR 2023), FNO in a modern variant (F-FNO, ICLR 2023), and CNO (NeurIPS 2023). Tier 2 (current SOTA on standard benchmarks): transformer operators — Transolver (ICML 2024 spotlight, 22% relative gain over six benchmarks), GNOT (ICML 2023), FactFormer, Latent Neural Operator (NeurIPS 2024). Tier 3 (the 2024–2026 story): PDE foundation models — Poseidon (NeurIPS 2024), DPOT (ICML 2024), MPP — plus diffusion/refinement surrogates (PDE-Refiner, NeurIPS 2023) and in-context operator learning (ICON, PNAS 2023). Cutting across all three, McGreivy & Hakim (Nature Mach. Intell. 6:1256–1269, 2024) found 79% of ML-beats-numerics claims in fluid PDEs rested on weak baselines, and DeepFDM (arXiv:2507.21269) shows a differentiable finite-difference scheme beating FNO/U-Net/ResNet by one to two orders of magnitude. The consequence for us is blunt: in 2026, a paper whose thesis is 'the sophisticated method fails' is held to a higher tuning standard than a paper whose thesis is 'my method wins' — and l5_fill2.log already proves our DeepONet grid did not bracket its own optimum.

(4) FOR OUR SPECIFIC PHYSICS, THE RELEVANT SOTA IS NOT AN OPERATOR AT ALL BUT A COORDINATE TRANSFORM. Registration-based model reduction (Taddei, arXiv:1911.06598; cross-correlation snapshot registration, arXiv:2501.01299) has attacked the slow-n-width-of-transport problem since 2019, and Adaptive Coordinate Transforms for Neural Operators (arXiv:2605.06203, May 2026) has now brought learned coordinate transforms inside the operator pipeline as a plug-and-play block. The project's two-wave warp sits precisely in this literature, cites none of it, and — critically — the ACT paper's end-to-end formulation is exactly the mechanism that would convert our oracle-warp 0.0233 into an achievable number instead of leaving 2.17x on the table.
implications: The headline finding is confirmed, not owned. Heinlein & Taraz (arXiv:2602.21910) reached 'the branch/coefficient map binds and error saturates in latent dimension' six months ago on KdV and Burgers, with a POD trunk, and even reported the per-mode spectral bias. The paper must cite them in the abstract-adjacent framing, state plainly that we independently reproduce their conclusion in a different regime, and relocate novelty to what they do not have.

What we still own, and it is not small: (a) their branch input is a function, ours is an 11-D physical descriptor vector, so the curse of parametric complexity cannot be the explanation and the wall is purely statistical/identifiability — a strictly different mechanism; (b) our split is extrapolation to unseen MATERIALS, not unseen initial conditions; (c) we have a measured physical cause they cannot have — L6 shows k_LDF is unrecoverable from observable descriptors (R^2 = -0.61), and k_LDF is precisely what sets the two-wave separation that modes 2+ encode; (d) we show the plateau SURVIVES a registration that cuts the n-width 2.4x. That last one is the strongest card in the deck and it is currently buried in comoving2.log.

The single most important unreported number in the repository is in comoving2.log and warp_predict.log: in the two-wave warped frame, oracle-warp error is 0.02053 / 0.02032 / 0.02034 / 0.02047 / 0.02027 at p = 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 — flat to three decimals across a 16x change in basis size, exactly as in the unwarped frame, but at a plateau 2.5x lower. The coefficient wall is invariant to the representation; only its height moves. That is a sharper and more general claim than anything currently in RESULTS.md and it is what makes our result distinct from Heinlein & Taraz.

L5's conclusion is currently a statement about linear-reconstruction operators only. run_l5.py tests families ['deeponet','deepokan']; both write u = sum_k b_k(params) t_k(z,t). Lanthaler et al. (ICLR 2023) proved that this exact class has lower bounds on advection-dominated/discontinuous problems and that FNO and shift-DeepONet escape them. fno_model_adsorption.py exists in the repo and was never entered into the ladder. Until a genuine nonlinear-reconstruction operator is tested, 'you need an operator -> eliminated' is not defensible.

The ladder metaphor now works against us on one rung. Every other rung kills a hypothesis by testing the strongest version of it. L5 kills 'you need an operator' having tested two members of the one operator family the theory predicts should fail. A referee will describe this as an experiment designed to fail, and that single sentence would sink the paper. Adding FNO + CNO + a modern U-Net converts it into the ladder's strongest rung.

The n-width prediction that L5 'refuted' (retraction A17) was never actually refuted — it was mis-specified. The Kolmogorov n-width bounds the achievable error given optimal coefficients; it is a floor, and a floor being inactive is not a refutation of the floor. The correct statement, in Lanthaler's PCA-Net language, is that obstruction (i) (eigenvalue decay) is inactive at our data budget while obstruction (ii) (coefficient complexity) is total. Reframing A17 this way turns a self-inflicted retraction into a precise positive result.

The alternative explanation we have not explicitly excluded is spectral bias in the branch MLP (arXiv:2503.13695, arXiv:2504.10932, arXiv:2602.19265) — it predicts the same flat-in-p curve for a completely different reason. Our own data already kills it: l5_bottleneck.py predicts coefficients with HistGradientBoostingRegressor, which has no spectral bias whatsoever, and still plateaus at 0.0510 with median mode-R^2 of -0.014 beyond mode 24. This argument must be made in the text, in one paragraph, with those numbers. It is close to free and it removes the most likely referee objection to the mechanism.

The project cannot use the word 'operator' as freely as it does. Under Bartolucci et al.'s ReNO criterion (arXiv:2305.19913), a model trained and evaluated at one frozen 128x128 encoding is learning a discretisation, not an operator. Either add a resolution-generalisation test (train 128x128, evaluate at 256x256 and at the native 512x256) or restate the L5 conclusion as being about fixed-grid surrogates. The test is cheap, the fields are already stored at full resolution, and the outcome is interesting either way.

The L1 verdict and learning_curve.log contradict each other, and the literature sides with learning_curve.log. Kovachki–Lanthaler–Mhaskar show that structured PDE solution operators have algebraic, not exponential, sample complexity — so a plateau observed at 48 training materials is not evidence of an intrinsic data limit, and 1.82x improvement from 12 to 48 materials with no saturation is exactly the algebraic behaviour their theory predicts. The paper must resolve this internally before a referee does: the honest statement is that L1 eliminated 'more data' on the CONDITION axis while the MATERIAL axis is unsaturated.

The two-wave warp needs to be re-framed from an ad-hoc trick into a contribution with two lineages: registration-based model order reduction (Taddei 2019; arXiv:2501.01299) and nonlinear-reconstruction operator learning (shift-DeepONet, in Lanthaler et al. ICLR 2023). Framed that way it is a physically-derived two-shift generalisation of shift-DeepONet whose shifts come from the Type V isotherm's two-wave structure — a genuinely publishable methodological contribution. Framed as it is now, it reads as a heuristic and it is exposed to arXiv:2605.06203 (May 2026) on priority.

The Damköhler sampling defect (open item 6: sampled Da 155–3885, median 626, informative regime Da ~1–50) is not merely a coverage issue, it may be causally upstream of the headline. Near local equilibrium the LDF rate barely influences the field, so k_LDF is weakly identifiable by construction — which is both why L6's identification failed (R^2 = -0.61) and, plausibly, why the parameters do not determine modes 2+. Re-sampling into Da ~1–50 is therefore the experiment that could either strengthen the mechanism enormously or reveal that the entire coefficient wall is an artefact of the sampling design. Do it before scaling to 240 materials.

On competitor architectures, the honest prediction is that most of them hit the same wall and two of them might not. Anything whose decoder is a linear combination of a learned basis — DeepONet, PCA-Net, DeepOKAN, GNOT, Latent Neural Operator, Transolver, FactFormer — is subject to the same argument and, given our HGB result in the optimal basis, will plateau. The two credible threats are (i) architectures with a genuinely nonlinear reconstruction that can represent a moving front at fixed latent dimension — FNO, CNO, NOMAD, shift-DeepONet and the ACT block — and (ii) the Laplace Neural Operator, whose pole–residue parameterisation of a transient step response is structurally close to the front-time variables our own warp analysis identifies as load-bearing. Test those five; cite the rest.
risks_to_our_claims: PRIORITY / SCOOP. Heinlein & Taraz (arXiv:2602.21910, Feb 2026, rev. Aug 2026) already report the branch-dominates-error result, the saturation in internal dimension, the POD-trunk substitution, and the per-mode spectral bias. A referee can reject on novelty in one line unless we cite it, differentiate on the parametric-input / material-extrapolation / physical-mechanism / warp-invariance axes, and say so up front.

DESIGNED TO FAIL. L5 tested only DeepONet and DeepOKAN — both linear-reconstruction. Lanthaler, Molinaro, Hadorn & Mishra (ICLR 2023) prove precisely this class is deficient for advection/discontinuity problems and that FNO and shift-DeepONet escape. A referee will say we eliminated 'operator learning' after testing only the family theory says cannot work, especially since fno_model_adsorption.py is sitting unused in the repository.

WEAK BASELINE. l5_fill2.log shows lr=3e-3 — outside the original grid — gives DeepONet ~0.0275 mean at p=128 versus the published 0.0296, and 0.0254 on the best seed. Our own logs prove the sweep did not bracket the optimum. McGreivy & Hakim (Nature Mach. Intell. 2024) makes this a named, citable failure mode, and it applies with double force to a paper whose thesis is that the method fails. The same applies to DeepOKAN's 10/45 training collapses, which a KAN advocate will attribute to optimisation, not architecture.

NOT AN OPERATOR. Everything is trained and evaluated at one frozen 128x128 encoding. Bartolucci et al. (ReNO, NeurIPS 2023) gives a referee a principled basis to say the study is about fixed-grid regression, not operator learning, and therefore that its negative conclusion does not transfer.

CONTRADICTION WITH THEORY, AT FACE VALUE. 'The n-width is not what binds' reads as a direct contradiction of the ICLR 2023 linear-reconstruction lower bounds for exactly our PDE class. It is reconcilable (approximation-theoretic worst case with optimal coefficients vs finite-sample achievable error) but only if we write the reconciliation ourselves. Retraction A17's language — 'the prediction built on it was wrong' — makes this worse than it needs to be.

INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY ON DATA. L1 says 'more data is eliminated'; learning_curve.log says 1.82x improvement from 12 to 48 training materials with no saturation. Kovachki–Lanthaler–Mhaskar (arXiv:2405.15992) supplies the theory that says the unsaturated curve is the expected behaviour. A careful referee reading both will conclude the ladder's rungs are not independent and that L1's verdict was reached on the wrong axis.

UNEXCLUDED ALTERNATIVE MECHANISM. Spectral bias in the branch MLP predicts the identical flat-in-p signature. Our HGB result excludes it, but the paper never says so, so the objection currently stands unanswered.

SAMPLING DESIGN UNDERCUTS THE PHYSICS. Da 155–3885 with median 626 is near local equilibrium. An adsorption referee will observe that k_LDF barely affects the solution in that regime, that L6's identifiability failure is therefore near-tautological, and that the whole parametric family is easier and less informative than claimed. This one objection can be used to discount L6, the coefficient-wall mechanism, and the practical relevance simultaneously.

MISSING BORING BASELINE. No U-Net, no CNN, no modern-recipe FNO anywhere in the ladder. Given Gupta & Brandstetter (TMLR 2023) and DeepFDM (arXiv:2507.21269), a referee can reasonably suspect a well-tuned U-Net or a differentiable coarse-grid solver would beat every arm in the study, which would recast the entire ladder.

UNCITED PRIOR ART ON THE WARP. Registration-based ROM (Taddei arXiv:1911.06598; arXiv:2501.01299; Greif & Urban on n-width decay for wave problems) has done transport-map registration since 2019, and Adaptive Coordinate Transforms for Neural Operators (arXiv:2605.06203, May 2026) learns the transform inside the operator. Presenting the two-wave warp without either lineage invites a prior-art rejection from a ROM referee.

EXTERNAL VALIDITY. Every conclusion comes from one 1-D PDE family on one dataset. Shikhman (arXiv:2601.11428, TMLR) explicitly demonstrates that failure patterns depend jointly on architecture and PDE family, and used five families and 750 models to say so. Generalised claims about operator learning from a single family will be cut.

UNADDRESSED MODERN COMPETITORS. Transolver, CNO, F-FNO, Poseidon/DPOT and PDE-Refiner are all named baselines a 2026 referee expects. Absent even a table row and a sentence of justification each, the review will read as 'the comparison set is three years out of date'.

concrete_actions.action: Add at least one genuine nonlinear-reconstruction operator to L5 — FNO first (fno_model_adsorption.py already exists), then CNO — at matched ~200k parameters, matched 8000 steps, and the widened learning-rate grid, swept over the same p where the notion applies. Report them in the same table as DeepONet/DeepOKAN.
concrete_actions.rationale: Lanthaler, Molinaro, Hadorn & Mishra (ICLR 2023, arXiv:2210.01074) prove that linear-reconstruction methods (DeepONet, PCA-Net) have lower bounds on advection-dominated and discontinuous PDEs while FNO and shift-DeepONet provably escape them. L5 currently tests only families=['deeponet','deepokan'], i.e. only the class the theory says must fail, on a problem whose defining feature is a self-sharpening cooperative shock. Without this the rung is not a falsification test, and one referee sentence ends the paper. If FNO/CNO also plateau, the claim becomes dramatically stronger and directly extends the ICLR 2023 theory into the finite-sample regime.

concrete_actions.action: Re-run the entire L5 p-sweep (both families, all five p, three seeds) with a learning-rate grid that demonstrably brackets the optimum on both sides — at minimum {3e-4, 1e-3, 3e-3, 1e-2} — and report the per-p tuning envelope, not a single best number. Update RESULTS.md and 03_LADDER_PROTOCOL.md, and log the protocol amendment honestly rather than silently.
concrete_actions.rationale: l5_fill2.log shows lr=3e-3, above the top of the original grid, yields DeepONet ~0.0275 mean and 0.0254 best-seed at p=128 versus the recorded 0.0296 — our own logs prove the published sweep did not bracket the baseline's optimum. McGreivy & Hakim (Nature Machine Intelligence 6:1256–1269, 2024) turned 'weak baselines' into a named, citable rejection reason covering 79% of the ML-for-PDE literature. A paper claiming the strong method fails is held to the highest tuning standard in the field, and this is the one defect that is both certain to be found and trivially fatal.

concrete_actions.action: Rewrite the L5 framing around Heinlein & Taraz (arXiv:2602.21910): cite them prominently, state that we independently reproduce the branch-dominance and dimension-saturation result, and relocate the novelty claim to (a) parametric descriptor input rather than function input, (b) material extrapolation, (c) the measured physical cause via k_LDF unidentifiability, (d) the invariance of the plateau under registration. Also run their two cheap ablations — shared vs stacked branch, and branch width vs mode coupling.
concrete_actions.rationale: They published the same experiment and the same conclusion in February 2026, revised August 2026, using a POD trunk on KdV and Burgers, including the per-mode spectral bias. Claiming discovery of the coefficient bottleneck is now indefensible; claiming independent confirmation in a materially different regime with a physical mechanism is both defensible and more interesting. Their finding that a shared branch generalises better on small modes than a stacked one is a concrete, hours-scale ablation that might actually improve our numbers.

concrete_actions.action: Fix the Damköhler sampling before any dataset scale-up: regenerate a parametric slice covering Da ~1–50 (the kinetically-controlled regime) alongside the existing Da 155–3885 near-equilibrium band, and re-run l5_bottleneck.py, the L6 identification, and the warp analysis on it. Abandon or postpone the incomplete 240-material data/parametric_scale run until this is settled.
concrete_actions.rationale: Open item 6 already flags the coverage defect, but its consequences are deeper than coverage. Near local equilibrium the LDF rate has little influence on the solution, so k_LDF is weakly identifiable by construction — which makes L6's R^2 = -0.61 nearly tautological and plausibly manufactures the very coefficient wall that is the paper's headline. This is the experiment that either establishes the mechanism as physics or reveals it as a sampling artefact, and it must be run before 4080 more simulations are generated in the wrong regime. It also fixes the adsorption community's strongest single objection.

concrete_actions.action: Promote the warped-frame plateau to the paper's central result: in the two-wave frame, oracle-warp error is 0.0205/0.0203/0.0203/0.0205/0.0203 at p=8..128 — flat across a 16x change in basis size, at a level 2.5x below the unwarped plateau. State the general claim: registration moves the height of the coefficient wall but not its existence; the wall is invariant to the representation.
concrete_actions.rationale: This is the strongest and most general finding in the repository, it is currently only in comoving2.log and absent from RESULTS.md, and it is precisely what Heinlein & Taraz do not have. It also cleanly separates the two obstructions in Lanthaler's PCA-Net language (arXiv:2303.16317): registration attacks obstruction (i), eigenvalue decay, and leaves obstruction (ii), coefficient complexity, untouched. Elevating it converts the paper from 'we reproduce a known bottleneck' into 'the bottleneck is representation-invariant', which is a genuinely new claim.

concrete_actions.action: Re-frame the two-wave warp as a physically-derived two-shift generalisation of shift-DeepONet and as registration-based model order reduction, citing Lanthaler et al. (ICLR 2023), Taddei (arXiv:1911.06598), the cross-correlation registration paper (arXiv:2501.01299), Greif & Urban on n-width decay for wave problems, and Adaptive Coordinate Transforms for Neural Operators (arXiv:2605.06203). Then implement it end-to-end — warp parameters learned jointly with the shape coefficients through a differentiable resampling layer, as in the ACT block — rather than predicted post-hoc by an HGB.
concrete_actions.rationale: Two separate risks close at once. Prior-art: registration ROM has done this since 2019 and ACT did the learned-transform version in May 2026; an uncited contribution here invites rejection from a ROM referee. Performance: warp_predict.log shows oracle warp 0.0233 vs predicted warp 0.0508 and the alpha-sweep shows the loss is entirely warp-prediction error (alpha=0.25 already gives 0.0269), so 2.17x is sitting on the table and end-to-end joint learning of the transform is exactly the published mechanism for capturing it. A predicted-warp result of 0.0508 that only ties the 0.0510 fixed frame is not publishable as a method; 0.025–0.030 would be.

concrete_actions.action: Add a resolution-generalisation experiment: train the best arms at 128x128, evaluate at 256x256 and at the native 512x256 without retraining, and report the degradation. If the arms are not resolution-robust, restate the L5 conclusion as being about fixed-grid surrogates rather than about operator learning.
concrete_actions.rationale: Bartolucci et al.'s ReNO framework (arXiv:2305.19913, NeurIPS 2023) makes continuous-discrete equivalence the criterion for calling something an operator, and everything in the ladder runs at one frozen encoding. A referee can currently deny the paper the word 'operator' entirely. The full-resolution fields are already stored, so this is a few hours of evaluation code with no new training, and it also cleanly discriminates FNO/CNO (designed to be resolution-robust) from DeepONet in our setting.

concrete_actions.action: Add a modern well-tuned U-Net baseline (Gupta & Brandstetter's pdearena recipe) and a NOMAD-style nonlinear-decoder DeepONet at matched parameter count. NOMAD is a one-layer change to PI_DeepONet in operator_models.py: replace sum_k b_k(params) t_k(z,t) with D([b(params), z, t]).
concrete_actions.rationale: The U-Net closes the 'boring baseline beats fancy operators' hole that Gupta & Brandstetter and DeepFDM (arXiv:2507.21269) have made a standard referee move; without it, a suspicion that a plain CNN beats everything in the ladder goes unanswered. NOMAD (Seidman et al., NeurIPS 2022) is the cheapest possible direct test of our central claim, since it removes exactly the linearity that our argument depends on while changing nothing else — if NOMAD is flat in p, the claim is close to bulletproof; if it is not, we need to know before a referee tells us.

concrete_actions.action: Write an explicit one-paragraph exclusion of the spectral-bias explanation, using our own numbers: l5_bottleneck.py predicts coefficients with HistGradientBoostingRegressor, a tree ensemble with no spectral bias, and it plateaus at 0.0515/0.0509/0.0510 for p=8/32/128 with mode-1 R^2 = 0.946 collapsing to a median of -0.014 beyond mode 24 on held-out materials. Therefore the wall is not an artefact of MLP frequency preference.
concrete_actions.rationale: The 2025–2026 spectral-bias literature (arXiv:2503.13695, arXiv:2504.10932, arXiv:2602.19265, and Heinlein & Taraz's own branch spectral bias) supplies a complete alternative explanation for the identical flat-in-p signature. It is the most likely mechanistic objection a reviewer will raise, we already have the data that refutes it, and the paper simply never makes the argument. Highest ratio of risk removed to effort spent in this entire list.

concrete_actions.action: Resolve the L1-versus-learning_curve contradiction explicitly in RESULTS.md and the manuscript: restate L1's verdict as scoped to the operating-condition axis, report the material-axis learning curve (0.0929 -> 0.0509, 1.82x, 12 -> 48 materials, unsaturated), and cite Kovachki, Lanthaler & Mhaskar (arXiv:2405.15992) for why algebraic sample complexity is the expected behaviour for a structured PDE solution operator.
concrete_actions.rationale: Two of the project's own artefacts disagree, and a careful referee will find it. Volunteering the resolution turns a credibility problem into evidence of rigour, and the data-complexity theory gives a principled reason why the two axes should behave differently rather than leaving it as an unexplained inconsistency. It also determines whether the 240-material scale-up is worth finishing — under this framing it is, but only after the Damköhler fix.

concrete_actions.action: Add the Laplace Neural Operator (Cao, Goswami & Karniadakis, Nature Machine Intelligence 2024; arXiv:2303.10528; public code at qianyingcao/Laplace-Neural-Operator) as a targeted competitor arm, swept in the same protocol.
concrete_actions.rationale: Of every architecture surveyed, this is the one whose inductive bias most closely matches our physics and therefore the one most likely to actually break the flat-in-p result. A breakthrough curve is a non-periodic transient step response of a 1-D system with a Danckwerts inlet; LNO's pole-residue parameterisation was built exactly for transient responses and reports better extrapolation than other operators. Its latent variables (pole locations) are close to the front-time variables our own warp analysis identifies as the load-bearing degrees of freedom. Finding out it wins after review would be far worse than finding out now.

concrete_actions.action: Re-implement the Wavelet Neural Operator honestly (Tripura & Chakraborty, CMAME 404:115783, 2023; arXiv:2205.02191; reference code at TapasTripura/WNO) and report it, explicitly noting in the text that an earlier mislabelled dilated-CNN arm was withdrawn as retraction A9.
concrete_actions.rationale: Turns a retraction into a contribution, and the architecture is well matched to the problem: wavelets localise in both space and frequency, which is what a sharp self-sharpening shock riding on a broad spreading Henry wave demands. Reference code exists, so the cost is small. Reporting the retraction alongside the corrected result is also the strongest possible signal of the integrity the falsification-ladder framing depends on.

concrete_actions.action: Add a transformer-operator arm — Transolver (arXiv:2402.02366, ICML 2024 spotlight) as first choice, GNOT (arXiv:2302.14376) as the alternative if heterogeneous parameter encoding is the point being tested — and add a single related-work paragraph that names Transolver, GNOT, FactFormer, Latent Neural Operator, F-FNO/geo-FNO/U-FNO and CNO, stating for each why it is or is not included.
concrete_actions.rationale: These are the named 2024–2026 baselines a referee will list; a table row plus a justified sentence each is the minimum defence. Transolver is the strongest choice on merit and on mechanism: its Physics-Attention slices the domain by physical state, and our field is exactly two coherent states separated by two moving interfaces, so it is the transformer with a real chance of absorbing the warp implicitly. geo-FNO and U-FNO can be excluded in one sentence (fixed 1-D domain, single-phase) rather than run.

concrete_actions.action: Run a bounded PDE-foundation-model probe: fine-tune Poseidon (arXiv:2405.19101) and, if time allows, DPOT (arXiv:2403.03542) on the existing 691-run training split, and report the transfer result honestly whatever it is.
concrete_actions.rationale: Given learning_curve.log's unsaturated material axis, the obvious 2026 referee question is 'why generate 4080 more simulations instead of using a pretrained PDE foundation model?'. The honest expectation is weak transfer — both are pretrained on 2-D fluids, our target is a 1-D coupled advection-reaction-energy column — but a measured negative transfer result is a legitimate finding, costs GPU-days rather than the stalled scale-up run, and pre-empts the question entirely.

concrete_actions.action: Add a PDE-Refiner-style refinement stage (Lippe et al., NeurIPS 2023, arXiv:2308.05732) on top of the best one-shot arm: predict the field, then iteratively add and remove noise of decreasing variance with the same network, 3 refinement steps.
concrete_actions.rationale: Their diagnosis — that models capture dominant modes and drop non-dominant frequency content — is the temporal-rollout analogue of our per-mode R^2 collapse. This is the cleanest test of whether our plateau is an information limit or a loss-weighting/optimisation artefact: an MSE loss on the field weights modes by singular value, which is exactly the mechanism Heinlein & Taraz identify as causing the branch to neglect small modes. If refinement moves 0.051, our 'the coefficient map is unlearnable' framing is too strong and needs softening to 'unlearnable under a variance-weighted loss'.

concrete_actions.action: Add an in-context / few-shot arm framed as the practical recommendation: instead of predicting a new material's field from 11 static descriptors, condition on 1-3 observed breakthrough curves for that material (an ICON-style data prompt, arXiv:2304.07993 / PNAS 2023). Report how many observed curves are needed to break the 0.051 plateau.
concrete_actions.rationale: This directly attacks the measured cause rather than the symptom. Our wall is that descriptors do not determine modes 2+ on an unseen material, and L6 independently found k_LDF unrecoverable from observable descriptors (R^2 = -0.61) — both are statements that the information is absent from the input, not that the model is inadequate. A few observed curves supply exactly the missing information. It gives the paper a constructive ending, converts a purely negative ladder into an actionable engineering result, and its 'how many curves' answer is a genuinely useful number for the AWH community.

concrete_actions.action: Adopt the F-FNO training recipe (arXiv:2111.13802) — Gaussian-noise augmentation, cosine learning-rate decay, improved residual connections — uniformly across every learned arm, and state in the methods that all arms share it.
concrete_actions.rationale: F-FNO's reported 83%/31%/57% error reductions come substantially from the training recipe rather than the layer alone. Applying one modern recipe uniformly is the cheapest structural defence against the weak-baseline critique, because it makes 'every arm got the same modern treatment' a checkable claim rather than an assertion, and it removes the possibility that any single arm's failure is attributable to a stale optimisation setup.

concrete_actions.action: Align the distribution-shift protocol with Shikhman (arXiv:2601.11428, TMLR) — report novel-material and novel-condition splits under their shift taxonomy — and add an explicit external-validity paragraph stating that all conclusions come from one PDE family on one dataset.
concrete_actions.rationale: Their study used five PDE families and 750 trained models specifically to show that failure patterns depend jointly on architecture and PDE family. Any unqualified generalisation from our single 1-D adsorption column will be cut by a referee. Pre-emptively scoping the claims and mapping onto an existing published taxonomy costs almost nothing and makes the paper read as field-aware rather than isolated.

concrete_actions.action: Add a differentiable coarse-grid version of solver_fd.py as a baseline arm, in the spirit of DeepFDM (arXiv:2507.21269): embed the existing finite-difference discretisation in a differentiable module at low N_z and learn the residual closure.
concrete_actions.rationale: DeepFDM reports one to two orders of magnitude lower error than FNO, U-Net and ResNet with 5-50x fewer parameters on advection, diffusion, advection-diffusion, reaction-diffusion and Burgers — the exact PDE class we are in. We already own a verified solver (L0, four closed-form checks) so the differentiable version is a modest engineering job. This would also give the speed claim (open item 5) an honest, self-consistent reference point, and if it beats every learned arm that is a far stronger and more publishable conclusion than L7's current 3.2x over Klinkenberg.

concrete_actions.action: Restate retraction A17 in Lanthaler's two-obstruction language: the Kolmogorov n-width is a floor, and a floor being inactive is not a refutation of it; obstruction (i), PCA eigenvalue decay, is inactive at our data budget while obstruction (ii), coefficient complexity, is total.
concrete_actions.rationale: A17 currently reads as the project having refuted its own pre-registered prediction, which invites a referee to conclude the pre-registration was ill-posed. The PCA-Net bounds paper (arXiv:2303.16317) supplies exactly the right vocabulary to say the same thing as a precise positive result about which of two known obstructions binds. This is a rewrite, not an experiment, and it converts a self-inflicted wound into the paper's theoretical anchor.

concrete_actions.action: Document the 988-run parametric dataset to The Well's conventions (arXiv:2412.00568, NeurIPS 2024 Datasets & Benchmarks) — splits, metadata schema, loaders, licence — and consider releasing it as a standalone benchmark contribution.
concrete_actions.rationale: The Well is now the reference standard for PDE-surrogate dataset releases, and chemical-engineering transport is not represented in it.
