Matching its conventions costs little and materially raises perceived rigour for a paper whose primary asset is a verified data generator; releasing the dataset gives the work a second, independent axis of impact and citation that does not depend on the negative results surviving review.

lens: Physics-informed learning: when a PDE residual loss actually helps, when it hurts, and the hard-constraint alternative — audited against the 2020-2026 literature and against the referee attack that McGreivy & Hakim's survey licenses.
state_of_the_art:
As of 2026 the field has largely abandoned the 2019-era default that "adding the PDE residual is free improvement." Three independent diagnoses converged: (i) the differential operators in the residual make the loss ill-conditioned and change the optimisation landscape (Krishnapriyan et al. NeurIPS 2021; Rathore et al. ICML 2024, who tie ill-conditioned operators directly to ill-conditioned PINN loss and show Adam+L-BFGS and a second-order NysNewton-CG step are needed); (ii) the loss terms have wildly imbalanced back-propagated gradient magnitudes and different NTK convergence rates (Wang, Teng & Perdikaris arXiv:2001.04536 / SISC 2021, reporting 50-100x accuracy gains purely from learning-rate annealing on the weights; Wang, Yu & Perdikaris arXiv:2007.14527); (iii) the terms' gradients actively conflict in direction, not just magnitude (ConFIG, Liu/Chu/Thuerey, ICLR 2025). A 2026 addition reframes the classic failure modes as plain overfitting to the collocation points (Andersen & Matsubara, arXiv:2605.30910). The practical consequence is that "physics as a loss" is now understood as a multi-task optimisation problem requiring an adaptive weighting scheme (gradient-norm annealing, NTK weights, self-adaptive per-point weights, causal/temporal weighting) — and results reported without one are considered uninterpretable.

Running in parallel, the hard-constraint line has become the preferred answer wherever the constraint admits an exact parameterisation. The lineage is Lagaris, Likas & Fotiadis (1998), which already wrote u = A(x) + B(x)N(x) so that BC/IC hold by construction with no penalty term at all; then distance-function / R-function ansatz (Sukumar & Srivastava, CMAME 2022), output transforms in DeepXDE (Lu et al., SIAM Rev. 2021), augmented-Lagrangian hPINN (Lu et al., SISC 2021), structural BC enforcement in neural operators (BOON, ICLR 2023, 2-20x L2 improvement), differentiable constrained-optimisation layers scaled with mixture-of-experts (Chalapathi, Du & Krishnapriyan, ICLR 2024), exact conservation by Bayesian update (ProbConserv, ICML 2023), and general input-dependent hard constraints with universal-approximation guarantees (HardNet, arXiv:2410.10807). The 2026 empirical literature is remarkably consistent with our L4b: hard-constrained variants beat soft-penalty variants and, importantly, "remove the need for loss-weight tuning" (Chung et al., arXiv:2604.08453), with error gaps as large as 1.42% vs 39.3% on stiff DAEs (Le et al., arXiv:2604.19930). Theory agrees on the boundary of the effect: Doumèche, Bach, Biau & Boyer (COLT 2024) show the PDE regulariser accelerates convergence only to the extent the physical prior carries information the data does not.

Two counterweights matter and are not yet common knowledge. First, hard constraints are not free: Xie et al. (arXiv:2512.23295) show hard-constraint ansatz functions act as spectral filters on the NTK and can induce "spectral collapse" — exact boundary satisfaction with stalled interior convergence. Second, the current 2026 consensus in hard/soft hybrid papers (Nguyen et al., arXiv:2606.23359) is that hard BCs plus soft residuals beats all-soft; nobody in the literature I could find reports the specific interaction we measured, namely that the residual becomes actively harmful once the same physical fact is imposed architecturally. That interaction is our novel contribution in this lens.

Finally, the meta-literature that governs how any of this will be received: Grossmann et al. (IMA J. Appl. Math. 89:143-174, 2024) find PINNs do not beat FEM on solution time and accuracy on standard PDEs, and McGreivy & Hakim (Nat. Mach. Intell. 6:1256-1269, 2024) find 79% (60/76) of ML-for-PDE papers claiming to beat standard numerics compare against a weak baseline, with widespread outcome-reporting and publication bias. Adsorption-specific PINN work exists but is thin, single-column and single-material (ChemEngineering 6:21, 2022; Processes 13:2824, 2025; An. Acad. Bras. Cienc. 2024; Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 2022) — a parametric, cross-material falsification study is genuinely new for this application.

papers.citation: Aditi S. Krishnapriyan, Amir Gholami, Shandian Zhe, Robert M. Kirby, Michael W. Mahoney, "Characterizing possible failure modes in physics-informed neural networks", NeurIPS 2021
papers.what_it_shows: PINNs with adequate capacity fail on convection/reaction/diffusion problems for optimisation reasons, not approximation reasons. Explicitly: soft regularisation using PDE differential operators "can introduce a number of subtle problems, including making the problem more ill-conditioned". Curriculum regularisation and sequence-to-sequence training recover 1-2 orders of magnitude.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the canonical citation for our L4b claim that the residual term is not a free addition. It supplies the mechanism (ill-conditioning of the soft term) for why bounded+physics (0.0194) is worse than bounded+data-only (0.0124). It also warns us: our physics arm may be under-optimised rather than intrinsically worse, which is the referee attack we must pre-empt.

papers.citation: Nick McGreivy, Ammar Hakim, "Weak baselines and reporting biases lead to overoptimism in machine learning for fluid-related partial differential equations", Nature Machine Intelligence 6(10):1256-1269
papers.what_it_shows: Systematic review: 79% (60/76) of articles claiming ML beats standard numerical methods for fluid-related PDEs compare to a weak baseline. Outcome-reporting bias and publication bias are widespread, so negative results are under-reported. Calls for cultural and structural change.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the exact referee attack the whole ladder is designed to survive, and it should be cited in the first page of the introduction, not buried. Our L7 (three closed-form classical controls, scored like-for-like on the exit curve), our pre-registered protocol, our 17 Part-A retractions and 23 Part-B pre-contamination defects, and our refusal to compare across rungs are all direct answers to this paper. Citing it converts our biggest vulnerability into the paper's stated contribution. It also indicts us in one place: the 11.5x hard-bounds claim is measured against a t*softplus head our own protocol calls not the right IC — that is a weak baseline by their definition.

papers.citation: Tamara G. Grossmann, Urszula Julia Komorowska, Jonas Latz, Carola-Bibiane Schönlieb, "Can physics-informed neural networks beat the finite element method?", IMA Journal of Applied Mathematics 89(1):143-174
papers.what_it_shows: Systematic head-to-head of PINNs vs FEM on Poisson (1D/2D/3D), Allen-Cahn (1D) and semilinear Schrödinger (1D/2D). PINNs did not outperform FEM in solution time or accuracy, though they were sometimes faster to evaluate once trained.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Sets the honest ceiling for our speed claim (open item 5: our own solver is 4.2 s/condition at N_z=2000). The defensible framing is not "our surrogate beats the solver" but "accuracy at a fixed inference budget, and amortised across many materials" — the one regime where Grossmann et al. concede an advantage. Also gives a precedent for publishing a rigorous negative comparison in a good venue, which is structurally what our ladder is.

papers.citation: Sifan Wang, Yujun Teng, Paris Perdikaris, "Understanding and mitigating gradient pathologies in physics-informed neural networks" (SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 43:A3055-A3081, 2021)
papers.what_it_shows: Identifies numerical stiffness producing unbalanced back-propagated gradients across loss terms as a fundamental PINN failure mode; proposes a learning-rate annealing scheme using gradient statistics to equilibrate terms, plus a resistant architecture. Reports 50-100x accuracy improvement across problems.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the scheme our L4/L4b physics weight uses (gradient-norm balancing), so it is already load-bearing in the protocol and must be cited precisely. Its own headline — 50-100x from the weighting alone — is also the strongest argument a referee has against us: it establishes that PINN results are dominated by the weighting scheme, so a single weighting choice cannot support a claim that physics-as-a-loss hurts.

papers.citation: Sifan Wang, Xinling Yu, Paris Perdikaris, "When and why PINNs fail to train: A neural tangent kernel perspective" (published in Journal of Computational Physics)
papers.what_it_shows: Derives the NTK of a PINN, shows it converges to a deterministic kernel in the infinite-width limit, and that the different loss components converge at drastically different rates. Proposes an adaptive weighting using NTK eigenvalues.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The second weighting scheme a referee will demand we try. Our L4b physics arm was balanced by gradient norm only; NTK weighting is the standard alternative and diagnoses a different pathology (rate mismatch, not magnitude mismatch). Running it is cheap insurance for the 'physics hurts' claim.

papers.citation: Pratik Rathore, Weimu Lei, Zachary Frangella, Lu Lu, Madeleine Udell, "Challenges in Training PINNs: A Loss Landscape Perspective", ICML 2024 (PMLR v235)
papers.what_it_shows: Connects ill-conditioned differential operators to ill-conditioning of the PINN loss landscape; shows Adam+L-BFGS beats either alone and introduces NysNewton-CG, a second-order optimiser that substantially improves PINN accuracy.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Our L4/L4b arms almost certainly used first-order Adam only. A referee can say the physics arm lost because it was optimised with the wrong optimiser for an ill-conditioned objective. Either run an Adam+L-BFGS finishing phase on the physics arms, or state explicitly that both arms used identical optimisers and that the claim is conditional on first-order training.

papers.citation: Nigel T. Andersen, Takashi Matsubara, "PINNs Failure Modes are Overfitting"
papers.what_it_shows: Argues the classic PINN failure modes are overfitting: the residual is minimised at the collocation points but not between them, shown by direct residual visualisation. Regularisation makes the failure modes disappear; extended double backpropagation over all residuals matches benchmarks with up to 23x fewer collocation points.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Directly relevant to our L4 observation that the residual bought consistency and not accuracy (seed spread 0.0074->0.0024 on c, 0.0125->0.0010 on T). It supplies a 2026 framing for that: the residual behaves as a regulariser with a collocation-overfitting failure mode. It also gives a concrete diagnostic we can run cheaply — plot the trained model's residual off the collocation grid, for training vs novel materials.

papers.citation: I. E. Lagaris, A. Likas, D. I. Fotiadis, "Artificial Neural Networks for Solving Ordinary and Partial Differential Equations", IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks
papers.what_it_shows: Constructs the trial solution as a fixed part that satisfies BC/IC exactly with no adjustable parameters plus a network term that cannot affect them. Boundary conditions hold by construction; the network is trained only on the differential equation.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The canonical ancestor of our bounded sigmoid head. We must cite it so that the paper never appears to claim hard output constraints as novel — the family is 28 years old. What is ours is the measured interaction (the penalty becomes counter-productive once the bound exists) and the axis-specificity, not the technique.

papers.citation: N. Sukumar, Ankit Srivastava, "Exact imposition of boundary conditions with distance functions in physics-informed deep neural networks", Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering 389:114333
papers.what_it_shows: Uses R-functions and generalized barycentric coordinates to build approximate distance functions to the domain boundary, then transfinite interpolation to satisfy inhomogeneous Dirichlet, Neumann and Robin conditions exactly. Notes a trade-off: second and higher derivatives of the ADF are unstable at boundary joins.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The modern reference for exact BC imposition and the natural citation next to our Danckwerts inlet condition. It also flags the failure mode of hard constraints (derivative pathology of the ansatz), which is the balanced caveat our L4b discussion currently lacks.

papers.citation: Lu Lu, Raphael Pestourie, Wenjie Yao, Zhicheng Wang, Francesc Verdugo, Steven G. Johnson, "Physics-informed neural networks with hard constraints for inverse design" (hPINN), SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 43(6):B1105-B1132
papers.what_it_shows: Replaces the all-soft PINN formulation with hard constraints imposed by the penalty method and the augmented Lagrangian method. Achieves objectives comparable to adjoint-based PDE-constrained optimisation, with simpler and smoother designs where the solution is non-unique.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Establishes in a top numerical-analysis venue that the soft/hard distinction is the axis that matters, and that the augmented Lagrangian is the principled middle ground between a fixed penalty weight and an exact ansatz. If we want a third arm for L4b beyond fixed-weight and gradient-norm balancing, augmented Lagrangian is the one with the strongest pedigree.

papers.citation: Lu Lu, Xuhui Meng, Zhiping Mao, George Em Karniadakis, "DeepXDE: A deep learning library for solving differential equations", SIAM Review 63(1), DOI 10.1137/19M1274067
papers.what_it_shows: The reference PINN library and review. Its 'output transform' facility is the standard practical route to hard-imposed BC/IC in PINN practice.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Establishes that output-transform hard constraints are standard tooling, not an exotic choice. Cite it alongside Lagaris so our sigmoid head is positioned as an instance of accepted practice applied to a maximum principle, rather than as a contribution.

papers.citation: Nithin Chalapathi, Yiheng Du, Aditi S. Krishnapriyan, "Scaling physics-informed hard constraints with mixture-of-experts", ICLR 2024
papers.what_it_shows: Embeds differentiable PDE-constrained optimisation as network layers (hard constraints) rather than loss penalties, and makes it scalable by decomposing the domain across experts. Reports greater accuracy on challenging nonlinear dynamics, improved training stability, and significantly less computation in training and inference.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: From the same group as the failure-modes paper, and it is the strongest recent statement of the position our L4b result supports: constraints belong in the architecture, not the loss. It also shows the community accepts hard-constraint work as a contribution when it is paired with a scalability story — useful framing if we ever extend beyond bounds to a hard mass-balance layer.

papers.citation: Derek Hansen, Danielle C. Maddix, Shima Alizadeh, Gaurav Gupta, Michael W. Mahoney, "Learning Physical Models that Can Respect Conservation Laws" (ProbConserv), ICML 2023, PMLR 202:12469-12510
papers.what_it_shows: Enforces the integral form of a conservation law by a Bayesian update on top of a generic SciML architecture. Tested on the Generalized Porous Medium Equation family spanning parabolic to hyperbolic (shock-forming) regimes; outperforms approaches that do not guarantee volume conservation specifically on the harder, shock-forming variants, while retaining uncertainty quantification.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Our system is exactly the hard case they identify: a self-sharpening cooperative shock in the second wave. It is the template for the next hard constraint we could impose after bounds — a column mass balance — and it makes the argument that hard structure matters more, not less, as the solution becomes shock-dominated. Also a natural companion citation for our two-wave frontier.

papers.citation: Nadim Saad, Gaurav Gupta, Shima Alizadeh, Danielle C. Maddix, "Guiding continuous operator learning through Physics-based boundary constraints" (BOON), ICLR 2023
papers.what_it_shows: Modifies the operator kernel structurally so that Dirichlet, Neumann and periodic BCs are satisfied by the neural operator; reports 2x-20x improvement in relative L2 error over the unconstrained operator across multiple PDEs.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Extends the hard-constraint result from PINNs to neural operators, which is the L5 function class in our ladder. A referee may ask why L5's DeepONet was not hard-constrained; BOON is both the answer to what that would look like and a possible cheap addition (bounded output head on the DeepONet trunk-branch product). Given that L4b measured 11.5x from bounding alone, a bounded DeepONet is an obvious untested arm.

papers.citation: "HardNet: Hard-Constrained Neural Networks with Universal Approximation Guarantees" (author list not independently verified)
papers.what_it_shows: Appends a differentiable closed-form projection layer so that affine and convex input-dependent constraints hold by construction, while retaining universal approximation. Motivated explicitly by the fact that soft penalties "offer no guarantee of constraint satisfaction, especially on inputs far from the training distribution".
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the single cleanest theoretical statement of the asymmetry our L4b measured: a soft penalty is a training-time object that is not evaluated at inference, whereas a hard constraint is active at test time and therefore on novel materials. That sentence should be the thesis of our L4b discussion. Confidence is lowered because I did not fetch the abstract page directly and have not verified the author list.

papers.citation: Seung Whan Chung, Stephen T. Castonguay, Sumanta Roy, Michael S. Penwarden, Yucheng Fu, Pratanu Roy, "Hard-constrained Physics-informed Neural Networks for Interface Problems"
papers.what_it_shows: Embeds interface physics in the solution representation, decoupling interface enforcement from PDE residual minimisation. Finds soft penalties give imperfect enforcement and degraded near-interface accuracy, while hard constraints "consistently improve interface fidelity and remove the need for loss-weight tuning"; windowing reaches O(1e-9), buffer O(1e-5).
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: A 2026 independent corroboration of our headline: hard constraint beats soft penalty AND eliminates the weight-tuning problem. That second half is the part of our result we currently under-sell — our fixed-weight cautionary arm (w_pde=1 sending the residual to 9.87 against a data loss of 0.130) is precisely the pathology this paper says the hard constraint deletes.

papers.citation: Huy Hoang Le, Haoguang Wang, Christian Moya, Marcos Netto, Guang Lin, "Physics-Guided Dimension Reduction for Simulation-Free Operator Learning of Stiff Differential-Algebraic Systems"
papers.what_it_shows: On a grid-forming inverter with stiffness ratio ~4712, an extended-Newton implicit (hard-constraint) layer reaches 1.42% error against 39.3% for the penalty (soft) method and 57.0% for standard Newton; validated further on the Robertson DAE at stiffness ~1e5. States soft-constraint methods leave algebraic residuals that stiffness amplifies into errors.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Our system is stiff and near local equilibrium (measured Damköhler 122-3312, median 626), which is structurally the same regime: the LDF driving force is a small difference of two large numbers. This is the strongest quantitative external precedent that soft constraints degrade specifically under stiffness — a mechanism we can claim in our discussion rather than merely asserting our null.

papers.citation: Yuchen Xie, Honghang Chi, Haopeng Quan, Yahui Wang, Wei Wang, Yu Ma, "Spectral Analysis of Hard-Constraint PINNs: The Spatial Modulation Mechanism of Boundary Functions"
papers.what_it_shows: Builds an NTK framework showing the hard-constraint boundary function B in u = A + B·N acts as a spectral filter on the network's kernel. Widely used boundary functions can induce 'spectral collapse' — optimisation stagnation with exact boundary satisfaction. Effective rank of the residual kernel predicts this better than condition number.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The essential counterweight and the honest caveat our L4b section is missing. It means 'hard bounds are the best single intervention' is not a general law — a badly chosen ansatz can stall training. It also gives a concrete self-check we should run: our sigmoid head saturates by construction, so we should report the fraction of predictions in the saturated tails and confirm gradients are not being killed at c ≈ c_in after breakthrough (where the true field is flat at 1, exactly the sigmoid saturation region).

papers.citation: Duc Tien Nguyen, Trinh Minh Tuan, Nguyen Duc Manh, Vu Linh Nguyen, Dinh Gia Ninh, "Adaptive Hard-Soft Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Robust Boundary-Constrained PDE Solving" (HSPINN)
papers.what_it_shows: Enforces Dirichlet and periodic BCs exactly by construction while keeping PDE residuals, fluxes and ICs as soft terms with an inverse-share softmax adaptive weighting. Reports improved convergence and robustness over all-soft PINNs on Poisson, Burgers and pure convection. The hybrid, not the removal of soft terms, is the recommended configuration.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the position our result partly contradicts, and that is why our finding is publishable. The 2026 consensus is hard-BC + soft-residual; we measured that once the bound is hard, the residual costs accuracy (bounded 0.0124 -> 0.0194 on the time axis, CI [-0.0112,-0.0020]). We should cite this paper as the prevailing view and state our result as a scoped exception, with the mechanism (our supervised data already covers the full (z,t) domain per training material, so the residual adds no information).

papers.citation: Sebastian Barschkis, "Exact and soft boundary conditions in Physics-Informed Neural Networks for the Variable Coefficient Poisson equation"
papers.what_it_shows: A dedicated study of how soft loss-based and exact distance-function-based BC imposition differ within PINNs, with reference Keras/TensorFlow implementations.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: A direct precedent for the experimental design of our L4b 2x2 (imposition method x arm). I fetched the abstract but it does not report the outcome numbers, so we should read the full PDF before citing it for a directional claim — cite it for the design, not for a result.

papers.citation: Nathan Doumèche, Francis Bach, Gérard Biau, Claire Boyer, "Physics-informed machine learning as a kernel method", COLT 2024, PMLR 247:1399-1450
papers.what_it_shows: For linear differential priors, empirical risk plus a PDE-inconsistency penalty is exactly a kernel regression. The regularised estimator converges at least at the Sobolev minimax rate, and faster rates are achieved depending on the physical error — i.e. the acceleration is conditional on the PDE prior carrying information about the problem.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The theoretical backbone for our mechanism claim. Our L4 discussion argues the residual is largely redundant because the training data samples the full (z,t) domain for every training material. This paper says exactly that in the language a theory-literate referee will want: the PDE penalty is a regulariser whose benefit scales with the information it adds beyond the data. It converts our hand-wave into a cited principle — and it predicts our missing experiment (sparsify the data and the physics arm should win).

papers.citation: Qiang Liu, Mengyu Chu, Nils Thuerey, "ConFIG: Towards Conflict-free Training of Physics Informed Neural Networks", ICLR 2025
papers.what_it_shows: Loss terms for IC/BC and the PDE frequently yield conflicting update directions, not merely imbalanced magnitudes. ConFIG constructs an update with positive dot product against every loss-specific gradient, with convergence proofs, and outperforms baselines on PINN and multi-task benchmarks.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Our protocol's own account of the bounded+physics degradation is that the penalty 'diverts gradient budget from fitting the data' (in-window error 0.0145 -> 0.0248). That is a gradient-conflict statement, and ConFIG is the method that removes it. If ConFIG-updated bounded+physics is still worse than bounded data-only, the L4b interaction claim is essentially referee-proof; if it closes the gap, we have learned that the effect was an optimisation artefact and must say so.

papers.citation: Sifan Wang, Shyam Sankaran, Paris Perdikaris, "Respecting causality is all you need for training physics-informed neural networks", Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering 421
papers.what_it_shows: Standard PINN losses violate the spatio-temporal causal structure of the problem; reweighting the residual so earlier times are fitted first is presented as a key source of accuracy gains on evolution equations.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Our L4 design already includes a pi_gradnorm_causal arm, so this citation is required. More importantly, our TIME axis is the one axis where physics-as-a-loss demonstrably helped (0.1425 -> 0.0639), and causal weighting is the state-of-the-art tool for exactly that axis. If we want a fair 'best physics-informed arm', causal weighting on the time axis is it.

papers.citation: Sifan Wang, Shyam Sankaran, Hanwen Wang, Paris Perdikaris, "An Expert's Guide to Training Physics-informed Neural Networks"
papers.what_it_shows: Consolidates best practice (non-dimensionalisation, Fourier features, random weight factorisation, curriculum/causal training, adaptive weighting) into a reproducible recipe with full ablations, plus a set of hard benchmarks.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the yardstick a referee will hold our PINN arms against. Our arms are matched to each other, which is the right internal design, but if the absolute performance sits far below this recipe, the reviewer will discount the whole rung. We should either adopt one or two of its cheapest ingredients (Fourier features, non-dimensionalisation — we already non-dimensionalise) or state explicitly that the comparison is internal and that both arms share the same non-expert baseline.

papers.citation: L. D. McClenny, U. M. Braga-Neto, "Self-adaptive physics-informed neural networks", Journal of Computational Physics 474:111722
papers.what_it_shows: Fully trainable per-collocation-point adaptation weights acting as a soft multiplicative attention mask, so the network autonomously up-weights hard regions of the solution.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The third standard weighting scheme (after gradient-norm annealing and NTK). Given that our two-wave physics has one sharp self-sharpening shock, per-point adaptive weights are the scheme most likely to rescue the physics arm, and therefore the one a referee is most likely to name. Worth one run.

papers.citation: Lukas Fesser, Luca D'Amico-Wong, Richard Qiu, "Understanding and Mitigating Extrapolation Failures in Physics-Informed Neural Networks"
papers.what_it_shows: PINN extrapolation failure is not caused by high-frequency content but by shifts in the support of the Fourier spectrum over time, quantified by a Weighted Wasserstein-Fourier distance. Without significant spectral shift, PINN predictions stay close to the true solution even in extrapolation; transfer learning cuts extrapolation error up to 82%.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Directly attacks the interpretation of our TIME-axis result. Our two-wave breakthrough involves a slow shock arriving at late times, i.e. a genuine spectral shift, so this paper predicts temporal extrapolation should be hard here — consistent with unbounded data-only 0.1425. But it also means our attribution of the improvement to 'the residual supervises where data is absent' is one hypothesis among two. Computing the WWF between our in-window and extrapolation windows is a cheap, novel diagnostic that would let us separate them.

papers.citation: Sifan Wang, Hanwen Wang, Paris Perdikaris, "Learning the solution operator of parametric partial differential equations with physics-informed DeepONets"
papers.what_it_shows: Adds PDE residuals as soft penalties to DeepONet, enabling training with no paired input-output data beyond IC/BC, reporting up to three orders of magnitude speedup over a conventional solver and improved accuracy plus reduced data requirements versus vanilla DeepONet.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The direct precedent for combining our L4 (physics loss) and L5 (operator) rungs, which we never did. A referee will ask why. Two honest answers: the L4b result predicts the residual would not help once outputs are bounded, and the L5 bottleneck is the params->coefficient map, which no residual addresses. Better still, run it: a bounded, physics-informed DeepONet is a one-experiment closure of an obvious gap, and its predicted outcome (no gain) is itself a ladder result.

papers.citation: Jan G. Rittig, Alexander Mitsos, "Thermodynamics-Consistent Graph Neural Networks"
papers.what_it_shows: Predicts molar excess Gibbs free energy and recovers activity coefficients through exact thermodynamic relations via automatic differentiation, so that thermodynamic consistency holds by architecture and 'additional loss terms are unnecessary'.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: A chemical-engineering-native instance of exactly our claim, from a group that had previously used the soft-penalty version (Gibbs-Duhem-informed NNs, arXiv:2306.07937). The pair is a clean before/after in our own community: penalty first, structure second, penalty then dropped. That is a much more persuasive citation for a chemical engineering journal audience than a fluid-dynamics PINN paper.

papers.citation: Jan G. Rittig, Kobi C. Felton, Alexei A. Lapkin, Alexander Mitsos, "Gibbs-Duhem-Informed Neural Networks for Binary Activity Coefficient Prediction"
papers.what_it_shows: Imposes the Gibbs-Duhem relation explicitly as a loss penalty rather than embedding a thermodynamic model; increases thermodynamic consistency, with results sensitive to the activation function.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The soft-penalty half of the pair above. Cite both together to make the hard-vs-soft argument in the vocabulary of chemical engineering rather than of ML.

papers.citation: Reese E. Jones, Jan N. Fuhg, "A hierarchy of thermodynamics learning frameworks for inelastic constitutive modeling"
papers.what_it_shows: Compares internal-variable, generalized-standard-material and metriplectic frameworks inside a unified neural potential architecture to isolate how the amount of imposed thermodynamic structure affects learnability and generalization across elastoplastic, viscoelastic and rate-dependent data.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the same experimental philosophy as our ladder — vary the amount of imposed structure, hold everything else matched, measure generalization — published in 2026. It is the closest methodological sibling to our paper and shows the design is currently valued. Worth reading in full to see whether they also find a non-monotone relationship between structure and generalization, which is what our L6 (separate arm worse than joint) and L4b (penalty harmful once bound present) jointly suggest.

papers.citation: Quercus Hernandez, Alberto Badias, David Gonzalez, Francisco Chinesta, Elias Cueto, "Deep learning of thermodynamics-aware reduced-order models from data"
papers.what_it_shows: Couples sparse autoencoders with structure-preserving (metriplectic/GENERIC) networks so that energy conservation and the entropy inequality hold by construction in a learned reduced-order model.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The reduced-order-model instance of by-construction physics, which is the function class of our POD + regressor and two-wave warp work rather than of our PINN. If we ever want the two-wave frontier to carry a physics guarantee, this is the template — and it is a more natural fit than a PINN residual, which our own L4b says buys nothing once structure exists.

papers.citation: Davor Runje, Sharath M. Shankaranarayana, "Constrained Monotonic Neural Networks"
papers.what_it_shows: Shows weight-sign constraints alone fail with unsaturated activations, then constructs additional activation functions that recover universal approximation of continuous monotone functions under the constraint.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Relevant to the live frontier rather than to L4b. Our two-wave warp requires predicting two smooth monotone 1-D front curves t_lo(z), t_hi(z), and the entire 2.17x remaining headroom sits in the error of that prediction. Monotonicity in z (and t_hi > t_lo) is a hard constraint we could impose by construction on the warp predictor instead of hoping HGB learns it. That is a direct application of this lens's central lesson to the part of the project with the most upside.

papers.citation: "Towards Surrogate Modeling for Adsorption Processes Using Physics-Informed Neural Networks", Processes 13(9):2824
papers.what_it_shows: Applies hybrid PINNs to adsorption process surrogate modeling, incorporating governing equations as constraints alongside labeled data with the stated aim of reducing data requirements and improving generalization under data scarcity.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The closest domain-adjacent PINN work and a required related-work citation, since a chemical engineering referee will know it. I could not retrieve the full text (the publisher blocks fetch and the PDF did not parse), so the specific quantitative claims are unverified and must be read before citing for any number.

papers.citation: "A First Approach towards Adsorption-Oriented Physics-Informed Neural Networks: Monoclonal Antibody Adsorption Performance on an Ion-Exchange Column as a Case Study", ChemEngineering 6(2):21
papers.what_it_shows: Early application of PINNs to column adsorption (ion-exchange chromatography, monoclonal antibody), single-system case study.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Establishes the domain baseline our work must be positioned against: existing adsorption PINN work is single-column, single-material and does not test transfer to unseen materials. That is exactly the gap our parametric 60-material design fills, and stating it plainly is a legitimate novelty claim that survives the A12-style scrutiny that killed the DeepOKAN claim.

implications: Our L4b result is on the right side of the 2026 consensus, and that is both good and dangerous. Good: five independent 2024-2026 papers (Chung et al. arXiv:2604.08453, Le et al. arXiv:2604.19930, Chalapathi et al. ICLR 2024, BOON ICLR 2023, HardNet arXiv:2410.10807) find hard constraints beat soft penalties, and Chung et al. specifically report that hard constraints 'remove the need for loss-weight tuning', which is our fixed-weight cautionary arm in one sentence. Dangerous: 'hard beats soft' is therefore not a contribution. Our contribution must be narrowed to the two things nobody else reports — the INTERACTION (the penalty becomes counter-productive, not merely redundant, once the same fact is imposed architecturally) and the AXIS-SPECIFICITY (helps on time, never on materials, with a stated mechanism).

The strongest, most transferable sentence available to us is an asymmetry the literature states but does not measure: a soft penalty is evaluated only at training-time collocation points on training materials and is not evaluated at inference at all, whereas a hard constraint is active at test time on every input including out-of-distribution ones. HardNet motivates itself in exactly those words. Our material-axis null is the direct empirical consequence of that asymmetry, and framing it that way turns an under-powered null into a structural prediction that a reader can carry to other systems.

The theory says our redundancy mechanism is correct. Doumèche, Bach, Biau & Boyer (COLT 2024) prove the PDE regulariser accelerates rates only to the extent the physical prior carries information the data does not. Our L4 training set samples the full (z,t) domain for every training material, so by that theorem the residual should buy approximately nothing — which is what we measured. This upgrades our explanation from plausible narrative to cited principle, and it makes a sharp prediction we have not tested: sparsify the supervised samples and the physics arm's advantage must reappear.

We have an unexploited positive result. L4 found the residual tightened seed-to-seed spread by 3-12x in every field (c 0.0074->0.0024, T 0.0125->0.0010) with no change in mean. The 2026 reading of this (Andersen & Matsubara, arXiv:2605.30910: PINN failures are collocation overfitting; Doumèche et al.: the residual is a ridge-like regulariser) is that a physics loss is a variance-reduction device, not an accuracy device. 'No change in mean, 3-12x tighter across seeds' is a publishable, quotable, and currently under-argued finding. It deserves its own subsection with a citation-supported interpretation, not a note inside a null.

There is a weak baseline inside our own ladder, and McGreivy & Hakim license a referee to say so. The 11.5x hard-bounds gain is measured against a t*softplus head that our own protocol describes as 'not the right IC anyway' because it forces c <= t everywhere including at the inlet. That baseline is both unbounded AND carrying a wrong IC, so the 11.5x confounds two defects. Any headline number stated against it is exactly the failure mode we are citing McGreivy & Hakim to criticise.

Our physics-hurts claim rests on a single weighting scheme from 2020. Gradient-norm balancing (Wang, Teng & Perdikaris) is defensible and was chosen for good documented reasons, but that same paper reports 50-100x swings from the weighting choice alone, and three subsequent standard alternatives exist (NTK weighting, self-adaptive per-point weights, ConFIG conflict-free updates), plus a second-order optimiser story (Rathore et al.). A referee does not need to believe physics helps here; they only need to argue we did not give it its best shot. This is the single largest attack surface in this lens.

Hard constraints have a known failure mode we have not checked. Xie et al. (arXiv:2512.23295) show hard-constraint ansatz functions act as spectral filters and can cause 'spectral collapse': exact constraint satisfaction with stalled interior convergence. Our sigmoid head saturates by construction precisely where the true field is flat at c_in after breakthrough — which is most of the late-time domain. We should verify empirically that gradients are not dying there before claiming hard bounds are unambiguously the best single intervention.

The lens's lesson applies most profitably not to L4b but to the live frontier. The two-wave warp's entire remaining 2.17x headroom lives in predicting two monotone 1-D front curves with t_hi(z) > t_lo(z) everywhere. Those are hard constraints with off-the-shelf architectural enforcement (constrained monotonic networks, arXiv:2205.11775; positivity via output transform on the span t_hi - t_lo). Our own L4b result says impose structure architecturally rather than penalise it — applying our own finding to our own frontier is a coherence argument the paper can make explicitly.

Two obvious cross-rung gaps exist that referees will name: nobody bounded the DeepONet outputs in L5 (BOON shows structural BC enforcement gives 2x-20x for neural operators; our own L4b measured 11.5x from bounding), and nobody combined the physics loss with the operator (physics-informed DeepONet, arXiv:2103.10974, is the standard method). Both are single experiments. Both have predicted outcomes from our own measurements — bounding should help, the residual should not — and either outcome is a ladder result.

Domain positioning is genuinely favourable and currently under-claimed. Existing adsorption PINN work is single-column, single-material, and does not test transfer to unseen materials. A parametric, 60-material, pre-registered falsification study of surrogate transfer in fixed-bed adsorption has no direct precedent that I found. That claim is narrow, checkable and survives the kind of scrutiny that retired the DeepOKAN novelty claim in A12.
risks_to_our_claims: WEIGHTING ARTEFACT (highest risk). A referee cites Wang/Teng/Perdikaris's own 50-100x weighting sensitivity, plus NTK weighting, self-adaptive weights, causal weighting and ConFIG, and argues that 'bounded + physics is worse' (0.0124 -> 0.0194) reflects one 2020-era balancing rule rather than a property of physics-as-a-loss. Our protocol already concedes the general form of this argument when it explains why a fixed w_pde manufactures a false negative. We currently have no defence beyond 'we used a published scheme'.

OPTIMISER ARTEFACT. Rathore et al. (ICML 2024) show the PINN objective is ill-conditioned by construction and that Adam alone is the wrong optimiser; Adam+L-BFGS and second-order methods materially change results. If both arms used Adam only, the physics arm was disadvantaged relative to what the literature considers correct practice, and the harm claim becomes conditional on first-order training.

WEAK-BASELINE SELF-INDICTMENT. The 11.5x hard-bounds figure compares against t*softplus, a head that is simultaneously unbounded and carries an IC our own text calls wrong. Under McGreivy & Hakim's criteria this is a weak baseline, and it appears in a paper that cites McGreivy & Hakim approvingly. A hostile referee will quote our own protocol against us.

EFFECT SIZE VS SEED COUNT. The interaction rests on 0.0124 -> 0.0194 with CI [-0.0112,-0.0020] at 3 seeds and one architecture, one budget, one lr. The CI barely excludes zero and the absolute difference is 0.007 nRMSE. Our own calibration work established the cluster bootstrap over-rejects at these cluster counts; a referee can reasonably ask whether the one POSITIVE finding in this rung deserves more scrutiny than the nulls, exactly as A13 required in L1.

MECHANISM ASSERTED, NOT MEASURED. The claim 'nothing in material A's residual constrains material B' is an argument, not a measurement. There is no reported number for the trained model's PDE residual on held-out materials versus training materials. Until that exists, the material-axis null has an alternative explanation (the physics arm was simply undertrained on the data term, consistent with train c degrading 0.0092 -> 0.0197).

COMPETING EXPLANATION FOR THE TIME-AXIS GAIN. Fesser et al. attribute PINN extrapolation failure to Fourier spectral shift, not to the absence of a residual. Our 0.1425 -> 0.0639 improvement may be generic regularisation of a badly parameterised head rather than physics per se. We have no non-physics regulariser control (matched-strength weight decay, matched-cost data augmentation) at the same budget, so 'the residual helps because it supervises where data is absent' is not isolated from 'any regulariser would have helped this head'.

NOVELTY EROSION. Hard output constraints date to Lagaris et al. (1998); distance-function BC imposition to Sukumar & Srivastava (2022); output transforms are a documented DeepXDE feature; and at least three 2026 papers report hard-beats-soft with the loss-weight-tuning benefit. If the paper presents 'hard bounds beat soft penalties' as a finding rather than as a confirmation, it invites an A12-class retraction (DeepOKAN) for the same reason: the technique is published.

CONTRADICTS PREVAILING 2026 PRACTICE WITHOUT ENOUGH EVIDENCE. Hard/soft hybrids (Nguyen et al., arXiv:2606.23359; Chung et al., arXiv:2604.08453) keep soft residuals alongside hard BCs and report that combination as best. Our claim that the residual becomes harmful is the minority position. Presenting it as a general lesson rather than a scoped result conditioned on dense full-domain supervision will read as overreach.

UNCHECKED HARD-CONSTRAINT PATHOLOGY. Xie et al. (arXiv:2512.23295) show hard-constraint ansatz choices can cause spectral collapse. Our sigmoid saturates exactly in the post-breakthrough plateau that dominates the late-time domain. If a referee suspects gradient starvation there, the 11.5x becomes 'we replaced one pathology with another that happened to be less severe on this metric'.

SCOPE OF THE BOUND ITSELF. 0 <= c <= c_in is the maximum principle for the transported species, but the T* head uses 1 + dT_max*tanh with a generous dT_max chosen so it 'never binds on a physical solution'. That is a NaN guard, not a physical bound. If the paper says 'hard bounds encode the maximum principle', a referee who reads output_head.py will note that only two of three fields are actually bounded by physics.

CROSS-RUNG COMPARABILITY. L4b's best material-axis number (0.0538) is not comparable to L1-L3 (0.0485) and the protocol correctly says so. But readers will compare them anyway, and the abstract must not place them adjacent. Any reviewer who notices the caveat only in a footnote will treat it as a hedge rather than as design.

concrete_actions.action: Run a supervised-data-sparsity sweep on the material axis: bounded data-only vs bounded physics-informed at 100%, 25%, 5% and 1% of the (z,t) supervised points per training material, matched steps, 5+ seeds. Report the crossing point where the physics arm overtakes.
concrete_actions.rationale: This is the experiment the whole L4/L4b mechanism claim implies and that Doumeche et al. (COLT 2024) theoretically predict: the PDE regulariser buys only what the data does not already supply. Right now we assert redundancy and measure a null. If the physics arm wins at 5% or 1% data, the null becomes a quantitative statement with a threshold ('the residual is worth nothing above X% domain coverage and Y-fold below it'), which is far more publishable and far harder to attack than 'no difference detected'. If it does NOT win even at 1%, that is a stronger and more surprising result still, and it kills the redundancy explanation honestly.

concrete_actions.action: Add a third and fourth output head to the L4b design: plain softplus with NO t* envelope, and a clamp or scaled-tanh bound. Recompute the boundedness effect against the strongest unbounded baseline, and report the 11.5x only if it survives.
concrete_actions.rationale: The current 11.5x is measured against t*softplus, which our own protocol describes as carrying the wrong IC. That confounds boundedness with a bad initial-condition envelope, and it is a weak baseline under McGreivy & Hakim's own criteria in a paper that cites them. Separating the two is cheap, and whichever way it lands the number becomes defensible. This is the single most likely place a referee will catch us being the thing we criticise.

concrete_actions.action: Referee-proof the 'physics hurts once bounded' claim by re-running the bounded 2x2 cell under (a) a w_pde sweep spanning at least four decades including w->0, (b) NTK-based weighting (Wang/Yu/Perdikaris), (c) self-adaptive per-point weights (McClenny & Braga-Neto), and (d) ConFIG conflict-free updates. State the claim as 'worse at every weighting scheme tested' or withdraw it.
concrete_actions.rationale: This is the highest-probability referee attack and it is fully anticipatable. The literature establishes that PINN outcomes are dominated by the weighting scheme (50-100x in Wang/Teng/Perdikaris alone), so a harm claim resting on one scheme is not defensible. The w_pde sweep alone is decisive and cheap: if the bounded physics arm's error is monotone increasing in w_pde with the minimum at w_pde = 0, the claim is essentially unassailable and can be stated in one figure. Note the ladder has already been bitten twice by not bracketing a hyperparameter grid (L5's learning rate, where l5_fill2 later found 3e-3 above the grid top beats the recorded optimum) - do not make it three.

concrete_actions.action: Convert the mechanism argument into a measurement: evaluate the trained physics-informed model's PDE residual magnitude on held-out-material collocation points versus training-material collocation points, and report the ratio. Do the same off-grid (between collocation points) for training materials.
concrete_actions.rationale: Our claim that 'nothing in material A's residual constrains material B' is currently an argument. A residual that is small on training materials and large on novel materials measures the failure to transfer directly, in one number, from checkpoints we already have. The off-grid version tests Andersen & Matsubara's 2026 collocation-overfitting hypothesis on our own model. Both are hours of work on existing checkpoints and both turn narrative into evidence, which is the standard the rest of this project holds itself to.

concrete_actions.action: Rewrite the L4b framing around the train-time/test-time asymmetry: a soft penalty is a training-time object evaluated only at collocation points on training materials and not evaluated at inference; a hard constraint is active at test time on every input. Cite HardNet (arXiv:2410.10807), Lagaris et al. (1998), Sukumar & Srivastava (2022), DeepXDE, hPINN, BOON and Chalapathi et al. so the sigmoid head is positioned as an instance of a known family, and claim ONLY the interaction and the axis-specificity as new.
concrete_actions.rationale: Hard-vs-soft is 28 years old and has five recent confirmations; presenting it as a finding invites an A12-class retraction for exactly the reason DeepOKAN's novelty claim was narrowed. The asymmetry sentence, by contrast, is the crispest transferable statement in the whole rung, it explains both the time-axis gain and the material-axis null with one mechanism, and it is supported rather than pre-empted by the literature.

concrete_actions.action: Cite McGreivy & Hakim (Nat. Mach. Intell. 2024) and Grossmann et al. (IMA J. Appl. Math. 2024) prominently in the introduction, and add a short 'design response' paragraph mapping each of their criticisms to a specific feature of this study: pre-registered frozen protocol, RETRACTIONS.md, calibrated alpha, matched-budget assertions, L7 classical controls, no cross-rung comparisons, honest wall-clock reference.
concrete_actions.rationale: These two papers are the frame every referee in this area now reads through, and 79%/60-of-76 is a number that will be in the reviewer's head. Our project is unusually well-defended against them - the retraction register and the pre-registration are genuinely rare - but only if we say so explicitly. Left unstated, the same reviewer applies the criticism to us by default; stated, it becomes the paper's methodological contribution and the reason the negative results are worth publishing.

concrete_actions.action: Promote the variance result to a named finding: 'a PDE residual buys consistency, not accuracy' (seed sd on c 0.0074 -> 0.0024, on T 0.0125 -> 0.0010 at unchanged mean), and support it with the regulariser reading from Doumeche et al. (COLT 2024) and the overfitting reading from Andersen & Matsubara (arXiv:2605.30910). Increase L4b to 8-10 seeds so the variance claim itself is well estimated.
concrete_actions.rationale: This is a real, quotable, under-argued positive result sitting inside a null, and it is the kind of thing that reviewers remember. It also fixes a second problem simultaneously: 3 seeds is thin for the interaction claim given our own calibration work showing the cluster bootstrap over-rejects, and A13 established that positive verdicts need more scrutiny than nulls. More seeds serves both the variance finding and the interaction claim at once.

concrete_actions.action: Run a non-physics regulariser control on the TIME axis at matched cost: unbounded head + weight decay (or dropout, or Sobolev/derivative smoothing) tuned to the same effective strength, against unbounded + physics. Also compute the Weighted Wasserstein-Fourier distance (Fesser et al.) between the in-window and extrapolation windows.
concrete_actions.rationale: Without this, 'physics helps on temporal extrapolation (0.1425 -> 0.0639)' cannot be distinguished from 'any regulariser rescues a badly parameterised head'. Fesser et al. offer the competing explanation (spectral shift) and a metric to test it. Our two-wave structure means the extrapolation window genuinely contains a spectral shift, so this is not a hypothetical. If physics beats the generic regulariser, the claim is properly isolated; if it does not, we learn something important about what the residual was actually doing.

concrete_actions.action: Add a causally-weighted physics arm on the TIME axis (Wang, Sankaran & Perdikaris, CMAME 421, 2024) and report it as the best-effort physics-informed configuration for the axis where physics demonstrably helps.
concrete_actions.rationale: The time axis is the one place physics wins, and causal weighting is the state-of-the-art tool for exactly that axis. Reporting the strongest physics arm where physics helps, alongside the finding that a hard bound still beats it (0.0124 vs 0.0639), makes the hard-constraint conclusion far stronger than beating a mediocre physics arm would. It also removes the 'you did not try causal training' objection, which is nearly free since pi_gradnorm_causal already exists in the L4 arm list.

concrete_actions.action: Audit the sigmoid head for spectral collapse (Xie et al., arXiv:2512.23295): report the fraction of predictions in the saturated tails, the gradient magnitude through the head in the post-breakthrough plateau, and confirm training is not stalling there. Also correct the manuscript language so that only c and q are described as physically bounded; the T* tanh is a NaN guard with a generous dT_max, not a physical bound.
concrete_actions.rationale: Our sigmoid saturates precisely where the true field is flat at c_in, which is a large fraction of the late-time domain - the exact configuration Xie et al. identify as risky. A one-paragraph audit converts a potential referee objection into a demonstrated non-issue. The T* wording fix is pure honesty maintenance: anyone reading output_head.py will see that dT_max is chosen so it 'never binds on a physical solution', which is the opposite of a binding physical bound, and this project's credibility rests on that kind of precision.

concrete_actions.action: Apply the lens's own lesson to the live frontier: impose monotonicity of t_lo(z) and t_hi(z) in z, and positivity of the span t_hi - t_lo, architecturally in the warp predictor (constrained monotonic networks, arXiv:2205.11775, or a cumulative-softplus parameterisation), rather than leaving HGB to learn them.
concrete_actions.rationale: This is where the project has the most value at stake: the two-wave frame reaches oracle 0.0203-0.0233 versus predicted-warp 0.0508, so 2.17x is sitting entirely in front-location error, and the fronts obey hard structural constraints we are not enforcing. Our own L4b finding says impose structure architecturally rather than penalise it. Doing so here is both the highest-expected-value experiment in the project and a coherence argument the paper can make explicitly - the physics-informed rung producing a method used by the frontier.

concrete_actions.action: Close two named cross-rung gaps with single experiments: (a) add a bounded output head to the L5 DeepONet (BOON precedent, plus our own 11.5x from bounding), and (b) run one physics-informed DeepONet arm (arXiv:2103.10974). Pre-register the predictions - bounding should help, the residual should not - before running.
concrete_actions.rationale: Both are obvious to any referee and both are currently absent, which reads as a gap rather than a choice. Both have predictions derivable from our own measurements, so either outcome is informative and pre-registering the prediction is exactly the ladder's methodology. (b) is also the standard method in the operator-learning literature; not having run it is the kind of omission that invites 'the authors did not try the obvious combination'.

concrete_actions.action: Add the adsorption-domain PINN related-work paragraph (ChemEngineering 6:21 2022; Processes 13:2824 2025; the sulfate-ion PINN with particle filter, An. Acad. Bras. Cienc. 2024; Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 2022 cyclic adsorption) and state the positioning claim precisely: existing work is single-column and single-material; no prior study tests surrogate transfer to unseen adsorbents. Read each in full before citing any number from it.
concrete_actions.rationale: A chemical engineering referee will know this literature and its absence signals unfamiliarity with the field. The positioning claim is narrow, checkable and true as far as my searches go, which makes it the kind of novelty claim that survives - unlike the DeepOKAN claim that A12 had to retract. The read-before-citing caveat is not optional: I could not retrieve full text for the two MDPI papers, so their quantitative claims are unverified.

lens: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN, PIKAN, DeepOKAN, Chebyshev-KAN, RBF-KAN): published claims vs. this project's measured L3/L5 reality, and what a referee will demand before accepting "KAN loses".

papers.citation: Ziming Liu, Yixuan Wang, Sachin Vaidya, Fabian Ruehle, James Halverson, Marin Soljačić, Thomas Y. Hou, Max Tegmark. "KAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks." arXiv, 30 Apr 2024 (v5 9 Feb 2025); accepted ICLR 2025.
papers.what_it_shows: The founding paper. Learnable univariate B-spline activations on edges instead of fixed activations on nodes; claims KANs beat MLPs in accuracy and interpretability, that 'much smaller KANs achieve comparable or better accuracy than much larger MLPs in data fitting and PDE solving', and that KANs have faster neural scaling laws. Introduces grid extension (progressive grid refinement) as a core mechanism.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the claim L3 is refuting. Note two things the paper says that we do NOT currently honour: (a) the canonical basis is the 3rd-order B-spline, which we never tested — we tested only Gaussian-RBF and Chebyshev; (b) grid extension is presented as part of the method, not an optional extra, and we never ran it. A referee will say our 'KAN' is not the paper's KAN.

papers.citation: Khemraj Shukla, Juan Diego Toscano, Zhicheng Wang, Zongren Zou, George Em Karniadakis. "A comprehensive and FAIR comparison between MLP and KAN representations for differential equations and operator networks." Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering 431:117290 (2024). arXiv 5 Jun 2024.
papers.what_it_shows: Fetched abstract: original B-spline KANs 'underperformed in both accuracy and efficiency'; 'modified versions based on low-order orthogonal polynomials have comparable performance to PINNs and DeepONet although they still lack robustness'; explicitly warns implementations 'may diverge for different random seeds or higher order orthogonal polynomials'. Uses loss-landscape visualisation and information-bottleneck analysis of learning dynamics.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Our strongest prior ally and we already cite it. Two of its specific statements are independently reproduced by our data: (i) higher-order orthogonal polynomials are unstable — our cheby_kan degrees 7/9/11 fail to leave initialisation; (ii) seed divergence — our 10/45 DeepOKAN collapses. But note the ceiling it sets: its verdict on tuned low-order variants is 'comparable', not 'worse'. Our L3 claims something strictly stronger than Shukla et al., so we carry the burden of proof.

papers.citation: Diab W. Abueidda, Panos Pantidis, Mostafa E. Mobasher. "DeepOKAN: Deep operator network based on Kolmogorov Arnold networks for mechanics problems." Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering 436:117699 (2025). arXiv 29 May 2024 (v3 7 Aug 2024).
papers.what_it_shows: Fetched abstract: DeepOKAN replaces branch/trunk MLPs with KANs using Gaussian RBFs rather than B-splines, and reports 'lower training losses and more accurate predictions compared to traditional DeepONets' on 1D sinusoidal waves, 2D orthotropic elasticity and transient Poisson. The abstract reports no optimisation difficulties, no parameter-matched protocol, and no caveats.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the paper our L5 arm is named after and the direct target of retraction A12. Critical asymmetry we should exploit in the manuscript: DeepOKAN's headline evidence is *lower training loss*, whereas our L5 measures *held-out-material* error. Our own audit shows RBF-KAN edges fit training data competitively and generalise worse — so we are not contradicting their measurement, we are showing their measurement does not transfer to the quantity a surrogate is for. Say that explicitly; it converts an apparent contradiction into a contribution.

papers.citation: Runpeng Yu, Weihao Yu, Xinchao Wang. "KAN or MLP: A Fairer Comparison." arXiv, 23 Jul 2024 (v2 17 Aug 2024).
papers.what_it_shows: Controls for BOTH parameter count and FLOPs across ML, CV, audio, NLP and symbolic tasks. Conclusion: 'except for symbolic formula representation tasks, MLP generally outperforms KAN.' Ablation: KAN's symbolic advantage 'mainly stems from its B-spline activation function' — bolting B-splines onto an MLP recovers the gain. Also finds KAN's forgetting in class-incremental continual learning is *more* severe than MLP's, contradicting the original KAN paper.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The canonical 'KAN loses at matched budget' citation and the methodological template we should mirror. Two things we must copy from it: (1) it controls FLOPs as well as parameters — we control parameters only, and our own L5 notes DeepOKAN costs 1.6–2.1x wall-clock per run, so a FLOP-matched comparison would strengthen us at no cost; (2) it runs the decisive ablation (give the MLP the KAN's basis). Our analogue is an MLP with a learnable-basis edge, or simply reporting the g→1 limit.

papers.citation: Pant et al. "MLPs and KANs for data-driven learning in physical problems: A performance comparison." arXiv, April 2025.
papers.what_it_shows: KANs substantially beat MLPs in SHALLOW (single-hidden-layer) configurations on Burgers, 1D Darcy and elastic-plate problems (e.g. 0.39% vs 2.89% on Darcy) but the advantage collapses in DEEP networks (0.07% difference on Burgers); 'simply stacking additional KAN layers does not result in comparable performance improvements'. Out-of-distribution testing: KANs show a 'significantly larger increase in error' than MLPs (3.68% vs 2.17%), i.e. KANs overfit more readily. KANs ~18x slower to train in one case. Notes 'training strategies designed for MLPs may not effectively translate to KAN-based architectures'.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Simultaneously our best mechanistic ally and our most dangerous unaddressed confound. Ally: their OOD result is exactly our novel-material result — richer edges buy in-distribution fit and lose out-of-distribution. Danger: they find KANs WIN at depth 1, and every one of our L3 arms is fixed at depth 3. We have not swept depth at all. A referee who knows this paper will ask for depth 1 and 2 immediately, and it is cheap to run.

papers.citation: Ziyao Li. "Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks are Radial Basis Function Networks." arXiv, 10 May 2024. (FastKAN)
papers.what_it_shows: Shows 3rd-order B-splines in KANs are well approximated by Gaussian RBFs, giving FastKAN. Secondary sources (emergentmind topic page, citing Li 2024 and Coffman et al. arXiv:2502.07176) state FastKAN applies layer normalization before the RBF activation specifically to keep features inside the fixed RBF window, and report ~30x faster forward / ~40x forward+backward vs efficient-KAN on MNIST with no accuracy loss.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the reference implementation our RBF-KAN is a variant of, and we deviate from it in the one place that matters. `run_l3.py:RBFKANBlock` has NO normalization and fixed centres on [-2,2] with h=4/(grids-1); `operator_models.py:PI_DeepOKAN` builds `RBFKANLayer(...)` with `use_layernorm` left at its default False. The literature's stated purpose for that LayerNorm is precisely to prevent the saturation we then measured as defect B22 (gradient norm 1.2e-11 by step 150, bit-identical cross-seed predictions). Our DeepOKAN collapse is therefore confounded with a known, documented, one-line omission.

papers.citation: Sidharth SS, Keerthana A. R., Gokul R., Anas K. P. "Chebyshev Polynomial-Based Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks: An Efficient Architecture for Nonlinear Function Approximation." arXiv, 11 May 2024.
papers.what_it_shows: Introduces Chebyshev-KAN: learnable edge functions parameterised by Chebyshev polynomials, with inputs squashed (tanh) into [-1,1] where the recursion is bounded. Reports gains on digit classification, synthetic function approximation and fractal generation.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Our `ChebyKANBlock` correctly applies tanh, so we are faithful on that point and can say so. But the canonical implementation and most PIKAN follow-ups also use inter-layer normalization and/or a residual base path, neither of which our block has — and our degree-7/9/11 arms never trained (train error pinned at ~0.118 vs 0.058 at degree 3). Author list beyond 'Sidharth SS' is from a search snippet and should be checked against the arXiv listing before it goes in a bibliography.

papers.citation: Spyros Rigas, Fotios Anagnostopoulos, Michalis Papachristou, Georgios Alexandridis. "Training Deep Physics-Informed Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks." arXiv, 27 Oct 2025 (rev. 18 Dec 2025); Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering (2026), doi:10.1016/j.cma.2026.000356 per ScienceDirect listing S0045782526000356.
papers.what_it_shows: Diagnoses WHY deep Chebyshev PIKANs diverge: default cPIKAN initialisation does not preserve activation variance across layers. Fixes: (1) a basis-agnostic Glorot-like variance-preserving initialisation; (2) Residual-Gated Adaptive KANs (RGA KANs), PirateNet-style, for cases where init alone is insufficient. Information-bottleneck analysis shows baseline cPIKANs stagnate in the diffusion phase while RGA KANs traverse all phases. Across nine forward-PDE benchmarks RGA KANs 'consistently outperform parameter-matched cPIKANs and PirateNets — often by several orders of magnitude — while remaining stable in settings where the others diverge'.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the single most dangerous paper for our L3 Chebyshev column. It says, with a mechanism and a parameter-matched fix, that exactly the failure we observed (deep Chebyshev KAN stagnating, never leaving initialisation) is an initialisation defect and is repairable by several orders of magnitude. Our cheby_kan arm at 200k is 6/6 runs stuck at step 0. If we publish that as 'Chebyshev-KAN generalises worse', this paper is the rebuttal, and it is parameter-matched, which removes our usual defence.

papers.citation: Spyros Rigas, Dhruv Verma, Georgios Alexandridis, Yixuan Wang. "Initialization Schemes for Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks: An Empirical Study." arXiv, 3 Sep 2025; accepted ICLR 2026.
papers.what_it_shows: First systematic study of initialisation for spline-based KANs. Compares LeCun-inspired, Glorot-inspired and a tunable power-law family across function fitting, PDE benchmarks, NTK analysis and the Feynman dataset. Glorot-inspired significantly beats the baseline in parameter-rich models; power-law initialisation is strongest overall, across tasks and across architecture sizes.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: We used PyTorch-default-style initialisation everywhere (`randn / sqrt(i*grids)` for RBF coefficients, `randn / sqrt(i*(degree+1))` for Chebyshev) and never swept init. This is now an ICLR-published, KAN-specific hyperparameter with a demonstrated large effect. 'We did not tune initialisation' is not a defensible answer for a paper whose central claim is a negative result about KANs.

papers.citation: Elham Kiyani, Khemraj Shukla, Jorge F. Urbán, Jérôme Darbon, George Em Karniadakis. "Optimizing the Optimizer for Physics-Informed Neural Networks and Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks." arXiv, 22 Jan 2025 (v6 8 Feb 2026).
papers.what_it_shows: Compares Adam against BFGS, L-BFGS with several line searches, Self-Scaled BFGS (SSBFGS) and Self-Scaled Broyden (SSBroyden) for PINNs and KANs. Reports 'orders-of-magnitude accuracy improvements' from SSBFGS/SSBroyden over standard practice, without adaptive weighting or other PINN enhancements.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Every arm in L3, L4 and L5 is Adam + cosine annealing, and only two learning rates. From the same group that wrote our main supporting citation. A referee will ask why a negative result about KANs was established with the optimiser that paper says leaves orders of magnitude on the table. This is also the honest counter to our own worry: the fix is to run the strongest KAN under a quasi-Newton finish and show the ordering survives.

papers.citation: Xianyang Zhang, Huijuan Zhou. "Generalization Bounds and Model Complexity for Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks." arXiv, 10 Oct 2024; ICLR 2025.
papers.what_it_shows: Margin/Rademacher generalisation bounds for KANs with activations that are linear combinations of basis functions or lie in a low-rank RKHS. Fetched abstract: the bound scales with the l1 norm of the coefficient matrices and the Lipschitz constants of the activations, with 'no dependence on combinatorial parameters (e.g., number of nodes) outside of logarithmic factors'; in the low-rank case it scales polynomially with the ranks.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Cuts BOTH ways and we must handle it honestly. It does not license 'more basis functions per edge ⇒ worse generalisation' — complexity enters through coefficient norms and Lipschitz constants, not through the basis count, so richer bases are theoretically free if coefficient norms stay controlled. That means our monotone dose-response in grids/degree is NOT theoretically expected, which makes an optimisation explanation more likely than a statistical one — and our own audit table agrees (RBF train error also rises with grids). It also hands us a real experiment: measure the l1 coefficient norm per arm and show whether it grows with the basis size. If it does, we have a theory-grounded mechanism instead of a stipulated one.

papers.citation: Amir Noorizadegan, Sifan Wang, Leevan Ling, Juan P. Dominguez-Morales. "A Practitioner's Guide to Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks." arXiv, 28 Oct 2025 (latest version 7 May 2026).
papers.what_it_shows: Review organised around basis choice as the central design axis, with a 'Choose-Your-KAN' guide. Fetched content: the optimal basis varies significantly with the PDE; B-splines are the safe default; Chebyshev for smooth high-order approximation; Fourier for periodic/oscillatory targets; Gaussian RBFs for localized/radial structure but requiring careful centre placement; Jacobi for fractional operators. Its Table 1 indicates KANs underperform on NON-SMOOTH targets, implying B-spline KANs are unsuitable for discontinuous or sharp-gradient solutions without modification (finite-basis or ensemble approaches). Reports KANs match or beat MLPs on accuracy/convergence but with up to 10x slower wall clock. States KAN advantages over well-designed MLPs 'depend strongly on the problem setting and architectural choices'.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Gives us the strongest available *physical* framing for the L3 result: our target is a self-sharpening cooperative shock — a non-smooth target — and this review already flags non-smooth targets as where KANs lose. That upgrades our finding from 'KANs lost on our problem' to 'KANs lost on our problem for the reason the review predicts, measured'. It also supplies the exact list of bases a referee will expect us to have tried, and warns that Gaussian RBFs need careful centre placement — which we never tuned (centres fixed on [-2,2] in L3).

papers.citation: Roberto Cavoretto, Alessandra De Rossi, Adeeba Haider, Amir Noorizadegan. "Adaptive RBF-KAN: A Comparative Evaluation of Dynamic Shape Parameters in Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks." arXiv, 20 May 2026.
papers.what_it_shows: Adaptive extension of FastKAN: RBF shape parameters initialised by leave-one-out cross-validation, then refined by gradient descent under a log-space reparameterisation θ=ln(h) to keep positivity. Sensitivity is large: FastKAN's fixed shape parameter (0.5714) gives 4.08e-2 error on a smooth test function where LOOCV initialisation gives 4.07e-3 — a tenfold improvement. Kernel choice matters too (Gaussian / Matérn / Wendland optimal for different targets; 0.456 → 0.062 on a high-frequency function).
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Direct, quantified evidence that the RBF shape parameter alone can move accuracy by 10x — and our L3 RBFKANBlock hard-codes h = 4/(grids-1) as a non-learnable Python float, so h SHRINKS as we increase grids. Our 'monotone in KAN-ness' dose-response is therefore confounded with a monotone narrowing of the kernel. That is a fatal confound for the mechanism claim as currently written, and it is cheap to break: sweep h independently of the grid count.

papers.citation: "Scale-Parameter Selection in Gaussian Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks." arXiv, 2026. (author list not captured in the fetch)
papers.what_it_shows: Identifies a stable operating interval for the Gaussian scale parameter, ε ∈ [1/(G-1), 2/(G-1)] with G centres, proposed as a design rule rather than a universal optimum. States accuracy and stability are 'highly sensitive to the scale parameter ε, which has not been studied systematically', and that the conditioning of the first-layer feature matrix determines reliability — degradation there 'propagates through the entire network'.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Our h equals exactly one grid spacing, i.e. the LOWER edge of their recommended interval — the narrowest, worst-conditioned end. Combined with no LayerNorm, this is a plausible published explanation for both the L3 grid dose-response and the L5 DeepOKAN gradient collapse, and it names first-layer conditioning as the diagnostic to measure. Verify the author list before citing.

papers.citation: Salvador K. Dzimah, Sonia Rubio Herranz, Fernando Carlos López Hernández, Antonio López Montes. "A Unified Benchmark of Physics-Informed Neural Networks and Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Ordinary and Partial Differential Equations." arXiv, 14 Feb 2026.
papers.what_it_shows: Nine problems (4 ODEs, 5 PDEs: logistic, oscillatory, harmonic oscillator, Airy, 2D Laplace, 2D Poisson, 1D heat, 1D wave, 1D Burgers), matched parameter budgets, 1–4 hidden layers, 10 independent runs per configuration, identical Adam/lr/collocation settings. Finding: PIKANs 'consistently achieve more accurate solutions, converge in fewer iterations, and yield superior gradient estimates' — roughly one order of magnitude better relative L2/Linf, and error standard deviations about TWO orders of magnitude smaller than PINNs. Example: logistic equation, best PINN 7.70e-2 vs best PIKAN 1.94e-3.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: THE adversarial citation. A 2026 matched-budget, 10-seed benchmark that finds the opposite of both our headline claims — KANs more accurate AND more seed-stable. We cannot ignore it. The distinction that saves us, and it is a real one, is the task: theirs is physics-informed solution of a single fixed PDE instance (a fitting problem, where training fit IS the objective); ours is supervised generalisation to unseen materials (where training fit and the objective come apart). Our L3 audit shows RBF-KAN fitting competitively and generalising worse — which is entirely consistent with their result. We should cite this paper prominently, state the task distinction explicitly, and scope our claim to out-of-distribution surrogate generalisation. Doing this pre-emptively is far better than being handed it by a referee.

papers.citation: Spotorno, Leal Filho, Frohlich. "Empirical Stability Analysis of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks in Hard-Constrained Recurrent Physics-Informed Discovery." arXiv, Feb 2026 (rev. Mar 2026).
papers.what_it_shows: KANs inside hard-constrained recurrent physics-informed architectures show 'severe hyperparameter fragility', 'instability in deeper configurations', and 'consistent failure on multiplicative terms' (Van der Pol), attributed to the limitations of KAN's additive inductive bias on state-coupling problems. Small KANs compete on univariate polynomial tasks (Duffing) but are 'generally outperformed by standard MLPs' overall.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: An independent 2026 replication of our qualitative verdict, in a hard-constrained setting close to our bounded-output head from L4b. Its 'additive inductive bias fails on multiplicative coupling' argument is a mechanism we can borrow directly: our Type V dual-term Do-Do isotherm coupled to LDF kinetics and an energy balance is multiplicatively coupled (van't Hoff exponential times loading), so an additive edge decomposition is a poor match. That is a physics-grounded reason for the L3 result rather than a purely empirical one.

papers.citation: Amanda A. Howard, Bruno Jacob, Sarah Helfert, Alexander Heinlein, Panos Stinis. "Finite basis Kolmogorov-Arnold networks: domain decomposition for data-driven and physics-informed problems." arXiv, 28 Jun 2024 (rev. 14 Nov 2025).
papers.what_it_shows: FBKAN: partition-of-unity domain decomposition so several small KANs train in parallel, motivated by the fact that 'KANs can be expensive to train, even for relatively small networks'. Demonstrated effective with noisy data and for physics-informed training on multiscale problems.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The standard remedy a referee will name for sharp/multiscale features when a monolithic KAN underperforms. Our two-wave breakthrough with a 40x spread in t(0.9)-t(0.1) is exactly a multiscale target. We should either run an FBKAN arm or state precisely why domain decomposition in (z,t) is out of scope — silence here reads as an unexplored fix.

papers.citation: Salah A. Faroughi et al. "Scientific Machine Learning with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks." arXiv, 30 Jul 2025 (rev. 3 Nov 2025).
papers.what_it_shows: Pro-KAN review across data-driven, physics-informed and deep-operator learning; asserts KANs give 'consistent improvements in accuracy, convergence, and spectral representation' and address MLP weaknesses on localized or high-frequency features. Openly lists computational efficiency, theoretical guarantees, hyperparameter tuning and algorithm complexity as unresolved.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the prevailing narrative our paper contradicts, so it must be cited and engaged, not omitted. Its own admission that hyperparameter tuning is an open problem is the lever: it concedes KAN results are tuning-dependent, which is precisely why our tuning protocol has to be airtight.

papers.citation: Salah A. Faroughi et al. "Kolmogorov-Arnold networks for data-driven, physics-informed, and deep-operator learning: a review, synthesis, and new analysis." Neural Networks (2026), ScienceDirect S0893608026002534; PubMed 41819622. Published ~1 Mar 2026.
papers.what_it_shows: Journal review covering the same three axes as our ladder (data-driven, physics-informed, deep-operator), framed around SciML shifting from MLPs to KANs.
