Full text was 403 to fetch; the framing above is from search metadata plus the closely related arXiv:2507.22959 by the same lead author.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The most current review venue for our claim, in a journal a reviewer of ours is likely to read. Our L3/L5 result is a direct counterexample to its framing. Get the full text through institutional access and cite the specific pages before submission — do not cite it from metadata alone.

papers.citation: "Is the Statistical Advantage Worth the Cost? An Empirical Comparison of KANs and MLPs for Structured Data Classification." arXiv, July 2026.
papers.what_it_shows: Twelve public tabular datasets (binary, multiclass, multilabel, ordinal). KANs statistically outperform MLPs on binary and multiclass and hold a significant aggregate advantage, but at medium effect size (d = -0.46) and at substantially higher parameter and computational cost. Conclusion: KANs for high-precision settings, MLPs for resource-constrained ones.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: A 2026 counterexample in a tabular/structured regime, which is close to our L1/L3 setting (11 material descriptors → 192 POD coefficients is a tabular regression problem, not a field-to-field one). Worth engaging because it blocks any sweeping 'KANs lose on tabular data' phrasing. Author list not captured; verify before citing.

papers.citation: Jin Lee, Ziming Liu, Xinling Yu, Yixuan Wang, Haewon Jeong, Murphy Yuezhen Niu, Zheng Zhang. "KANO: Kolmogorov-Arnold Neural Operator." arXiv, 20 Sep 2025 (rev. 24 Feb 2026).
papers.what_it_shows: Dual-domain (spectral + spatial) neural operator with symbolic interpretability. Claims KANO stays expressive for position-dependent / variable-coefficient PDEs where FNO is practical only for spectrally sparse operators, and that KANO 'robustly generalizes but FNO fails to' on position-dependent operators. Quantum Hamiltonian learning: ~6e-6 state infidelity vs ~1.5e-2 for FNO. No matched-parameter comparison in the abstract.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The current state of the art in KAN-based operator learning, published after our DeepOKAN arm was designed. If we claim to have tested 'the KAN operator family', a referee will note we tested the 2024 architecture and not the 2025/2026 one. Either add a KANO arm or scope the claim to 'DeepOKAN-style Gaussian-RBF branch/trunk operators' explicitly in the abstract.

papers.citation: Zavareh Bozorgasl, Hao Chen. "Wav-KAN: Wavelet Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks." (Semantic Scholar corpus ID 8199e26d20281b3e4f64d72ff63e00eb8eae2987; code at github.com/zavareh1/Wav-KAN). Related: "On the study of frequency control and spectral bias in Wavelet-Based Kolmogorov Arnold networks: A path to physics-informed KANs", arXiv:2502.00280.
papers.what_it_shows: Replaces spline edges with wavelet edges, which are localized in BOTH position and scale — presented as advantageous when the target contains sharp transitions, oscillations, or multi-resolution features. Reported to train faster than spline-KAN by avoiding grid machinery.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The most obviously well-matched KAN basis for our physics that we never tried: our target is a shock front whose position moves and whose width varies 40x. If we publish 'KANs lose' without a wavelet arm, the reviewer's one-line objection is 'you chose the two bases least suited to a moving sharp front'. The arXiv identifier for the primary Wav-KAN paper was not confirmed in my searches — resolve it from the Semantic Scholar record before it enters a bibliography.

papers.citation: Alireza Afzal Aghaei. "fKAN: Fractional Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with trainable Jacobi basis functions." arXiv:2406.07456 (Jun 2024); Neurocomputing (2025), ScienceDirect S0925231225000864.
papers.what_it_shows: Trainable adaptive fractional-orthogonal Jacobi basis (Fractional Jacobi Neural Block) with a trainable fractional order that adapts the basis during training; non-piecewise, so more efficient than splines, and active for both positive and negative inputs.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The 'trainable basis order' variant a referee lists alongside Chebyshev when arguing our polynomial arm was under-specified — our Chebyshev degree is a fixed hyperparameter, theirs is learned. Cheap to add as a third polynomial arm and it directly answers 'you fixed the polynomial family by hand'.

papers.citation: Ziming Liu, Pingchuan Ma, Yixuan Wang, Wojciech Matusik, Max Tegmark. "KAN 2.0: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks Meet Science." arXiv:2408.10205, 19 Aug 2024. Journal version appears at Phys. Rev. X, doi 10.1103/4t7t-v19l (APS page returned 403; verify).
papers.what_it_shows: Bidirectional science↔KAN framework: injecting scientific knowledge into KANs and extracting symbolic formulas out of them, via MultKAN, kanpiler and a tree converter. MultKAN adds multiplication nodes to the purely additive KAN structure.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: MultKAN is the authors' own answer to the additive-inductive-bias failure that Spotorno et al. document and that our multiplicatively coupled isotherm/energy balance would trigger. Naming MultKAN and saying whether we tested it closes an obvious hole. Also relevant to L7 and the SINDy work: KAN 2.0's symbolic-extraction pipeline is the natural 'interpretability' rebuttal if we claim KANs buy us nothing — they claim KANs buy interpretability, which our nRMSE metric cannot measure. Confirm the PRX DOI independently; I could not fetch the APS page.

state_of_the_art:
As of mid-2026 the literature has NOT converged, and anyone who says it has is selling something. Three things are settled and three are actively contested.

Settled. (1) At matched parameters AND matched FLOPs, on general-purpose supervised tasks, MLPs generally beat KANs; KAN's genuine edge is symbolic-formula representation and it traces to the B-spline basis rather than to the Kolmogorov-Arnold structure — bolt B-splines onto an MLP and the gap closes (Yu, Yu & Wang, arXiv:2407.16674). (2) Vanilla B-spline KANs are slow and fragile; the practical KAN of 2026 is a non-spline variant — Gaussian RBF (FastKAN), Chebyshev (cPIKAN), wavelet (Wav-KAN), or fractional Jacobi (fKAN). (3) KAN training is genuinely more fragile than MLP training, and this is documented by KAN proponents themselves: Shukla et al. (CMAME 431:117290, 2024) warn implementations "may diverge for different random seeds or higher order orthogonal polynomials".

Contested, and this is where our paper lands. (4) In physics-informed SOLVING of a fixed PDE, the 2026 evidence has swung toward KANs: Dzimah et al. (arXiv:2602.15068) report PIKANs about an order of magnitude more accurate than parameter-matched PINNs across nine ODE/PDE benchmarks with error standard deviations two orders of magnitude smaller — the opposite of our stability finding. (5) In data-driven surrogate generalisation, the evidence runs the other way: Pant et al. (arXiv:2504.11397) find KANs win only at depth 1, lose the advantage with depth, and degrade substantially more out-of-distribution. (6) The field has moved from "is KAN better?" to "KAN training is an optimisation problem with known fixes": variance-preserving/Glorot and power-law initialisation (Rigas et al., ICLR 2026, arXiv:2509.03417), residual gating for deep stacks (RGA KAN, arXiv:2510.23501), quasi-Newton finishing with SSBFGS/SSBroyden for orders-of-magnitude gains (Kiyani et al., arXiv:2501.16371), LOOCV-initialised adaptive RBF shape parameters worth ~10x (arXiv:2605.21534), and a published stable interval for the Gaussian scale, ε ∈ [1/(G-1), 2/(G-1)] (arXiv:2604.21174).

The practical consequence: in 2026, an untuned KAN failure is no longer publishable as a KAN result. The reviewer's default hypothesis for any KAN that underperforms or collapses is bad initialisation, missing normalization, a mis-scaled basis, or Adam-only optimisation — and there is now a named, parameter-matched fix in the literature for each one.

There is, separately, a clean gap we own: I found no work applying KANs to adsorption breakthrough curves or column dynamics. Our physical setting is genuinely unoccupied.
implications: Our L3 headline is currently STRONGER than the literature supports and stronger than our own data supports. The defensible claim is: at matched parameters, on out-of-distribution material generalisation for a sharp-front adsorption surrogate, a well-tuned Gaussian-RBF KAN does not beat an MLP. The claims 'architecture family is eliminated' and 'monotone in the KAN-ness of the edge' do not survive scrutiny as written.

The mechanism sentence in RESULTS.md is contradicted by our own audit. RESULTS.md says richer per-edge bases 'buy training fit and not generalisation'. But `results/l3_audit.json` plus `l3_audit.log` show RBF-KAN TRAIN error rising monotonically with grids (0.0553 at g=4 to 0.0688 at g=24), worse than the MLP's 0.0514 at every grid. Richer bases bought neither fit nor generalisation. That is an optimisation/conditioning signature, not a bias-variance one — and Zhang & Zhou's bound (ICLR 2025) agrees, since complexity there enters through coefficient l1 norms and Lipschitz constants, not basis count.

The grid dose-response is confounded by a shrinking kernel. `run_l3.py:RBFKANBlock` hard-codes h = 4.0/(grids-1), so raising grids from 4 to 24 simultaneously (a) enriches the basis and (b) narrows each Gaussian by 6x, at fixed centres on [-2,2] with no input normalization. Cavoretto et al. (arXiv:2605.21534) show the shape parameter alone moves accuracy ~10x, and arXiv:2604.21174 puts our h at the narrow, worst-conditioned edge of the stable interval. The 'monotone in KAN-ness' claim cannot be separated from 'monotone in kernel narrowness' with the runs we have.

Eleven of fifty-four L3 runs never trained. `l3_rerun.log` shows `best@0/400` — meaning the early-stopping checkpoint was the model AT INITIALISATION — for all 6 cheby_kan runs at the 200k budget, all 3 cheby_kan 800k lr=1e-3 runs, and 2 mlp 800k lr=3e-3 runs. The cheby_kan 200k row quoted in both RESULTS.md and 03_LADDER_PROTOCOL.md is an untrained network's error. The same signature (train error ~0.118 versus 0.058 at degree 3) appears for audit degrees 7, 9 and 11, so the 'cheby 0.0889 → 0.1250 as degree goes 3 → 11' trend is largely a record of which configurations failed to leave initialisation. This is the B14 strawman pattern for a fourth time, on the arm being argued against.

Every RBF-KAN arm in L3 picks the TOP of the learning-rate grid. From `results/l3_results.json`: rbf_kan best lr = 3e-3 at 50k, 200k and 800k, where 3e-3 is the maximum of the swept set {3e-3, 1e-3}. The MLP picks 1e-3 (the minimum) at all three. Neither optimum is bracketed, and the KAN's is unbracketed in the direction that would help it. This is exactly defect B22 ('a single lr saturates the narrow RBF-KAN stack') recurring, and `audit_l3.py` inherits the same two-point grid. The l5_fill2 result — DeepONet improving to ~0.0275 at lr=3e-3, above the old grid top — is the third instance of this same failure in the project.

The DeepOKAN collapse is confounded with a documented one-line omission. `operator_models.py:PI_DeepOKAN` constructs `RBFKANLayer(...)` without arguments, so `use_layernorm` stays at its default False — while FastKAN, the reference implementation of exactly this Gaussian-RBF layer, applies layer normalization before the RBF specifically to keep inputs inside the fixed grid window. Our own B22 diagnosis (96% of edges alive at init, gradient norm 1.2e-11 by step 150) is the saturation that LayerNorm exists to prevent. The 10/45 collapses are therefore currently attributable to our implementation, not to KANs.

We never tested the canonical KAN. No B-spline arm (pykan / efficient-KAN) exists anywhere in the repository, despite B-splines being the basis of the original paper, the default recommendation of the 2026 practitioner's guide, and the source of the only KAN advantage that survives Yu et al.'s ablation. We also never ran grid extension, which the original paper presents as part of the method.

Depth was never swept. All L3 arms are depth 3. Pant et al. (arXiv:2504.11397) find KANs beat MLPs decisively at depth 1 and lose the advantage with depth. A single-hidden-layer arm is cheap and is the first thing a knowledgeable referee will request.

03_LADDER_PROTOCOL.md contains a stale L3 table that contradicts its own verdict. The table at approximately lines 514-524 reports 50k: mlp 0.1260, rbf_kan 0.1037, cheby_kan 0.1875 — in which RBF-KAN BEATS the MLP — immediately above the sentence 'the ordering mlp < rbf_kan < cheby_kan is identical at all three budgets'. Those numbers match neither `results/l3_results.json` nor RESULTS.md (0.0585 / 0.0768 / 0.1220). For a project whose entire credibility rests on a frozen pre-registered protocol, a superseded table inside the frozen document that reverses the verdict is the worst possible thing for a referee to find.

`audit_l3.py`'s docstring overstates what it swept. It states it sweeps 'rbf_kan: num_grids 4..24, and learnable vs fixed centres/widths'. The code sweeps only `grids` and `degree`; it imports `RBFKANBlock` and never uses it, and no learnable-centre arm is run. The learnable-centre RBF layer exists in `kan_model.py` but was never entered into the audit.

There is a real and defensible task distinction that rescues most of the result, and we are not currently making it. The 2026 pro-KAN evidence (Dzimah et al.) is about physics-informed SOLVING, where training fit is the objective. Ours is out-of-distribution surrogate generalisation, where fit and objective come apart — and DeepOKAN's own headline evidence is training loss. Stating this explicitly turns our most dangerous counter-citation into a scoping argument and makes the contribution sharper.

We have an unoccupied niche worth claiming carefully. No KAN work on adsorption breakthrough curves or column dynamics appears in the literature. Combined with the practitioner's guide flagging non-smooth/sharp-gradient targets as where KANs underperform, the framing 'first controlled KAN evaluation on a self-sharpening two-wave adsorption front, and it fails in the way the basis-choice literature predicts' is both novel and defensible.
risks_to_our_claims: FATAL IF UNFIXED: 'Your Chebyshev-KAN never trained.' Eleven of fifty-four L3 runs early-stopped on the initialisation checkpoint, including 6/6 of the cheby_kan 200k arm you tabulate. You reported an untrained network's error as an architecture result and then built a monotone dose-response on top of it. Reject.

FATAL IF UNFIXED: 'Your learning-rate grid is one-sided.' The RBF-KAN's best learning rate is the maximum of your two-point sweep at all three budgets. You retracted exactly this defect as B22 and then repeated it in L3 and in the audit. The negative result is not established.

SEVERE: 'Your RBF-KAN is not FastKAN.' No layer normalization (default False, never enabled in DeepOKAN), fixed non-learnable centres on [-2,2], non-learnable width h = 4/(grids-1) at the narrow edge of the published stable interval. Your 10/45 collapses and your grid dose-response are both consistent with a mis-specified kernel rather than with KAN edges. Cite Li (arXiv:2405.06721), Cavoretto et al. (arXiv:2605.21534), arXiv:2604.21174.

SEVERE: 'You did not test a B-spline KAN.' The original architecture, the practitioner's guide's default, and the only basis whose advantage survives Yu et al.'s ablation. Testing two non-canonical variants and concluding against 'KANs' is a category error.

SEVERE: 'You used only Adam with a two-point learning-rate sweep and default initialisation.' Kiyani et al. (arXiv:2501.16371, Karniadakis group — the same group as your main supporting citation) report orders-of-magnitude gains from SSBroyden/SSBFGS. Rigas et al. (ICLR 2026, arXiv:2509.03417) show KAN-specific initialisation is worth large factors. You tuned neither.

SEVERE: 'A 2026 matched-budget benchmark finds the opposite.' Dzimah et al. (arXiv:2602.15068): nine ODE/PDE problems, 10 seeds each, PIKANs about an order of magnitude more accurate with error standard deviations two orders of magnitude SMALLER than PINNs. Your paper claims KANs are both less accurate and less stable and does not cite this.

MODERATE: 'Your deep-KAN failure is a solved problem.' Rigas et al. (arXiv:2510.23501) diagnose deep cPIKAN divergence as a variance-preservation failure at initialisation and fix it with Glorot-like init plus residual gating, beating parameter-matched cPIKANs by orders of magnitude. Your untrained Chebyshev arms are their Figure 1.
MODERATE: 'You tested only depth 3.' Pant et al. (arXiv:2504.11397) find the KAN advantage lives at depth 1 and dies with depth. Your design cannot see the regime where KANs win.

MODERATE: 'You picked the two bases least suited to a moving shock.' Wav-KAN's wavelets are localized in position AND scale — the obvious match for a front whose position moves and whose width varies 40x across your dataset. You did not try it, nor fKAN's trainable fractional order, nor MultKAN's multiplicative nodes for your multiplicatively coupled isotherm.

MODERATE: 'Your stated mechanism is contradicted by your own audit table.' You claim richer bases buy training fit but not generalisation; your audit shows train error rising from 0.0553 to 0.0688 as grids go 4 to 24, worse than the MLP at every grid. That is an optimisation failure you have relabelled as a generalisation finding. Zhang & Zhou's bound (ICLR 2025) does not predict your effect either: it depends on coefficient l1 norms and Lipschitz constants, not on basis count.

MODERATE: 'Your frozen protocol contradicts itself.' 03_LADDER_PROTOCOL.md's L3 table shows RBF-KAN beating the MLP at 50k, directly above a sentence asserting the ordering is identical at all budgets, and neither matches your results JSON. For a paper selling pre-registration, this is disproportionately damaging.

MODERATE: 'Your audit docstring claims a sweep the code does not perform.' `audit_l3.py` says it swept learnable versus fixed centres and widths; it did not. If a reviewer diffs the docstring against the loop, every other audit claim in the paper becomes suspect.

MILD: 'You tested the 2024 KAN operator, not the current one.' KANO (arXiv:2509.16825) postdates your DeepOKAN arm and claims robust generalisation on position-dependent operators. Either add it or scope the claim explicitly.

MILD: 'You matched parameters but not FLOPs or wall-clock.' Yu et al. control both and note the ranking can flip. Your L5 already records DeepOKAN at 1.6-2.1x wall clock per run — that favours you, so report it rather than leaving the gap open.

MILD: 'nRMSE cannot see the property KANs are sold on.' KAN 2.0 claims interpretability and symbolic extraction. A one-metric refutation does not address the claim actually being made by the KAN literature.

concrete_actions.action: Quarantine every L3/L5 run whose best checkpoint was step 0. Add a hard assertion in `run_l3.py:train_one` that raises if `best_step == 0`, re-run all 11 affected configurations with warm-up plus a much longer patience (currently patience=400 with validation every 25 steps = only 16 non-improving evaluations, far too aggressive for a KAN), and withdraw the current cheby_kan 200k and 800k rows from RESULTS.md and 03_LADDER_PROTOCOL.md until they are replaced by genuinely trained models. Log `best_step` in `audit_l3.py`, which currently does not print it, and re-check degrees 7/9/11 whose train error of ~0.118 shows the same never-trained signature.
concrete_actions.rationale: Reporting a network at initialisation as an architecture result is the single most reject-worthy defect in the project, it is the B14 pattern for a fourth time, and it lands on precisely the arm the paper argues against. It is also fully diagnosable from data already on disk (`l3_rerun.log`, `l3_audit.log`).

concrete_actions.action: Widen the learning-rate sweep until every arm's optimum is interior. Extend to at least {1e-2, 3e-3, 1e-3, 3e-4, 1e-4} for all three L3 families at all three budgets and re-run `audit_l3.py` on the same grid. Add a protocol rule — and a programmatic check in the analysis script — that refuses to report any arm whose selected hyperparameter sits on a grid boundary.
concrete_actions.rationale: rbf_kan selects lr=3e-3, the maximum of the swept set, at all three budgets, so its optimum is unbracketed in the direction that would help it; the MLP selects the minimum. This is defect B22 recurring for the third time in the project, and l5_fill2 already showed DeepONet improving above the old grid top. Until this is fixed the L3 negative result is not established.

concrete_actions.action: Rebuild the RBF-KAN arm to match the FastKAN reference before re-running anything: enable layer normalization before the RBF basis in both `run_l3.py:RBFKANBlock` and `operator_models.py:PI_DeepOKAN` (the latter currently leaves `use_layernorm` at its default False), make centres and widths learnable as `kan_model.py:RBFKANLayer` already supports, and decouple the kernel width from the grid count — sweep h independently, spanning the published stable interval ε ∈ [1/(G-1), 2/(G-1)], with LOOCV initialisation per Cavoretto et al. Then re-test whether the grid dose-response and the DeepOKAN collapses survive.
concrete_actions.rationale: Layer normalization exists in FastKAN specifically to stop inputs drifting outside the fixed RBF window, which is exactly the saturation our own B22 diagnosis measured (gradient norm 1.2e-11 by step 150, 96% of edges alive at init). And h = 4/(grids-1) means our grid sweep also narrows the kernel 6x, confounding basis richness with conditioning. Both the collapse result and the dose-response mechanism are currently attributable to our implementation rather than to KANs.

concrete_actions.action: Add the missing KAN arms so the comparison cannot be called a strawman: (1) B-spline KAN via efficient-KAN or pykan, with and without grid extension — the canonical architecture, currently absent from the entire repository; (2) Wav-KAN wavelet edges, the basis best matched to a moving sharp front; (3) fKAN trainable fractional-Jacobi edges, so the polynomial order is learned rather than fixed; (4) depth 1 and depth 2 versions of every family, since Pant et al. locate the KAN advantage at depth 1 and all our arms are depth 3. Report all of them at matched parameters AND matched FLOPs.
concrete_actions.rationale: These are the four objections a KAN-literate referee raises in the first paragraph of their report. Each is individually cheap on our existing harness, and together they convert 'the authors tested two non-canonical variants' into 'the authors tested the field'.

concrete_actions.action: Give the strongest surviving KAN configuration the strongest available training recipe and show the ordering holds: power-law and Glorot-like variance-preserving initialisation (Rigas et al., ICLR 2026), a residual-gated variant for the deep Chebyshev stack (RGA KAN), and an SSBroyden or L-BFGS finishing phase after Adam (Kiyani et al.). Report the best-of-everything KAN against the best-of-everything MLP.
concrete_actions.rationale: In 2026 an untuned KAN failure is not a publishable KAN result — the reviewer's default explanation is bad initialisation or Adam-only optimisation, and there is a named parameter-matched fix in the literature for each. Kiyani et al. is from the same group as our main supporting citation, which makes ignoring it especially conspicuous. If the ordering survives this, the result becomes very hard to attack.

concrete_actions.action: Rewrite the L3 mechanism claim to match the evidence. Replace 'parameters spent on per-edge basis richness buy training fit and not generalisation' with what the audit actually shows — that at fixed budget, increasing basis richness degrades train AND novel-material error together, an optimisation and conditioning signature rather than a bias-variance one. Then measure the l1 norm of the edge coefficient matrices and the per-layer Lipschitz constants across the grid sweep, since Zhang & Zhou's bound (ICLR 2025) makes those, not basis count, the complexity carriers.
concrete_actions.rationale: The current sentence is contradicted by `results/l3_audit.json` (train error 0.0553 at g=4 rising to 0.0688 at g=24, worse than the MLP's 0.0514 at every grid). A referee who reads the audit table will see the contradiction. Measuring the coefficient norms replaces a stipulated mechanism with a theory-grounded, falsifiable one.

concrete_actions.action: Reconcile 03_LADDER_PROTOCOL.md with `results/l3_results.json`. The L3 RESULT table at approximately lines 514-524 reports 50k as mlp 0.1260 / rbf_kan 0.1037 / cheby_kan 0.1875 — RBF-KAN winning — directly above a verdict asserting the ordering is identical at all three budgets, and matches neither the results JSON nor RESULTS.md. Replace it with the current numbers, annotate what superseded what, and add a CI-style check that regenerates every protocol table from the JSON so this cannot recur.
concrete_actions.rationale: The project's whole epistemic pitch is a frozen pre-registered protocol. A stale table inside that frozen document, whose numbers reverse the verdict printed beneath it, does more damage to reviewer trust than the underlying error would.

concrete_actions.action: Fix `audit_l3.py` so it performs the sweep its docstring claims. Either add the learnable-centres/widths RBF arm (the layer already exists in `kan_model.py`; `RBFKANBlock` is imported and never used) or correct the docstring — and add the omission to RETRACTIONS.md as a new B-defect.
concrete_actions.rationale: An audit script that claims a sweep it did not run is exactly the kind of discrepancy this project logs as a defect, and the paper's credibility depends on the audit being what it says it is. It is a few lines either way.

concrete_actions.action: Restructure the KAN narrative around the task distinction and cite the adversarial 2026 evidence head-on. Add Dzimah et al. (arXiv:2602.15068) and Faroughi et al. (Neural Networks 2026) to the introduction, state that the pro-KAN evidence concerns physics-informed solving of a fixed PDE where training fit IS the objective, and that DeepOKAN's own headline evidence is training loss — then position our contribution as the out-of-distribution surrogate-generalisation regime where fit and objective diverge, which our audit measures directly.
concrete_actions.rationale: A referee who knows the 2026 literature will otherwise open with 'a matched-budget benchmark this year found PIKANs an order of magnitude better and two orders more stable, and the authors do not cite it'. Raising it ourselves converts the strongest attack into a scoping argument that makes the contribution sharper, and it is consistent with, not contradicted by, our data.

concrete_actions.action: Scope every KAN claim in the abstract and conclusions to what the design can support: name the specific variants, the depth, the budget range, the optimiser, and the out-of-distribution material split. Retire 'architecture family is eliminated' and 'monotone in the KAN-ness of the edge'. Note explicitly that we tested DeepOKAN-style Gaussian-RBF branch/trunk operators and not KANO (arXiv:2509.16825), and that nRMSE cannot assess the interpretability claims of KAN 2.0.
concrete_actions.rationale: Overclaiming is the failure mode this project was built to avoid, and the L3/L5 language currently outruns the evidence in exactly the way the ladder was designed to prevent. Precise scoping also makes the result more citable, not less.

concrete_actions.action: Add a FLOP and wall-clock column to every L3 and L5 table, alongside the existing parameter match. L5 already records DeepOKAN at 1.6-2.1x wall clock per run (median 420 s), which is currently buried in the protocol.
concrete_actions.rationale: Yu et al. control FLOPs as well as parameters and note the ranking can flip between the two. Our numbers happen to favour us on both axes, so reporting them costs nothing and closes the 'matched parameters is not a fair comparison' objection pre-emptively.

concrete_actions.action: Add an FBKAN (domain-decomposed KAN) arm, or state explicitly in the limitations why partition-of-unity decomposition in (z,t) is out of scope.
concrete_actions.rationale: FBKAN (Howard, Jacob, Helfert, Heinlein & Stinis) is the standard published remedy when a monolithic KAN underperforms on multiscale or sharp-featured targets, and our two-wave front with a 40x spread in t(0.9)-t(0.1) is textbook multiscale. Leaving it unmentioned reads as an unexplored fix; one sentence of scoping closes it if we choose not to run it.

concrete_actions.action: Claim the empty niche carefully in the introduction: no published work applies KANs to adsorption breakthrough curves or column dynamics, and the 2026 practitioner's guide independently flags non-smooth and sharp-gradient targets as where KANs lose. Frame the contribution as the first controlled matched-budget KAN evaluation on a self-sharpening two-wave adsorption front, failing in the manner the basis-choice literature predicts.
concrete_actions.rationale: This turns a negative result into a positive contribution with an independent theoretical prediction behind it, and it is the framing most likely to survive review at a top-tier venue. It also gives the physics of the Type V two-wave structure a load-bearing role in the machine-learning argument rather than leaving it as background.

concrete_actions.action: Before the bibliography is frozen, independently verify the four citations I could not fully confirm: the Wav-KAN arXiv identifier (I have only the Semantic Scholar record), the full author list of Chebyshev-KAN (arXiv:2405.07200), the author list of arXiv:2604.21174 and arXiv:2607.13413, and the Phys. Rev. X DOI 10.1103/4t7t-v19l for the KAN journal version (the APS page returned 403 to me). Obtain the Faroughi et al. Neural Networks 2026 review through institutional access rather than citing it from metadata.
concrete_actions.rationale: A paper whose contribution is methodological rigour cannot ship an unverified reference. Every other citation in this report was fetched and read; these five were not, and they should not enter the manuscript on search-snippet evidence alone.

lens: Symbolic/sparse discovery and interpretability for adsorption kinetics — what is credible in 2026, and what it says about the project's identifiability claims (retraction A7, identify_kinetics.py, identifiability.py, and the L6/H1 verdict)

papers.citation: J. C. Knox, A. D. Ebner, M. D. LeVan, R. F. Coker, J. A. Ritter, "Limitations of Breakthrough Curve Analysis in Fixed-Bed Adsorption", Industrial & Engineering Chemistry Research 55(16):4734-4748
papers.what_it_shows: Fetched in full. Shows that extracting the axial dispersion coefficient and/or the LDF mass-transfer coefficient from an exit breakthrough curve is unreliable: near-wall channelling produces non-plug flow even at bed/pellet diameter ratio ~20; the five standard D_L correlations disagree by a factor of 2 (CO2) to nearly 3 (H2O); and for steep isotherms fitting the exit curve required an LDF coefficient '~50 times larger' than correlation values. Their recommendation is to measure concentration AND temperature at multiple interior axial positions on the centreline, because the exit curve is dominated by mechanical dispersion while the interior temperature profile is what actually carries the mass-transfer kinetics.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the single most important domain citation for the whole project. It is independent, peer-reviewed, adsorption-specific confirmation of exactly what L6 measured (k_LDF unrecoverable, R^2 = -0.61) — which is simultaneously our best support and our biggest novelty risk, because it means a referee can say we spent a pre-registered rung rediscovering a known 2016 result. It also tells us the fix: our surrogate sees only c, q, T at a probe; the informative observable is the interior thermal wave.

papers.citation: S. Sircar, J. R. Hufton, "Why Does the Linear Driving Force Model for Adsorption Kinetics Work?", Adsorption 6:137-147
papers.what_it_shows: Bibliographic record verified via Crossref (title, author, journal, volume, pages, DOI). The paper's established result is that the LDF approximation reproduces integral (column- or particle-averaged) uptake well even when the actual intraparticle profile is nothing like the LDF's, and that the lumped LDF coefficient therefore absorbs process conditions rather than being an intrinsic material constant. I verified existence and citation, not the sentence-level content.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Directly attacks the framing of H1. If k_LDF is a lumped, process-dependent quantity rather than a material property, then 'identify the kinetic object separately from the equilibrium object' is ill-posed as posed, and 'k_LDF is not recoverable from observable material descriptors' becomes almost a definition rather than a finding. We must either cite this and reframe, or a referee will.

papers.citation: S. Brandani, "The zero length column technique to measure adsorption equilibrium and kinetics: lessons learnt from 30 years of experience", Adsorption 27:319-351
papers.what_it_shows: Bibliographic record verified via Crossref. ZLC is the standard technique for measuring adsorption kinetics on ~<10 mg of adsorbent (MOFs, zeolites) precisely because the small sample and high carrier flow suppress external mass- and heat-transfer resistances, decoupling the kinetic measurement from equilibrium and from bed hydrodynamics.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the published answer to 'what experimental design makes k_LDF identifiable': not a breakthrough column at all. Our paper currently has no sentence saying how a practitioner would actually obtain the parameter our separate-identification arm needs. Adding one, with this citation, converts a bare negative result into an actionable methodological statement.

papers.citation: E. Glueckauf, "Theory of chromatography. Part 10. Formulae for diffusion into spheres and their application to chromatography", Transactions of the Faraday Society 51:1540-1551
papers.what_it_shows: Bibliographic record verified via Crossref. Origin of the LDF approximation and of the k = 15 D_e/r_p^2 identification.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Our solver uses LDF but the manuscript has no canonical citation for it or for its validity range. Any adsorption referee expects Glueckauf 1955 plus Sircar & Hufton 2000 as the pair.

papers.citation: D. A. Messenger, D. M. Bortz, "Weak SINDy for Partial Differential Equations", Journal of Computational Physics 443:110525 (arXiv:2007.02848)
papers.what_it_shows: Fetched abstract. Eliminating pointwise derivative approximation via the weak (integral) form gives machine-precision coefficient recovery on clean data and robust PDE identification 'in the large noise regime (with signal-to-noise ratio approaching one in many well-known cases)'. Uses separable convolutional test functions with FFT, worst-case cost O(N^(D+1) log N), plus an a-priori spectral test-function selection algorithm and a learned STLS threshold.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the 2026 default for PDE discovery and our replacement script is not it. identify_kinetics.py estimates dq/dt with np.gradient and then does strong-form least squares — the exact noise-amplifying step WSINDy exists to remove. Our conclusion 'the estimator is not the problem, the driving force is' currently rests on a single strong-form estimator. Redoing it in weak form makes that conclusion unassailable. The journal DOI came from a search summary, not a fetch.

papers.citation: D. M. Bortz, D. A. Messenger, V. Dukic, "Direct Estimation of Parameters in ODE Models Using WENDy: Weak-form Estimation of Nonlinear Dynamics", Bulletin of Mathematical Biology (arXiv:2302.13271)
papers.what_it_shows: Fetched abstract. WENDy estimates parameters of a KNOWN model structure with no forward ODE solves, by converting to weak form against C-infinity bump test functions and solving an errors-in-variables regression with iteratively reweighted least squares. Robust to large measurement noise; for stiff/higher-dimensional systems typically orders of magnitude faster and more accurate than forward-solver nonlinear least squares.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is precisely our 'structured' estimator's problem: dq/dt = k(q*_obs - q) with k the only unknown. WENDy is the correct 2026 tool for it, it handles the errors-in-variables structure our problem literally has (q*_obs carries fingerprint reconstruction error of 0.22-0.47 mol/kg against a 0.061 mol/kg signal — a textbook EIV setting), and it is a ~1-day drop-in. A follow-up (arXiv:2502.08881) extends WENDy to nonlinear-in-parameters ODEs; I saw that only in search results.

papers.citation: K. Kaheman, J. N. Kutz, S. L. Brunton, "SINDy-PI: a robust algorithm for parallel implicit sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics", Proceedings of the Royal Society A 476(2242):20200279 (arXiv:2004.02322)
papers.what_it_shows: Fetched abstract. Handles implicit ODEs/PDEs and rational nonlinearities, which standard SINDy cannot; claims several orders of magnitude better noise robustness than prior implicit-SINDy variants; demonstrated on the double pendulum and the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Our kinetics are dq/dt = k(q*(c,T) - q) with a dual-term Do-Do q* that is rational in c and Arrhenius/van't Hoff in T. That is an implicit/rational target, i.e. exactly the class standard SINDy cannot represent and SINDy-PI can. If any symbolic-discovery experiment survives into the paper, SINDy-PI (not polynomial STRidge) is the defensible method choice, and saying so pre-empts 'you used the wrong variant'.

papers.citation: U. Fasel, J. N. Kutz, B. W. Brunton, S. L. Brunton, "Ensemble-SINDy: Robust sparse model discovery in the low-data, high-noise limit, with active learning and control", Proceedings of the Royal Society A 478(2260):20210904 (arXiv:2111.10992)
papers.what_it_shows: Fetched abstract. Bootstrap aggregating (bagging) over data subsets and over library sublibraries; recovers PDE models 'from data with more than twice as much measurement noise' as prior approaches; produces inclusion probabilities per candidate term at essentially the cost of standard SINDy, enabling UQ, active learning, and robust MPC.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Our stridge() reports one thresholded coefficient vector per condition and we then report 'fraction of conditions selecting a q term with negative sign'. Ensemble inclusion probabilities are the modern, statistically meaningful version of that statistic, and they are cheap. Given this project's own standing rule 3 (no single-seed numbers in any table), reporting a single-draw sparse selection is internally inconsistent.

papers.citation: S. M. Hirsh, D. A. Barajas-Solano, J. N. Kutz, "Sparsifying priors for Bayesian uncertainty quantification in model discovery", Royal Society Open Science 9(2):211823 (arXiv:2107.02107)
papers.what_it_shows: Fetched abstract. UQ-SINDy: MCMC sparse Bayesian inference with spike-and-slab and regularized horseshoe priors; yields posterior coefficient distributions and per-term inclusion probabilities instead of point estimates; robust under observation noise and limited samples.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The alternative to Ensemble-SINDy if we want a fully probabilistic statement. More importantly it sets the 2026 bar: a discovery result reported without inclusion probabilities or coefficient posteriors reads as dated. This applies to any surviving version of sindy_discovery.py.

papers.citation: S. H. Rudy, S. L. Brunton, J. L. Proctor, J. N. Kutz, "Data-driven discovery of partial differential equations", Science Advances 3(4):e1602614
papers.what_it_shows: Bibliographic record verified via Crossref. PDE-FIND: builds a library of candidate spatial derivative terms and products and solves with sequentially thresholded ridge (STRidge). The canonical strong-form PDE discovery reference.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The method our retracted A7 pipeline was an implementation of. It must be cited as the origin, and then explicitly superseded by the weak-form line, so the manuscript reads as 'we used the modern method' rather than 'we used the 2017 method badly'.

papers.citation: Z. Chen, U. Fasel, A. Bizyaeva, "Fourier Weak SINDy: Spectral Test Function Selection for Robust Model Identification", L4DC 2026 (arXiv:2604.20141)
papers.what_it_shows: Fetched abstract. Replaces hand-chosen weak-form test functions with orthogonal sinusoidal test functions whose frequencies are selected automatically from a multitaper estimate of the data's power spectrum, turning weak-form regression into a problem over Fourier coefficients.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The current (2026) frontier of weak-form discovery, and the right thing to cite when we say what state of the art is. Its practical value to us is the automated test-function scale selection — our two-wave breakthrough has two very different intrinsic timescales (t(0.9)-t(0.1) varies 40x across the dataset), so a single hand-picked test-function width would be wrong for most conditions.

papers.citation: A. Raue, C. Kreutz, T. Maiwald, J. Bachmann, M. Schilling, U. Klingmüller, J. Timmer, "Structural and practical identifiability analysis of partially observed dynamical models by exploiting the profile likelihood", Bioinformatics 25(15):1923-1929
papers.what_it_shows: Bibliographic record verified via Crossref; content confirmed by multiple search summaries. The profile likelihood distinguishes three cases: a flat profile means structural non-identifiability; a profile with a maximum but a plateau on one or both sides means practical non-identifiability (finite data/noise); a profile decaying on both sides means identifiable, with a finite confidence interval read directly off the threshold.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the standard, referee-recognised way to state what identifiability.py is trying to say. 'R^2 = -0.61 for a regressor' is an ML statistic; 'the profile likelihood for k_LDF is flat above Da ~ 100, so k is practically non-identifiable with a one-sided infinite confidence interval' is an identifiability result. Our solver is 4.2 s/run, so a profile over ~40 k values for ~10 representative conditions is a few CPU-hours.

papers.citation: M. K. Transtrum, B. B. Machta, K. S. Brown, B. C. Daniels, C. R. Myers, J. P. Sethna, "Perspective: Sloppiness and emergent theories in physics, biology, and beyond", Journal of Chemical Physics 143(1):010901 (arXiv:1501.07668)
papers.what_it_shows: Fetched arXiv abstract; journal record verified via Crossref. Sloppy models are those whose behaviour is controlled by a small number of parameter combinations; the Fisher information matrix acts as a Riemannian metric whose eigenvalues span many decades (the 'hyper-ribbon' picture), and the manifold boundary approximation method systematically removes the sloppy directions to yield a reduced effective model.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This gives the whole ladder a unifying theoretical frame it currently lacks. Three independent function classes (POD+rf, POD+HGB, DeepONet) are flat in rank while the POD floor falls 28.7x (retraction A17); k_LDF is unrecoverable; only mode 1 has R^2 = 0.946. That is the signature of a sloppy model in which one or two stiff directions (front position, equilibrium capacity) carry everything and the rest is sloppy. Computing the FIM eigenspectrum over our 11 generative parameters would let us say this quantitatively instead of anecdotally — and would likely be the single most citable idea in the paper.

papers.citation: A. P. Browning, M. Tașcă, C. Falcó, R. E. Baker, "Structural identifiability analysis of linear reaction-advection-diffusion processes in mathematical biology", Proceedings of the Royal Society A 480(2286):20230911 (arXiv:2309.15326)
papers.what_it_shows: Fetched arXiv record. Extends the differential-algebra approach to structural identifiability to PDE models that are linear in unobserved quantities, covering reaction-advection-diffusion systems; finds that adding advection and diffusion to a non-spatial model cannot decrease structural identifiability. Note: a Correction to this paper was published in Proc. R. Soc. A 482(2340):20260384, which should be cited alongside it.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The nearest published machinery for making a structural (not just practical) identifiability statement about our column: advection + dispersion + linear exchange with a solid phase, observed at the boundary. In the Henry/linear limit our system is exactly of this class, so a structural result there is derivable and citable rather than merely empirical.

papers.citation: H. Byrne, H. Harrington, A. Ovchinnikov, G. Pogudin, H. Rahkooy, P. Soto, "Algebraic identifiability of partial differential equation models", arXiv:2402.04241
papers.what_it_shows: Fetched abstract. Develops theory and algorithms based on differential algebra for testing identifiability of polynomial PDE models, explicitly addressing the initial/boundary-condition complications that had blocked a general PDE identifiability theory. The abstract does not confirm advection-diffusion-reaction with boundary-only observation as a worked example — I could not verify that from the abstract alone.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Together with Browning et al. and StructuralIdentifiability.jl, this is the toolchain for the structural half of the argument. Our system is polynomial/rational after clearing the Do-Do denominators, so it is in scope in principle.

papers.citation: S. Prabhu et al., "Derivative-Free Domain-Informed Data-Driven Discovery of Sparse Kinetic Models", Industrial & Engineering Chemistry Research 64(5):2601-2615
papers.what_it_shows: Bibliographic record verified via Crossref (first author Siddharth Prabhu, IECR 64(5):2601-2615, 2025). Search summaries describe a derivative-free (integral-form) sparse discovery of kinetic ODEs from batch and plug-flow reactor exit-concentration data, with domain constraints built in. I did not fetch the full text.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The chemical-engineering-native version of the weak-form argument, published in the journal family our paper is closest to. It is the natural citation for 'derivative-free sparse kinetics from reactor exit data' and shows that our exit-curve-only setting is a recognised, hard case in the CRE literature too.

papers.citation: M. Á. de Carvalho Servia, I. O. Sandoval, K. K. Hii, K. Hellgardt, D. Zhang, E. A. del Rio Chanona, "The automated discovery of kinetic rate models — methodological frameworks", Digital Discovery 3:954-... (2024); preprint arXiv:2301.11356
papers.what_it_shows: Record retrieved via Semantic Scholar (DOI, venue, authors, abstract snippet). Proposes ADoK-S and ADoK-W — automated discovery of kinetic rate models via genetic-programming symbolic regression in a 'strong' (fit the rate) and 'weak' (fit the integrated concentration trajectory) formulation, with a principled model-selection criterion. Explicitly states that ALAMO, SINDy and plain genetic programming suffer from needing model-structure assumptions, poor scalability, and noise sensitivity. Page range not verified.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The direct domain analogue of what our retracted A7 claimed to do, published two years before our submission, in a venue a reviewer will know. It sets the bar for what 'discovery of kinetics' has to look like in 2026: a model-selection criterion over a Pareto front, not a threshold sweep. It also names the strong-vs-weak distinction in exactly our vocabulary.

papers.citation: M. Á. de Carvalho Servia, I. O. Sandoval, K. K. Hii, K. Hellgardt, D. Zhang, E. A. del Rio Chanona, "Constraint-Guided Symbolic Regression for Data-Efficient Kinetic Model Discovery" (PI-ADoK), arXiv:2507.02730
papers.what_it_shows: Fetched abstract. Embeds physical constraints directly in the symbolic-regression search to shrink the space, plus Metropolis-Hastings uncertainty quantification over discovered models; claims a substantial reduction in the number of experiments needed for model convergence across catalytic case studies. The abstract gives no numeric reduction and does not explicitly say 'model-based design of experiments'.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Shows the 2025-2026 direction of travel: constrained symbolic regression + UQ + experiment-count as the headline metric. If we run any symbolic experiment, 'how many simulated conditions did it take' is a more publishable metric than 'did it recover the planted law'.

papers.citation: R. Aliaga Medina, P. Quintanilla, A. E. del Rio Chanona, "DASyR-LLM: Domain-Aware Symbolic Regression with LLMs for Kinetic Model Discovery", arXiv:2608.05120
papers.what_it_shows: Fetched abstract. An LLM embedded inside an iterative symbolic-regression loop, critiquing candidate rate expressions physicochemically and proposing new ones; reduces iterations to find the ground-truth model by 41.7-79.3% versus a state-of-the-art SR framework, with the LLM proposing the correct structure outright in over half of guided runs, at matched R^2 > 0.98.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is what 'current' looks like in 2026 for kinetic model discovery. It matters mainly as a positioning fact: a paper whose symbolic-discovery component is 2017-era polynomial STRidge will read as two generations behind. Either modernise the component or drop it and say why.

papers.citation: Y. Hou, T. Ji, D. Zhang, A. Stefanidis, "Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks: A Critical Assessment of Claims, Performance, and Practical Viability", arXiv:2407.11075
papers.what_it_shows: Fetched abstract. Under parameter- and compute-matched comparison, KANs outperform MLPs ONLY on symbolic regression, and consistently underperform on ML, vision and NLP benchmarks; computational overhead 1.36-100x; the claimed advantages trace to B-spline activations rather than architecture; the curse-of-dimensionality claims lack rigorous foundation. Search summaries additionally report a systematic absence of statistical rigour in the KAN literature (single-seed point estimates, ignoring B-spline optimisation instability) — that specific sentence I saw in search summaries, not in the fetched abstract.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Two-edged. It is a strong ally for L3 (MLP beats RBF-KAN and Chebyshev-KAN at matched parameters, 8/9 significant) and for defect B22 (our own observed KAN training collapse — 10/45 DeepOKAN collapses vs 0/45 DeepONet — is precisely the instability this paper says the field under-reports). But it also scopes L3's claim: KANs' one documented advantage is symbolic regression, which is the one thing we did not test. A referee will point that out.

papers.citation: Z. Liu, P. Ma, Y. Wang, W. Matusik, M. Tegmark, "KAN 2.0: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks Meet Science", arXiv:2408.10205
papers.what_it_shows: From search results only. Framework for using KANs in scientific discovery along three axes — identifying relevant features, revealing modular structure, and extracting symbolic formulas — plus MultKAN (multiplication nodes) and 'kanpiler', which compiles symbolic formulas into KANs. I did not fetch the abstract.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: If we want to close the interpretability gap L3 leaves open, this is the documented pipeline. The honest test is on a LOW-dimensional target where symbolic extraction is plausible — the two-wave warp shifts t_lo(z), t_hi(z) as functions of descriptors — not on the full field.

papers.citation: M. Cranmer, "Interpretable Machine Learning for Science with PySR and SymbolicRegression.jl", arXiv:2305.01582
papers.what_it_shows: From search results only. Multi-population evolutionary symbolic regression with an evolve-simplify-optimize loop and a high-performance Julia backend; designed for scientific use including constant optimisation in discovered expressions. A peer-reviewed review of PySR also exists in Genetic Programming and Evolvable Machines (2024).
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The pragmatic tool for the one genuinely-unknown low-dimensional function in this project: the warp predictor. Our best warp predictor is currently an HGB black box at R^2 = +0.895/+0.919 giving predicted-warp nRMSE 0.0508 against an oracle 0.0233. A symbolic warp law would be both more interpretable and more likely to extrapolate to novel materials, and it would fill the slot A7 vacated with something that is actually a discovery rather than a recovery.

papers.citation: S.-M. Udrescu, M. Tegmark, "AI Feynman: A physics-inspired method for symbolic regression", Science Advances 6(16):eaay2631
papers.what_it_shows: From search results only. Recursive symbolic regression combining neural-network fitting with physics-inspired simplifications (symmetry, separability, dimensional analysis); recovers all 100 Feynman equations vs 71 for prior public software, and lifts a harder benchmark from 15% to 90% success.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Mainly as the canonical prior citation, and for one transferable idea we should adopt regardless of tool: dimensional-analysis-constrained search. Our warp/kinetics targets have known units and known limiting behaviour (Henry's law as c->0, constant-pattern as N->inf), which are exactly the constraints that make symbolic search tractable.

papers.citation: W. La Cava, P. Orzechowski, B. Burlacu, F. O. de França, M. Virgolin, Y. Jin, M. Kommenda, J. H. Moore, "Contemporary Symbolic Regression Methods and their Relative Performance", NeurIPS 2021 Datasets and Benchmarks Track (arXiv:2107.14351)
papers.what_it_shows: From search results only. SRBench: 14 symbolic-regression methods and 7 other ML methods across 252 problems, including ground-truth and real-world datasets; a living benchmark framework.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: If we run symbolic regression we must justify the method choice against a benchmark rather than by availability. It is also the counter-citation to any claim that a particular SR tool is 'best'.

papers.citation: A. A. Kaptanoglu et al., "PySINDy: A comprehensive Python package for robust sparse system identification", Journal of Open Source Software 7(69):3994
papers.what_it_shows: Bibliographic record verified via Crossref. The reference implementation, which now ships weak/integral-form SINDy, SINDy-PI, ensembling, and SINDy with control as first-class features, plus a documented 'practical tips' page on derivative estimation and library conditioning.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Reviewers will ask why we hand-rolled stridge() rather than using the standard package. Using PySINDy's weak-form and ensemble features costs almost nothing and removes an entire class of 'implementation defect' objection — particularly given retraction A7 already documents a hand-rolled library with condition number 1.07e44 and numerical rank 1 of 12.

papers.citation: R. Kober et al., "D-optimal experimental designs for precise parameter estimation of adsorption equilibrium models", Chemometrics and Intelligent Laboratory Systems 192:103823 (2019); and "...: initial concentration and solvent volume to adsorbent mass ratio as independent variables", Adsorption 27:1013-1022 (2021)
papers.what_it_shows: Both bibliographic records verified via Crossref. D-optimal (maximise det of the Fisher information matrix) designs for adsorption equilibrium models — Langmuir, Freundlich, Sips, Redlich-Peterson, BET — choosing which concentrations and solid/liquid ratios to measure so parameters are precisely estimable.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Establishes that FIM-based design is already standard in adsorption for EQUILIBRIUM parameters, which sets up an obvious and defensible gap we can fill: the same treatment for the KINETIC parameter in a column. Our 17 operating conditions per material were chosen by hand; choosing them to maximise information about k_LDF is a cheap, novel methodological contribution that would directly rescue L6.
