L/d_p = 50 and D_in/d_p = 25 sit right at the conventional lower bounds for neglecting channelling and wall bypass in an axially-dispersed plug-flow model; defensible, but state it. Δz/d_p = 0.025 means your grid cell is 40× smaller than a particle — numerically fine (you are resolving a PDE, not a packing), but say so explicitly before someone else says it for you. And check the Anzelius (1926, ZAMM) citation — I could not verify it in Crossref; Schumann (1929, J. Franklin Inst. 208:405) I did verify, and the safe form is "Anzelius–Schumann" citing Schumann.

papers.citation: Shrinjay Sharma, Salvador R. G. Balestra, Richard Baur, Umang Agarwal, Erik Zuidema, Marcello S. Rigutto, Sofia Calero, Thijs J. H. Vlugt, David Dubbeldam — "RUPTURA: simulation code for breakthrough, ideal adsorption solution theory computations, and fitting of isotherm models", Molecular Simulation 49(9):893–953
papers.what_it_shows: The reference open-source breakthrough simulator for the MOF community. I read src/breakthrough.cpp directly: it uses FIRST-ORDER UPWIND advection with SSP-RK(3,3) explicit time stepping, grid points read from input, and NO energy balance — mass/pressure only. Supports 13 isotherm models (Langmuir, anti-Langmuir, BET, Henry, Freundlich, Sips, Langmuir-Freundlich, Redlich-Peterson, Toth, Unilan, O'Brien-Myers, quadratic, Temkin); Do-Do is not among them.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the single strongest defense of our numerics. The community's own reference code uses the same advection scheme we do, integrates it EXPLICITLY (we use implicit BDF with an analytic Jacobian sparsity pattern), and does not solve an energy balance at all. Cite it in the methods paragraph: our solver is a strict superset of the field-standard tool. It also tells us the expected isotherm vocabulary — 'Langmuir-Freundlich', not 'Do-Do'.

papers.citation: Jan Michael Breuer, Samuel Leweke, Johannes Schmölder, Gregor Gassner, Eric von Lieres — "Spatial discontinuous Galerkin spectral element method for a family of chromatography models in CADET", Computers & Chemical Engineering 177:108340
papers.what_it_shows: Arbitrary-order DG spectral element discretisation for the general rate model and simpler column models, coupled to implicit adaptive BDF (up to 5th order) in time; reports ~an order of magnitude speed-up over finite volume at engineering-relevant error levels.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the highest bar a numerics referee could hold us to, and it defines the honest framing: higher-order methods win on COST at fixed accuracy, not on validity. We should say explicitly that DG/WENO would let us reach the same accuracy at far fewer cells, that we chose monotone upwind because the limiter wrecks BDF Newton convergence (we measured 9x), and that we paid for it with N_z = 2000 — with the Pe_cell < 0.05 bound as proof the payment was sufficient.

papers.citation: Bijan Medi, Mohammad Amanullah — "Application of a Finite-Volume Method in the Simulation of Chromatographic Systems: Effects of Flux Limiters", Industrial & Engineering Chemistry Research 50(3):1739–1748
papers.what_it_shows: Systematic comparison of flux limiters for column chromatography; finds the van Leer limiter best on the accuracy/CPU trade-off across linear and nonlinear conditions.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: We already implemented van Leer MUSCL (_van_leer_div in solver_fd.py) and rejected it on wall time. This paper is the citation that shows we picked the right limiter to test, and it lets us frame our rejection as a measured trade-off against the recommended scheme rather than an untested shortcut. Our 9x cost / 6x Jacobian-factorisation measurement is a publishable observation in its own right, because their comparison is against explicit integrators where the limiter is cheap.

papers.citation: Shumaila Javeed, Shamsul Qamar, Andreas Seidel-Morgenstern, Gerald Warnecke — "Efficient and accurate numerical simulation of nonlinear chromatographic processes", Computers & Chemical Engineering 35(11):2294–2305
papers.what_it_shows: Semi-discrete high-resolution flux-limiting finite-volume scheme for nonlinear fixed-bed models with axial dispersion and finite mass-transfer kinetics; benchmarks against analytical solutions and other discretisations.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Establishes the norm this referee community holds: a numerics claim in fixed-bed adsorption is validated against analytic limits AND against an independent higher-order discretisation. We currently do only the first. A scheme-independence spot-check (upwind at N_z=2000 vs van Leer at N_z=500 on ~10 production cases) closes that gap cheaply.

papers.citation: Reza Haghpanah, Aniruddha Majumder, Ricky Nilam, Arvind Rajendran, Shamsuzzaman Farooq, Iftekhar A. Karimi, Mohammad Amanullah — "Multiobjective Optimization of a Four-Step Adsorption Process for Postcombustion CO2 Capture Via Finite Volume Simulation", Industrial & Engineering Chemistry Research 52(11):4249–4265
papers.what_it_shows: The standard reference comparing high-resolution TVD (van Leer, Superbee) against WENO finite volume for adsorption column simulation; concludes WENO permits far fewer finite volumes without sacrificing accuracy.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the paper a Sep&Pur/AIChE J referee will have in mind when they ask 'why not WENO?'. The answer we should give is quantitative and disarming: at N_z=2000 our numerical dispersion is bounded at 2.5% of the physical D_L everywhere in the parameter space, so a higher-order scheme would buy speed, not accuracy — and speed was never the binding constraint (4.2 s/condition).

papers.citation: Howard Brenner — "The diffusion model of longitudinal mixing in beds of finite length. Numerical values", Chemical Engineering Science 17(4):229–243
papers.what_it_shows: The canonical closed-form solution for the finite-length axially-dispersed plug-flow column with Danckwerts inlet and outlet boundary conditions, with tabulated numerical values.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: We verify the tracer case against van Genuchten & Alves (1982), a USDA soil-physics technical bulletin. That solution is correct, but for a Chemical Engineering Science / AIChE J audience Brenner (1962) is THE reference for exactly this problem and is the one the referee expects to see. Cite Brenner alongside (or instead of) van Genuchten — same physics, right community, zero cost.

papers.citation: Adriaan Klinkenberg — "Numerical Evaluation of Equations Describing Transient Heat and Mass Transfer in Packed Solids", Industrial & Engineering Chemistry 40(10):1992–1994
papers.what_it_shows: The closed-form approximation to the Anzelius/Schumann J-function for the linear-isotherm LDF column, accurate over the practical range.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the primary citation for our L0 LDF benchmark AND for the L7 classical baseline. We should make sure the same reference is doing both jobs explicitly, and be careful not to double-count: a solution used to verify the solver cannot then be presented as an independent competitor without saying so.

papers.citation: T. E. W. Schumann — "Heat transfer: A liquid flowing through a porous prism", Journal of the Franklin Institute 208(3):405–416
papers.what_it_shows: The original two-equation transient packed-bed heat-exchange solution whose kernel is the J-function used in our L0 Anzelius-Schumann check.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Verified and citable. NOTE: I could NOT verify the companion Anzelius (1926, ZAMM 6:291) citation in Crossref — it predates DOI coverage. Either verify it against a physical copy or cite the pair as 'Anzelius-Schumann (Schumann 1929)'. A fabricated or mis-paged 1926 citation is exactly the kind of thing a careful referee spot-checks.

papers.citation: J. B. Rosen — "Kinetics of a Fixed Bed System for Solid Diffusion into Spherical Particles", The Journal of Chemical Physics 20(3):387–394
papers.what_it_shows: Exact transient solution for a linear fixed bed with combined film resistance and intraparticle solid diffusion.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The benchmark we are MISSING. Our four L0 checks verify advection+dispersion+BC, equilibrium retardation, a passive thermal wave, and LDF. None verifies an intraparticle diffusion model — because we don't have one. If we add the pore-diffusion spot-check recommended below, Rosen is its verification case, and adding it makes the L0 rung look like a real code-verification suite rather than four convenient limits.

papers.citation: K. R. Hall, L. C. Eagleton, Andreas Acrivos, Theodore Vermeulen — "Pore- and Solid-Diffusion Kinetics in Fixed-Bed Adsorption under Constant-Pattern Conditions", Industrial & Engineering Chemistry Fundamentals 5(2):212–223
papers.what_it_shows: The canonical constant-pattern analysis for favourable isotherms in fixed beds, including the closed-form constant-pattern profiles used throughout the adsorption literature.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Two uses. (1) Verification: our cooperative branch IS a self-sharpening constant-pattern shock; driving the solver to the constant-pattern limit and matching this closed form would verify the NONLINEAR isotherm in the production regime, which nothing currently does. (2) Provenance: L7's 'constant-pattern' baseline needs a real citation and this is it.

papers.citation: S. Sircar, J. R. Hufton — "Why Does the Linear Driving Force Model for Adsorption Kinetics Work?", Adsorption 6(2):137–147
papers.what_it_shows: Although isothermal batch uptake curves from LDF and Fickian diffusion differ substantially, the particle-level kinetic distinction is repeatedly averaged away when computing packed-column breakthrough curves and process separation efficiency — which is why LDF works in column dynamics specifically.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the defense of our LDF choice and it must be cited in the methodology section. It is the pre-emption of the most predictable referee objection. Crucially it defends LDF FOR BREAKTHROUGH, which is exactly our observable — do not overstate it into a defense of LDF for uptake kinetics.

papers.citation: D. D. Do, R. G. Rice — "Validity of the parabolic profile assumption in adsorption studies", AIChE Journal 32(1):149–154
papers.what_it_shows: Establishes when the parabolic intraparticle concentration profile — the assumption that yields k = 15D/R^2 — is and is not valid, and shows it degrades for nonlinear systems and at high fractional uptake.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Direct evidence that a single constant k_LDF is least trustworthy exactly where our Type V cooperative shock lives (fractional uptake -> 1, extreme isotherm nonlinearity). Cite as an acknowledged limitation rather than letting a referee introduce it.

papers.citation: Andreas Georgiou, Krzysztof Kupiec — "Nonlinear driving force approximation for intraparticle mass transfer in adsorption processes", Chemical Engineering Journal 92(1-3):185–191; and Andreas Georgiou — "Asymptotically exact driving force approximation for intraparticle mass transfer rate in diffusion and adsorption processes: nonlinear isotherm systems with macropore diffusion control", Chemical Engineering Science 59(17):3591–3600
papers.what_it_shows: Explicit nonlinear-driving-force (NLDF) corrections built specifically because constant-coefficient LDF carries large errors for nonlinear isotherm systems under macropore diffusion control; the NLDF forms are accurate over the whole time domain where LDF is not.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The concrete, cheap upgrade path if we want to answer the LDF objection with a computation rather than a citation. An NLDF variant is a drop-in replacement for the one line `dq_dt = k_LDF*(q_star - q)` in solver_fd.py, so a bounded-error study over ~20 production conditions is a day of work and converts a limitation into a quantified sensitivity.

papers.citation: Chunye Ma, Jiawang Li, Guang Wang, Zhigang Li, Wei Su, Yanguang Zhou — "Microscopic Kinetics of Water Adsorption in Metal–Organic Frameworks", Nano Letters 25(14):5778–5783
papers.what_it_shows: At low relative humidity water molecules adsorb and diffuse freely in MOFs, consistent with linear-driving-force / Fickian description; at high RH water condenses into liquid clusters before diffusing, requiring a two-concentration framework. Validated across UiO-66, CAU-10-H, MOF-801, MIL-101 and MOF-303.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The most dangerous single citation for our kinetics assumption, and it is recent enough that a MOF-water referee will certainly know it. It says the LDF coefficient should CHANGE across the Type V step — precisely the step our entire two-wave physics story is built on. We must acknowledge it explicitly. It also independently supports our qualitative picture (two mechanisms, two regimes), so framed correctly it is corroboration, not refutation.

papers.citation: D. D. Do, H. D. Do — "A model for water adsorption in activated carbon", Carbon 38(5):767–773
papers.what_it_shows: The actual Do–Do model: water hydrogen-bonds onto surface functional groups, clusters nucleate and grow to a critical size (~5 molecules), and only then does micropore filling begin. Expressed in relative pressure with 5–6 parameters (q_sat, f, K_f, K_mu, cluster size n, m).
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: CRITICAL: our isotherm is NOT this model. isotherm.py implements q_max[f_H*bc/(1+bc) + (1-f_H)(b_C c)^n/(1+(b_C c)^n)], which is a dual-site Langmuir–Freundlich / Langmuir+Sips form in concentration with 4 parameters, sharing neither the functional form nor the physical mechanism. Every 'Do–Do' label in isotherm.py, 03_LADDER_PROTOCOL.md, RESULTS.md and the manuscript drafts is a misattribution that a water-adsorption referee catches instantly and that would cast doubt on everything else. This must be renamed before anything is submitted.

papers.citation: Anutosh Chakraborty, Baichuan Sun — "An adsorption isotherm equation for multi-types adsorption with thermodynamic correctness", Applied Thermal Engineering 72:190–199
papers.what_it_shows: The Sun–Chakraborty isotherm: a Fermi–Dirac-distribution-derived reformulation of Langmuir including loading, adsorbate–adsorbent interaction and surface heterogeneity, validated against all IUPAC isotherm types including S-shaped Type V (silica gel + water, ACF + ethanol, Maxsorb + HFC-134a).
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The model most likely to be named by a referee from the adsorption-cooling / AWH community as 'the standard for S-shaped water isotherms'. We should name it, say why we did not use it (it does not decompose into a Henry-carrying site plus a cooperative site, which is the structure H1/L6 requires us to identify separately), and thereby show we know the field. A one-paragraph comparison here is worth more than another experiment.

papers.citation: Shiue-Min Shih, Li-Chiang Lin — "Water Adsorption in Metal–Organic Frameworks: Characteristics, Mechanisms, and Structure–Property Relationships", Journal of the American Chemical Society 147:34791–34803
papers.what_it_shows: Current canonical review of MOF water adsorption: S-shaped/Type V isotherms with steps typically between ~15–35% RH, mechanisms of pore filling, and structure–property relationships governing step position.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The 2025-2026 reference a referee expects in the introduction of any MOF-water paper, and the correct source for justifying our step_rh sampling range (0.08–0.45). Our range extends below the reported ~15% lower edge — either justify the extension as deliberate coverage or cite this to narrow it. Also the right place to source real material parameters to replace the uncited MOF-303 placeholders in retraction A4.

papers.citation: Mathijs H. B. Born, Niels De Witte, Joeri F. M. Denayer, Tom R. C. Van Assche — "An insulated column for lab-scale non-isothermal breakthrough: Impact of thermal effects during CO2 adsorption", Chemical Engineering Science 276:118810
papers.what_it_shows: Lab-scale breakthrough measured under adiabatic, near-adiabatic and non-adiabatic conditions with axial and radial temperature profiles; an uninsulated steel column showed a temperature rise of only ~12 K and roughly 20% lower efficiency versus the insulated case, because of wall heat loss and wall thermal mass.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Our energy balance has a wall-loss term -(4 h_w/D_in)(T - T_w) with h_w hard-coded at 10 W/m2/K and NO wall thermal capacitance. This paper is the experimental evidence that at lab scale that is a first-order modelling decision, not a detail. Either add a lumped wall energy balance or run and report the two bracketing limits (adiabatic h_w=0 and isothermal-wall h_w->inf) so the referee sees the sensitivity bounded rather than ignored.

papers.citation: Ugochukwu David Uche, Shamsul Qamar, Andreas Seidel-Morgenstern — "Analytical solution of non-isothermal two-dimensional general rate model of liquid chromatography", Adsorption 25:1487–1509; and Abdulaziz Garba Ahmad, Shamsul Qamar, Andreas Seidel-Morgenstern — "Linearized non-equilibrium and non-isothermal two-dimensional model of liquid chromatography for studying thermal effects in cylindrical columns", J. Liquid Chromatography & Related Technologies 42:436–451
papers.what_it_shows: Closed-form (Laplace/eigenfunction) solutions for column models in which the energy balance is COUPLED to the mass balance through a linearised temperature-dependent isotherm — i.e. adsorption heat feeds back into equilibrium.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the missing fifth L0 benchmark. Every one of our current four checks decouples the physics (adsorption off, or linear isotherm, or thermal wave with adsorption off). The coupling term — heat_factor*dq_dt feeding q_star(c,T) — is the most error-prone line in solver_fd.py and is verified by nothing. Linearising our isotherm about a reference state and matching one of these solutions converts the strongest available referee objection into a table row.

papers.citation: Patrick J. Roache — "Code Verification by the Method of Manufactured Solutions", Journal of Fluids Engineering 124(1):4–10 (see also Salari & Knupp, SAND2000-1444)
papers.what_it_shows: Standard methodology for verifying a code's full nonlinear coupled operator by manufacturing an exact solution and adding the corresponding source terms, together with the grid-convergence-index framework for reporting observed order of accuracy.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The gold-standard answer to 'but your benchmarks all switch off part of the physics'. MMS on the full 3-equation coupled system with the actual Type V isotherm — add source terms so a chosen smooth (c,q,T) is exact — would demonstrate the observed order of accuracy of the ACTUAL production operator, which no analytic limit can. Also: we report 'error halves as N_z doubles' but never a fitted observed order p or a GCI, which is the number this framework expects.

papers.citation: Disha Brahma, N. Dwarkanath, S. Balasubramanian — "Insights into Isotherm Step and Pore-Filling Mechanisms for Water Adsorption in Covalent Organic Frameworks", Chemistry of Materials
papers.what_it_shows: Molecular-level analysis of the isotherm step and pore-filling mechanism for water adsorption specifically in COFs.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Directly addresses open item #3 — the title claims a COF case and none exists. This gives real COF water-adsorption step behaviour to parameterise at least one genuine COF material, which would both fix the title and broaden the material axis where the learning curve (1.82x over 12->48 materials, not saturated) says we have the most to gain.

papers.citation: Muhammad Hassan, Sunghyun Yoon, Yu Chen, Pilseok Kim, Hongryeol Yun, Hyuk Taek Kwon, Youn-Sang Bae, Chung-Yul Yoo, Dong-Yeun Koh, Chang-Seop Hong, Ki-Bong Lee, Yongchul G. Chung — "AIM: A User-friendly GUI Workflow program for Isotherm Fitting, Mixture Prediction, Isosteric Heat of Adsorption Estimation, and Breakthrough Simulation", arXiv:2504.20713
papers.what_it_shows: Current-generation community workflow tool: 13 isotherm models, IAST mixture prediction, isosteric heat estimation and breakthrough simulation; validated against literature experimental data for a ternary CO2/H2/N2 mixture including outlet compositions AND temperature profiles.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Two things. (a) It shows the 2025 community validation norm is 'compare to an experimental breakthrough including the temperature profile' — which is exactly our open item #2 (no experimental validation at all). Even ONE literature comparison would move us from 'verified' to 'verified and validated'. (b) Neither AIM's 13 models nor RUPTURA's 13 include Do-Do, reinforcing that our isotherm should be named by the standard vocabulary (dual-site Langmuir-Freundlich) that these tools use.

papers.citation: S. W. Rutherford — "Application of cooperative multimolecular sorption theory for characterization of water adsorption equilibrium in carbon", Carbon 41:622–625
papers.what_it_shows: Applies the cooperative multimolecular sorption (CMMS) framework (originating with Malakhov & Volkov) to Type V water isotherms in carbons.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: One of the named alternatives a referee may raise alongside Do-Do, GAB and Dubinin-Serpinsky. Worth a single sentence in the isotherm-choice paragraph so the paragraph reads as a survey rather than a defense of one arbitrary form. Low priority relative to the naming fix.

papers.citation: M. Th. van Genuchten, W. J. Alves — "Analytical Solutions of the One-Dimensional Convective-Dispersive Solute Transport Equation", USDA Technical Bulletin No. 1661, U.S. Department of Agriculture
papers.url_or_id: USDA Tech. Bull. 1661 (reviewed in Earth-Science Reviews 19:177-178, DOI 10.1016/0012-8252(83)90054-5)
papers.what_it_shows: Compendium of closed-form solutions to the 1-D advection-dispersion equation under first-, second- and third-type inlet conditions — the source of our third-type (flux-type) tracer benchmark.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The underlying solution is real and our use of it is correct. But I could only verify it in Crossref via a 1983 Earth-Science Reviews REVIEW of the bulletin, not the bulletin itself — it is a USDA technical bulletin without a DOI. Two consequences: (a) format the citation as a technical bulletin, not a journal article, or a referee will fail to find it; (b) for a ChemE venue, pair it with or replace it by Brenner (1962) CES 17:229, which is the same physics in the referee's own literature.

papers.citation: S. Nakao, M. Suzuki — "Mass transfer coefficient in cyclic adsorption and desorption", Journal of Chemical Engineering of Japan (1983)
papers.what_it_shows: Reported in secondary sources as establishing that the conventional LDF coefficient 15 D/R^2 is inadvisable for transient/cyclic operation, and that the LDF proportionality constant must be modified when the dimensionless half-cycle time falls below ~0.1 of the diffusion time constant.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Relevant only if we report the cyclic-drift metric promised in protocol section 4 (mass and energy imbalance after N adsorption/desorption cycles) — in a cyclic setting the constant-k LDF assumption acquires an additional, well-documented failure mode. I did NOT verify volume, pages or DOI; do not cite it without checking the primary source. If the cyclic metric is dropped, drop this citation too.

papers.citation: Ng and co-workers — "A Universal Isotherm Model to Capture Adsorption Uptake and Energy Distribution of Porous Heterogeneous Surface", Scientific Reports 7
papers.what_it_shows: Energy-distribution-based 'universal' isotherm claimed to capture all IUPAC isotherm types including Type V, widely used in the adsorption-cooling and water-sorption community.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Third named alternative in the isotherm-choice paragraph, alongside Sun-Chakraborty and Dubinin-Astakhov. I located it by search but did not fetch the article body, so verify the author list and article number before citing. Low priority.

implications: THE UPWIND CHOICE IS SAFE AND WE ARE UNDER-SELLING IT. Because D_L is set by the Ruthven correlation (which itself scales with u), the ratio of numerical to physical dispersion is bounded ANALYTICALLY at D_num/D_L <= dz/d_p = 2.5%, independent of velocity, over the whole parameter space. Evaluated at the corners of CONDITION_SPACE: 1.95% (v=0.03, eps=0.48), 2.34% (v=0.10, eps=0.40), 2.46% (v=0.30, eps=0.30). Cell Peclet number u*dz/D_L is 0.039 / 0.047 / 0.049, bounded by dz/(0.5*d_p) = 0.05 — forty times below the Pe_cell = 2 threshold where upwind's artificial diffusion becomes significant. Energy equation likewise: Pe_cell,T = 0.06, D_num,T/alpha_T = 3.0%. This is a proof, not a convergence anecdote, and it belongs in the paper.

RUPTURA — the MOF community's own reference breakthrough code, published in Molecular Simulation 2023 — uses first-order upwind with EXPLICIT SSP-RK3 and has no energy balance whatsoever (verified by reading src/breakthrough.cpp). Our solver is a strict superset: same advection scheme, implicit BDF with analytic Jacobian sparsity, plus a coupled energy equation. The 'is upwind defensible' question is settled in our favour by the field's own tooling.

THE REAL VERIFICATION HOLE IS THE COUPLING, NOT THE SCHEME. All four L0 checks switch off part of the physics: inert tracer, LINEAR-isotherm retarded front, thermal wave with ADSORPTION OFF, LDF against Anzelius-Schumann with a linear isotherm. Nothing verifies the production operator — nonlinear Type V equilibrium with heat of adsorption feeding back into b(T). The line `heat_factor * dq_dt` coupled to `q_star_np(c, T, physics)` is the most error-prone code in the solver and has zero verification coverage. A referee who reads verify_solver.py will notice this in five minutes.

WE REPORT MASS CLOSURE (0.050%) AND NO ENERGY CLOSURE. In a paper whose headline physics is a thermal wave outrunning the mass front, that asymmetry is conspicuous. The Danckwerts inlet fix in laplacian() makes the mass integral telescope exactly; whether the same holds for the energy integral is untested and could be hiding a bug.

THE ISOTHERM IS MISNAMED, AND THIS IS THE HIGHEST-RISK ITEM IN THE WHOLE LENS. isotherm.py implements a dual-site Langmuir-Freundlich (Langmuir + Sips/Hill) equation in concentration with 4 parameters. Do & Do (Carbon 2000) is a cluster-nucleation model in relative pressure with 5-6 parameters and a completely different mechanism (hydrogen bonding to functional groups, critical cluster size ~5, then micropore filling). Neither RUPTURA's nor AIM's 13-model libraries contain Do-Do. Every 'Do-Do' label across isotherm.py, 03_LADDER_PROTOCOL.md, RESULTS.md and the manuscript drafts is a misattribution. The underlying argument — that a bare Hill form violates Henry's law and that adding a Henry-carrying site fixes it — is good and survives the rename intact.

THE k_LDF SAMPLING MAY BE MANUFACTURING THE L6 RESULT. At the reported Damkohler range 155-3885 the column is near local equilibrium, where front width is dispersion-controlled and sensitivity to k_LDF scales like 1/N_TU. That is the most parsimonious physical explanation for L6's finding that k_LDF is unrecoverable from observable descriptors (R^2 = -0.61). If so, L6's conclusion is not a general identifiability statement but a statement about the regime we sampled. This is a threat to a PRE-REGISTERED PRIMARY-HYPOTHESIS result and it must be tested before submission.

TRANSPORT PARAMETERS ARE INTERNALLY INCONSISTENT. D_L is correlated to d_p = 2 mm and v; k_z is a hard-coded 0.10 W/m/K that never varies with velocity, when the standard closure lambda_ax = lambda_static + 0.5*rho_g*c_pg*v*d_p gives 0.036 / 0.120 / 0.360 W/m/K at v = 0.03 / 0.10 / 0.30 — a 3.6x under-dispersion of heat at the top of the range, with the static bed conductivity omitted entirely. Separately, k_LDF in (0.002, 0.05) s^-1 implies D_eff ~ 3e-9 m^2/s, i.e. crystallite control, while D_L is computed from a 2 mm pellet: the two resistances describe different particles unless we say otherwise.

OUR CONSTANT ISOSTERIC HEAT IS A LIMITATION SOLD AS A FEATURE. Because both sites carry the same Delta-H, q_st = -Delta-H exactly at every loading. Real Type V water systems show q_st falling from ~55-60 kJ/mol at low loading toward the enthalpy of vaporisation (~44 kJ/mol) through the pore-filling step. The current framing ('Clausius-Clapeyron satisfied by construction') will be read by a referee as an admission that the model cannot represent the loading dependence that matters for regeneration energy.

THE 2025 MOF-WATER KINETICS LITERATURE DIRECTLY CONTRADICTS A SINGLE CONSTANT k_LDF ACROSS THE STEP. Ma et al. (Nano Lett. 2025) show free diffusion / LDF below the step and cluster condensation requiring a two-concentration framework above it, validated on MOF-303 among others. Sircar & Hufton (2000) is our defense — column breakthrough averages away particle-level kinetic detail — but that defense is about breakthrough specifically and must not be overstated.

THE GEOMETRY NEEDS A SENTENCE OF JUSTIFICATION. L/d_p = 50 and D_in/d_p = 25 sit at the conventional lower bounds for neglecting channelling and wall bypass in an axially-dispersed plug-flow model. And dz/d_p = 0.025 means the grid cell is 40x smaller than a particle — numerically legitimate (we resolve a PDE, not a packing) but it looks odd unless stated. Separately, real AWH devices are thin sorbent layers and monoliths in cyclic operation, not 10 cm packed beds of 2 mm pellets; the honest analogue for our geometry is a desiccant/dehumidification breakthrough column, and framing it that way is more defensible than framing it as an AWH device.
risks_to_our_claims: FATAL-IF-UNFIXED: 'We use a dual-term Do-Do isotherm.' A referee from the water-adsorption community knows the Do-Do model is a cluster-nucleation equation in relative pressure with a critical cluster size, not a Langmuir+Sips sum in concentration. Once they catch one misattributed model name in the methods, they read the remaining 1500 lines of protocol with the assumption that other claims are equally loosely sourced. This single word threatens the credibility of the entire ladder.

'Verified against 4 closed-form solutions.' A careful referee will open the verification script and observe that all four solutions require switching off the very physics that makes the paper interesting: no nonlinear equilibrium, no adsorption-heat feedback, no two-wave structure. The natural sentence in the report is: 'the authors verify a solver they do not use.' Since the solver IS the dataset, this undermines every rung above L0 simultaneously.
'Global mass balance closes to 0.050%.' Immediate follow-up: and the energy balance? Silence here is worse than a mediocre number, because the paper's distinguishing physics is thermal.

'k_LDF is unrecoverable from observable descriptors (R^2 = -0.61)' — the measured cause behind the L6 / H1 negative result. A referee computes the Damkohler range from our own reported parameters, sees 155-3885, and points out that near local equilibrium the breakthrough curve is asymptotically insensitive to k_LDF by construction. The identifiability finding then reads as an artifact of the sampling design rather than a property of surrogate models. This is the single most damaging attack available, because it lands on the PRIMARY PRE-REGISTERED hypothesis.

'Ruthven correlation for axial dispersion, d_p = 2 mm — defensible to a referee.' The same referee immediately asks why k_z is a hard-coded constant while D_L is correlated, and why k_LDF (implying D_eff ~ 3e-9 m^2/s, crystallite-scale) is sampled independently of the 2 mm pellet that sets D_L. Selective rigour is more damaging than uniform simplification, because it shows we knew the right standard and applied it only where convenient.

'Clean first-order grid convergence.' Numerics referees expect an observed order of accuracy fitted from three or more grids plus a grid convergence index (Roache), not a table where errors approximately halve. As written it is an observation; they want a number with an uncertainty attached.

NOVELTY/FRAMING RISK on the two-wave finding. Dual-site isotherms producing two waves — a spreading proportionate-pattern wave plus a self-sharpening constant-pattern shock — is textbook equilibrium theory (Rhee/Aris/Amundson; Hall et al. 1966 for the constant-pattern branch). If we present the two-wave structure as a discovery rather than as a correctly-reproduced known consequence of dual-site equilibrium, a referee will call it naive. Present it as verification that our solver reproduces classical multi-wave behaviour, and reserve the novelty claim for the two-wave WARP (n-width 31 -> 13-17 modes, oracle 0.0203 beating DeepONet's 0.0281), which is genuinely ours.

WALL EFFECTS. h_w = 10 W/m^2/K constant, no wall thermal capacitance, no correlation. Born et al. (CES 2023) demonstrate experimentally that at lab scale this is a first-order choice — an uninsulated column showed ~20% lower efficiency and a strongly suppressed temperature rise. A referee who works on lab breakthrough will ask which limit we are in, and we currently cannot say.

SPEED CLAIM. Open item #5 already flags this. Any claim of surrogate speedup benchmarked against our OWN unoptimised solver (4.2 s/condition at N_z = 2000) is circular. RUPTURA's explicit upwind solver and CADET's DG-SEM are both orders of magnitude faster per solve; if either would run our cases in milliseconds, the speedup motivation for a surrogate evaporates. Benchmark against a competent implementation or drop the claim entirely.

MISSING EXPERIMENTAL VALIDATION (open item #2) is now measurably below the 2025 community norm: the AIM workflow paper validates against literature experimental breakthrough data INCLUDING temperature profiles. A verification-only paper with a Type V water isotherm and zero contact with data will draw the comment that the entire 988-simulation dataset is a self-consistent fiction.

CITATION HYGIENE: I could not verify the Anzelius (1926, ZAMM) reference in Crossref. Schumann (1929, J. Franklin Inst. 208:405-416) is verified. Also, van Genuchten & Alves (1982) is a USDA technical bulletin without a DOI and is cited in a ChemE venue where Brenner (1962, CES 17:229) is the expected reference for the identical problem. Neither is an error of substance, but both are the kind of thing that gets spot-checked.

concrete_actions.action: Rename the isotherm everywhere: 'dual-site Langmuir-Freundlich (Langmuir + Sips/Hill cooperative term)', NOT 'Do-Do'. Update isotherm.py's docstring, 03_LADDER_PROTOCOL.md section 6, RESULTS.md, 01_INTRODUCTION.md, 02_METHODOLOGY_JUSTIFICATION.md, and log it in RETRACTIONS.md as a correction. Keep the Henry's-law argument verbatim — it is correct and it is ours. Add a one-paragraph survey naming Do & Do (Carbon 2000), Sun-Chakraborty (Appl. Therm. Eng. 2014), Dubinin-Astakhov, GAB and CMMS, and stating why the DSLF decomposition is required by H1 (it is the only common form that cleanly separates a Henry-carrying equilibrium object from a cooperative one).
concrete_actions.rationale: The current name is a factual misattribution to a model with a different functional form, different variables and a different physical mechanism, in the one area (water adsorption) where our referee pool is most expert. It costs an hour to fix and it is the difference between a methods section that reads as expert and one that reads as generated. Nothing else on this list matters if this stays.

concrete_actions.action: Add the numerical-dispersion bound to the methods, as an analytic result rather than a convergence table. State: D_num/D_L = (u*dz/2)/(0.7*D_m + 0.5*d_p*u) <= dz/d_p = 2.5% for ALL velocities; evaluated at the corners of CONDITION_SPACE it is 1.95%, 2.34%, 2.46%; cell Peclet u*dz/D_L is 0.039-0.049, bounded by dz/(0.5*d_p) = 0.05, i.e. 40x below the Pe_cell = 2 threshold; for the energy equation Pe_cell,T = 0.06 and D_num,T/alpha_T = 3.0%. Add a table column reporting max Pe_cell over all 988 runs. Then cite RUPTURA (Mol. Simul. 2023) — first-order upwind, explicit SSP-RK3, no energy balance — as the community reference implementation, and Breuer et al. (2023) / Haghpanah et al. (2013) to acknowledge that DG/WENO would buy cost, not accuracy.
concrete_actions.rationale: Converts the single most predictable numerics objection ('first-order upwind in 2026?') from a defense into an offense. 'Error halves as N_z doubles' is an anecdote; a velocity-independent 2.5% bound on the equivalent dispersion is a proof, and it happens to be true because we correlated D_L to d_p. All numbers verified by direct computation from the frozen config.

concrete_actions.action: Compute and report global ENERGY balance closure alongside the existing 0.050% mass closure: d/dt integral[C_term*T]dz = v*rho_g*C_pg*(T_in - T_exit) + (1-eps)*rho_p*(-dH)*integral[dq/dt]dz - (4*h_w/D_in)*integral[(T - T_w)]dz. Verify that the inlet-face treatment in laplacian() makes the energy sum telescope exactly the way it does for mass. Stamp the closure per sample in the dataset manifest exactly as the grid-convergence error is stamped.
concrete_actions.rationale: The paper's distinguishing physics is thermal; reporting only mass closure invites the question and may be hiding a real defect. The Danckwerts inlet bug that produced the 1.02% mass gap was found precisely by this kind of check, and the same class of error in the T equation is currently invisible.

concrete_actions.action: Re-run the L6 identification on a Damkohler-controlled slice. Generate ~200 runs with k_LDF chosen so Da (transfer units on the retarded front, k_LDF*L/u_front) lands in 1-50, holding everything else fixed, and re-fit the k_LDF recovery. Report R^2 versus Da. Then re-scope the L6 claim accordingly: either 'k_LDF is unrecoverable even where the observable is sensitive to it' (much stronger) or 'k_LDF is unrecoverable in the near-equilibrium regime, and recoverable at Da ~ 1-50' (honest, narrower, and a genuinely useful design rule).
concrete_actions.rationale: Our own open item #6 flags Da = 155-3885 (median 626) as under-sampling the informative regime, but the project has not connected that to the L6 result. At Da >> 1 the breakthrough curve is asymptotically insensitive to k_LDF, so 'k_LDF is unrecoverable' may be a restatement of the sampling design rather than a finding about surrogates. This lands on the PRIMARY pre-registered hypothesis, so it is the highest-stakes open question in this lens.

concrete_actions.action: Add a fifth L0 benchmark that verifies the COUPLED mass-energy system. Linearise the DSLF isotherm about a reference (c_ref, T_ref) so that q* = K0 + K_c*c + K_T*(T - T_ref), retain the adsorption-heat source in the energy equation, and match the closed-form solution of Ahmad/Qamar/Seidel-Morgenstern (JLCRT 42:436, 2019) or Uche/Qamar/Seidel-Morgenstern (Adsorption 25:1487, 2019). Report max |c_num - c_ana| and max |T_num - T_ana| in the L0 table.
concrete_actions.rationale: Every current L0 check decouples the physics. The adsorption-heat feedback into b(T) is the most error-prone line in the solver and is verified by nothing. This is the objection that would actually stick in review, and closed-form solutions for exactly this coupled linearised problem exist and are citable.

concrete_actions.action: Add a sixth L0 benchmark in the NONLINEAR production regime, using the equilibrium limit. Drive k_LDF -> large and D_L -> small and check the shock velocity against the exact jump condition u_sh = v/(eps + (1-eps)*rho_p*(dq/dc)) — no fitting, no free parameters. Then verify the finite-kinetics constant-pattern profile of the cooperative branch against Hall/Eagleton/Acrivos/Vermeulen (I&EC Fundam. 5:212, 1966). Report both in the L0 table and note explicitly that Klinkenberg and constant-pattern now serve double duty as L0 verification and L7 baselines.
concrete_actions.rationale: This is the only way to verify the nonlinear Type V equilibrium in the regime the dataset actually occupies, and it costs almost nothing because the classical machinery already exists in classical.py for L7. It also transparently declares the double-use of those solutions, which is better than having a referee notice it.

concrete_actions.action: Replace the hard-coded k_z = 0.10 W/m/K with a velocity-dependent closure lambda_ax = lambda_bed_static + 0.5*rho_g*c_pg*v*d_p (Pe_h,ax -> 2), matching the treatment already given to D_L. Take lambda_bed_static ~ 0.1-0.3 W/m/K for a packed MOF and state the source. Likewise replace h_w = 10 W/m^2/K with a wall-Nusselt correlation, OR keep it fixed and run the two bracketing limits (adiabatic h_w = 0; isothermal wall h_w -> infinity) over ~20 conditions and report the spread on t_50 and dT_max. Cite Born et al. (CES 276:118810, 2023) for why this is first-order at lab scale.
concrete_actions.rationale: Selective rigour is worse than uniform simplification. We correlate D_L and then hard-code the thermal analogue at a value 3.6x too small at the top of our velocity range with the static conductivity missing entirely, in a paper whose headline physics is a thermal wave. NOTE: changing k_z regenerates the dataset and invalidates every rung, so it must be decided now, not after another training campaign. If regeneration is unacceptable, the bracketing-limits sensitivity study is the honest fallback.

concrete_actions.action: Reconcile k_LDF with d_p, in one paragraph. State that k_LDF in (0.002, 0.05) s^-1 corresponds to crystallite/micropore-controlled diffusion (D_eff ~ 3e-9 m^2/s with a crystal-scale radius), NOT to macropore control in the 2 mm pellet that sets D_L via the Ruthven correlation (which would give k ~ 15 s^-1). Either justify the two-scale picture explicitly, or make k_LDF a derived quantity 15*D_c/R_c^2 with R_c sampled as a material property, which has the side benefit of making k_LDF a function of descriptors the surrogate can actually see.
concrete_actions.rationale: As written the two transport resistances describe different particles, which a transport-focused referee will spot. The derived-parameter route additionally changes the L6 identification problem from 'recover a free-floating rate constant' to 'recover a crystallite size', which is a far more physically meaningful and defensible identification target.

concrete_actions.action: Run a scheme-independence check: solve ~10 representative production conditions (spanning the isotherm_n, k_LDF and velocity ranges) with the existing van Leer MUSCL path at N_z = 500 and compare against upwind at N_z = 2000 on the exit curve, t_05/t_50/t_95 and dT_max. Report max discrepancy. Cite Medi & Amanullah (2010) for van Leer being the recommended limiter and Javeed et al. (2011) for the HR-FVS norm.
concrete_actions.rationale: The code already has _van_leer_div; this is running it, not writing it. It converts 'upwind is fine because it converges' into 'upwind agrees with an independent second-order scheme', which is the standard this literature applies and which no grid-refinement study can substitute for (both grids share the same discretisation error mode).

concrete_actions.action: Bound the LDF error for the step isotherm. Implement either a pore/surface-diffusion particle model (verifiable against Rosen 1952) or the Georgiou-Kupiec nonlinear driving force (CEJ 92:185, 2003 / CES 59:3591, 2004) as a drop-in replacement for the single line `dq_dt = k_LDF*(q_star - q)`, and compare breakthrough curves over ~20 conditions spanning the step. Report the discrepancy in t_50 and in nRMSE(c). Frame with Sircar & Hufton (2000) as the defense and Ma et al. (Nano Lett. 2025) and Do & Rice (1986) as the acknowledged limits.
concrete_actions.rationale: Turns the most credible physics objection into a measured, bounded number. If the discrepancy is small, Sircar & Hufton's argument is confirmed on our own system and the LDF assumption is fully defended. If it is large, we would rather find out before a referee does — and given that the cooperative shock sits exactly where fractional uptake -> 1, it may well be large.

concrete_actions.action: Upgrade the grid study to standard V&V reporting: fit the observed order of accuracy p from the three finest grids by Richardson extrapolation and report a Grid Convergence Index with a safety factor, per Roache. Present it as a table with p and GCI columns for both the generic and the production configuration, and add the max cell Peclet number over the full dataset.
concrete_actions.rationale: 'Error halves as N_z doubles' is the right observation stated in the wrong currency. Numerics-literate referees in AIChE J / CES expect an observed order with an uncertainty band. The data already exists in grid_study.log — this is a fitting exercise, not new computation.

concrete_actions.action: Add a short 'model scope and geometry' paragraph: state L/d_p = 50 and D_in/d_p = 25 against the conventional lower bounds for neglecting channelling and wall bypass; state that dz/d_p = 0.025 is legitimate because we resolve a PDE rather than a packing; and reframe the geometry honestly as a lab-scale desiccant/dehumidification breakthrough column rather than as an AWH device (real AWH hardware is thin layers and monoliths in cyclic operation).
concrete_actions.rationale: Three small vulnerabilities closed by three sentences. The AWH framing point matters most: a referee who works on atmospheric water harvesting will ask why a 10 cm packed bed of 2 mm pellets at 0.03-0.30 m/s represents their technology, and the correct answer is that it represents the sorption dynamics, not the device.

concrete_actions.action: Add a method-of-manufactured-solutions verification of the FULL coupled operator (Roache, J. Fluids Eng. 124:4, 2002): choose a smooth analytic (c, q, T), substitute into the three governing equations with the actual DSLF isotherm, add the residual source terms to rhs(), and measure the observed order of accuracy on the complete nonlinear system.
concrete_actions.rationale: This is the only technique that verifies the production operator itself rather than a limit of it, and it is the definitive answer to 'all your benchmarks switch off part of the physics'. Deferred below the coupled-analytic benchmark only because it is more work for a partly overlapping payoff — do it if we want the L0 rung to be unimpeachable.

concrete_actions.action: Add at least one experimental validation point. Use a published water (or CO2) breakthrough dataset with a REPORTED TEMPERATURE PROFILE, fit only the isotherm and k_LDF, and predict the rest. The AIM workflow paper (arXiv:2504.20713) validates against a literature ternary CO2/H2/N2 breakthrough including outlet temperature, which is the current community norm; Born et al. (CES 2023) provides insulated/non-insulated lab data with axial temperature profiles.
concrete_actions.rationale: Open item #2 says 'no experimental validation at all'. A single honest comparison — even an imperfect one, clearly scoped — moves the paper from 'verified' to 'verified and validated' and removes the strongest available framing attack, that the 988-simulation dataset is a self-consistent fiction. Everything downstream in the ladder inherits its credibility from this.

concrete_actions.action: Parameterise at least one real COF using Brahma/Dwarkanath/Balasubramanian (Chem. Mater. 2024, DOI 10.1021/acs.chemmater.4c00673) for the isotherm step and pore-filling behaviour, and replace the uncited MOF-303 placeholders (retraction A4) with parameters sourced from the Shih & Lin JACS 2025 review and the primary MOF-303/MOF-801/CAU-10 literature.
concrete_actions.rationale: Closes open items #1 and #3 together. The title claims a COF and none exists; every MOF-303 parameter is an uncited placeholder that currently forbids naming any result. It also feeds the material axis, which the learning curve says is where the remaining headroom is (1.82x improvement from 12 to 48 training materials, not yet saturated).

lens: Kolmogorov n-width barrier for transport-dominated problems, and every published remedy — with a specific verdict on whether the project's two-wave warp sigma = (t - t_lo(z))/(t_hi(z) - t_lo(z)) is novel prior art, and on the state of the art for predicting registration/warp parameters (the project's current binding constraint).

papers.citation: Jan S. Hesthaven, Benjamin Peherstorfer, Benjamin Unger, "Nonlinear model reduction for transport-dominated problems", Acta Numerica 35, 173-272
papers.what_it_shows: The definitive current survey. Organises nonlinear MOR around nonlinear parametrisations, reduced dynamics and online solvers, and taxonomises the field into (i) transformation-based methods (registration, optimal transport, shifted/dynamically-transformed modes), (ii) online-adaptive methods, and (iii) generic nonlinear parametrisation plus instantaneous residual minimisation. It states explicitly that no single method universally solves transport-dominated problems.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the reference the referee will hold us to. Any claim we make about 'the n-width barrier' or 'the remedy' must be located inside this taxonomy in the first two paragraphs of our related work, or we look unaware of the field. Our two-wave warp is a transformation-based method in their category (i); our fixed-frame POD+GBM is their baseline; our DeepONet arm is neither. Published February 2026 - so it is brand new and citing it signals currency.

papers.citation: Florian Arbes, Constantin Greif, Karsten Urban, "The Kolmogorov N-width for linear transport: Exact representation and the influence of the data"
papers.what_it_shows: Exact Fourier representations and sharp bounds for the n-width of linear transport. Proves the n-width decays as c_r N^{-r} for data with Sobolev regularity g in H^{r-eps} for all eps>0, even when g is not in H^r. The famous N^{-1/2} rate for transport is the special case of a jump (H^{1/2-}).
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the theory that turns our measured d_n ~ n^-1.23 from a curve fit into a statement about the data. Our exponent 1.23 is exactly what their theorem predicts for solution profiles of Sobolev regularity ~H^1.23 - i.e. our fronts are smoothed by LDF kinetics and axial dispersion, not true discontinuities, which is why we see n^-1.23 rather than n^-0.5. Citing this converts our 'algebraic n-width, scoped to n=8-64' caveat into a principled claim: the exponent measures front regularity. Strongly recommend adding one sentence connecting the two.

papers.citation: Julius Reiss, Philipp Schulze, Joern Sesterhenn, Volker Mehrmann, "The shifted proper orthogonal decomposition: A mode decomposition for multiple transport phenomena", SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 40(3), A1322-A1344 (journal details from search, not fetched)
papers.what_it_shows: Extends POD with time-dependent shift operators, determines MULTIPLE transport velocities and separates them. Explicitly states that a single shift is insufficient when different transport velocities are present.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Two consequences, one good one bad. Bad: our 'single-front alignment is refuted' result is CONFIRMATORY of the founding premise of sPOD, published in 2018 - it is not a discovery and must not be framed as one. Good: sPOD's answer to multiple transports is an ADDITIVE decomposition (a sum of co-moving fields), whereas ours is a COMPOSITIONAL reparameterisation (one warp of the time axis). Those are genuinely different objects and that distinction is the cleanest way to carve out space. A referee will ask why we did not run sPOD as a baseline.

papers.citation: Neeraj Sarna, Jan Giesselmann, Peter Benner, "Data-driven snapshot calibration via monotonic feature matching", Finite Elements in Analysis and Design 230, 104065
papers.what_it_shows: Induces faster singular-value decay by computing snapshots on a transformed spatial domain (snapshot calibration). Treats discontinuities AND kinks as features and computes the spatial transform by MONOTONIC FEATURE MATCHING across multiple features, for shock collisions, shock/rarefaction-fan collisions and shock formation. Proves fast m-width decay of the calibrated manifold, and observes that after calibration the m-width also depends on the accuracy of the full-order model.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: THIS IS THE CLOSEST PRIOR ART TO OUR TWO-WAVE WARP. Our sigma = (t - t_lo)/(t_hi - t_lo) is exactly a monotone two-landmark feature-matching calibration, transposed from the space axis to the time axis, with the landmark curves depending on z. If we do not cite this and distinguish ourselves from it, a referee who knows it will reject on novelty. Their extra observation - that the calibrated m-width depends on FOM accuracy - is also a direct hit on our interpolation-floor guard and should be cited there.

papers.citation: Tommaso Taddei, Lei Zhang, "Space-time registration-based model reduction of parameterized one-dimensional hyperbolic PDEs", ESAIM: M2AN 55, 99-130
papers.what_it_shows: An adaptive SPACE-TIME registration-based data compression procedure that aligns LOCAL FEATURES (plural: parameter-dependent shock waves and contact discontinuities) in a fixed reference domain, for parameterized 1-D hyperbolic PDEs, plus space-time Petrov-Galerkin and hyper-reduction. Demonstrated on Burgers and shallow water.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The second closest prior art, and arguably the most dangerous: same dimensionality (1-D hyperbolic), same setting (space-time), same goal (align multiple features), same author group that dominates registration MOR. Our warp is a closed-form, landmark-supervised instance of exactly their space-time registration map, restricted to maps that are affine in t at each z. We must cite it and say so ourselves, then argue what we add.

papers.citation: Samuel Lanthaler, Roberto Molinaro, Patrik Hadorn, Siddhartha Mishra, "Nonlinear Reconstruction for Operator Learning of PDEs with Discontinuities", ICLR 2023
papers.what_it_shows: Proves LOWER approximation bounds: any operator-learning method with a LINEAR reconstruction step (DeepONet, PCA-Net) has expected squared L2 error bounded below by C/p in p trunk functions, so at best linear decay in network size, for prototypical PDEs with discontinuities. Methods with NONLINEAR reconstruction (FNO, and their new shift-DeepONet) escape this and can decay exponentially. Crucially, shift-DeepONet is N(u)(y) = sum_k beta_k(u) tau_k(A_k(u).y + gamma_k(u)) - a learned per-mode SCALE A_k and SHIFT gamma_k of the trunk's evaluation coordinate.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Two things, both critical. (1) Our two-wave warp IS a scale-and-shift of the evaluation coordinate: A = 1/(t_hi - t_lo), gamma = -t_lo/(t_hi - t_lo). shift-DeepONet is therefore the direct neural analogue of our contribution, published in 2023 at ICLR. It must be cited AND run as a baseline. Our differences are real (our scale/shift vary with z, are shared across modes, and are supervised on measured crossing times rather than learned end-to-end) but they must be argued, not assumed. (2) Our whole L5 rung tested only DeepONet and DeepOKAN - BOTH linear-reconstruction architectures. Their theorem says such methods must fail here. So L5 as currently designed cannot support 'you don't need an operator'; it only supports 'linear-reconstruction operators do not help', which was already known.

papers.citation: Simona Cucchiara, Angelo Iollo, Tommaso Taddei, Haysam Telib, "Model order reduction by convex displacement interpolation", J. Comput. Phys. (2024)
papers.what_it_shows: Identifies coherent structures via a scalar sensor plus point-set registration, yielding SORTED POINT CLOUDS. For a new parameter, predicts the new point cloud by regression, then builds boundary-aware bijective mappings to neighbouring snapshots and returns a weighted combination of composed snapshots. I read the paper: the regression is POD of the sorted point clouds followed by RBF (Gaussian kernel) regression on each POD coefficient, with cross-validation for the regularisation lambda and kernel width; they use kappa = 4 nearest neighbours; the point-set registration uses a Gaussian/optimal-transport map between the clouds.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the state-of-the-art recipe for the exact problem that is now our bottleneck: predicting the registration for an unseen parameter. Their pipeline (POD of landmark locations -> RBF regression on POD coefficients, CV-tuned) is a strict generalisation of ours (PCA of t_lo/t_hi curves -> HGB on 4 modes). We should adopt it as our comparison, and note that our (t_lo, t_hi) pair IS a two-point sorted point cloud - which makes CDI the framework our method sits inside.

papers.citation: Jon Labatut, Jean-Baptiste Chapelier, Angelo Iollo, Tommaso Taddei, "Parametric vector flows for registration fields in bounded domains with applications to nonlinear interpolation of shock-dominated flows"
papers.what_it_shows: Registration for parametric MOR in bounded domains. Diffeomorphisms are vector flows of velocity fields with vanishing normal component on the boundary; a sensor extracts point clouds from snapshots; an expectation-maximisation procedure simultaneously solves point-cloud matching and determines the velocity field. Combined with Iollo-Taddei nonlinear interpolation for shock-dominated fields. Targets multiple coherent structures (shocks, shear layers, cracks).
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The current (Jan 2026) frontier of registration MOR. Citing it shows we are up to date, and its EM-based joint matching + map identification is a concrete alternative to our two-stage 'measure crossings, then regress' pipeline.

papers.citation: Donsub Rim, Scott Moe, Randall J. LeVeque, "Transport reversal for model reduction of hyperbolic partial differential equations", SIAM/ASA J. Uncertainty Quantification (journal details from search)
papers.what_it_shows: An iterative algorithm that decomposes a snapshot matrix into MULTIPLE shifting profiles, each with its own speed, to restore fast singular-value decay for hyperbolic PDEs.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Another multi-wave prior art, and again ADDITIVE (a sum of profiles) rather than compositional. Together with sPOD it establishes that 'more than one wave' has been the central concern of this literature since 2015-2017. Our claim to novelty cannot be 'we noticed there are two waves'.

papers.citation: G. Welper, "Transformed snapshot interpolation" (arXiv:1505.01227, 2015) and "Transformed Snapshot Interpolation with High Resolution Transforms" (arXiv:1901.01322, 2019; SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 2020)
papers.what_it_shows: Allows a transformation of the physical coordinate before using a snapshot in reconstruction, realigning moving discontinuities and recovering high convergence rates. The transforms are computed automatically by minimising a training error. The 2019 paper specifically moves BEYOND low-resolution transforms (constant shifts, low-order polynomials, Fourier modes) to high-resolution transforms with correct behaviour near singularities.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Welper 2019 is the theoretical umbrella under which our warp sits: he explicitly argues that constant shifts are too coarse and that higher-resolution transforms are needed. Our two-parameter warp is a two-degree-of-freedom high-resolution transform. Cite it as the framework, not as a competitor.

papers.citation: Mario Ohlberger, Stephan Rave, "The method of freezing as a new tool for nonlinear reduced basis approximation of parameterized evolution equations"
papers.what_it_shows: Decomposes the solution into a Lie-group component and a spatial shape component (a group action, i.e. a shift), reformulates as a PDAE, and projects onto a reduced basis. Strongly improved performance for moving discontinuities versus no freezing.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The canonical single-transform ancestor. It is precisely the single-front alignment we refuted. Our comoving.py result is a well-controlled negative for freezing-type methods applied to a two-wave system, and should be presented as such: 'the method of freezing, and every single-group-action descendant, cannot represent a varying front WIDTH, only a varying position'. That is the crisp mechanistic reason our shift failed and our two-parameter warp worked.

papers.citation: Tommaso Taddei, "A registration method for model order reduction: data compression and geometry reduction", SIAM J. Sci. Comput. (2020)
papers.what_it_shows: An equation-independent registration procedure that, given snapshots, returns a parameter-dependent bijective mapping Phi(.,mu) designed to make the mapped manifold better suited to linear compression, with a theoretical result establishing rigour.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The foundational registration-MOR paper. Its key structural point - the mapping is parameter-dependent and must be constructed so it generalises - is exactly our bottleneck. Must-cite.

papers.citation: Nicolas Barral, Tommaso Taddei, Ishak Tifouti, "Registration-based model reduction of parameterized PDEs with spatio-parameter adaptivity", J. Comput. Phys. 499, 112727
papers.what_it_shows: Registration-based MOR combined with metric-based mesh adaptation and spatio-parameter adaptivity for advection-dominated problems.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Shows that the field has moved to ADAPTIVE registration (adapt where the features are). Our fixed 128x128 encoding and fixed level pair (0.05, 0.95) are the non-adaptive version; a referee may ask why the alignment levels were not chosen adaptively per sample.

papers.citation: Tobias Blickhan, "A registration method for reduced basis problems using linear optimal transport", SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 46(5), A3177-A3204 (journal details from search)
papers.what_it_shows: Constructs the registration mapping purely data-driven via Monge embeddings from linear optimal transport, with a single interpretable hyper-parameter. Explicitly discusses how it relates to prior MOR + optimal transport work, and handles both density-valued and non-density-valued solutions.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The cleanest, lowest-hyper-parameter competitor to a hand-designed warp, and it is data-driven so it needs no knowledge of the wave structure. If a linear-OT registration recovers our two-wave alignment automatically, our hand-designed warp loses its claim to necessity; if it does not, that is a strong result for us. Worth one experiment.

papers.citation: V. Ehrlacher, D. Lombardi, O. Mula, F.-X. Vialard, "Nonlinear model reduction on metric spaces. Application to one-dimensional conservative PDEs in Wasserstein spaces", ESAIM: M2AN 54, 2159-2197 (journal details from search)
papers.what_it_shows: Reformulates model reduction in general metric spaces with barycentric and tangent-space (Riemannian) approximations, both automatically nonlinear; demonstrated for 1-D conservative PDEs in the L2-Wasserstein space.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The canonical optimal-transport ROM reference and the closest to our setting dimensionally (1-D). Note the caveat: our c-field is not mass-conserving in the Wasserstein sense (it is a saturating breakthrough profile, not a density), so Wasserstein barycentres do not apply directly. Saying that explicitly is a good way to justify why we used a landmark warp instead - and it pre-empts the 'why not optimal transport?' referee question.

papers.citation: Kookjin Lee, Kevin T. Carlberg, "Model reduction of dynamical systems on nonlinear manifolds using deep convolutional autoencoders", J. Comput. Phys. 404, 108973 (journal details from search)
papers.what_it_shows: Manifold Galerkin and manifold LSPG projection onto a nonlinear manifold parameterised by a deep convolutional autoencoder, with a posteriori error bounds; significantly outperforms even the OPTIMAL linear-subspace ROM on advection-dominated benchmarks, thereby overcoming the intrinsic n-width limitation of linear subspaces.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the standard baseline for 'nonlinear manifold beats the POD floor'. Our POD floor is quoted as a hard lower bound throughout the ladder; Lee-Carlberg is the published demonstration that a nonlinear decoder goes BELOW it. If we claim the POD floor bounds anything other than linear-reconstruction methods, this paper refutes us. A convolutional-autoencoder arm is the single most obviously missing baseline in the whole project.

papers.citation: Jacob H. Seidman, Georgios Kissas, Paris Perdikaris, George J. Pappas, "NOMAD: Nonlinear Manifold Decoders for Operator Learning", NeurIPS 2022
papers.what_it_shows: Shows that even when target functions form a low-dimensional submanifold, a linear (basis-expansion) decoder can need a very large number of basis elements. Introduces a nonlinear decoder that learns finite-dimensional representations of nonlinear submanifolds, outperforming larger linear models and matching state-of-the-art operator learning at much smaller model size.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Our measured L5 diagnosis - 'DeepONet is flat in p and performs like a 4-mode oracle reconstruction; the params-to-coefficient map is the binding constraint' - is precisely the failure mode NOMAD was built to fix. NOMAD is therefore both a must-cite and the fairest neural baseline to run alongside shift-DeepONet. If POD+GBM in the two-wave frame beats NOMAD, that is a genuinely strong headline.

papers.citation: Rambod Mojgani, Maciej Balajewicz, "Physics-aware registration based auto-encoder for convection dominated PDEs"
papers.what_it_shows: An autoencoder whose unsupervised training learns a DIFFEOMORPHIC spatio-temporal grid that registers the PDE output onto a non-uniform parameter/time-varying grid such that the Kolmogorov n-width of the mapped data is MINIMISED. Emphasises interpretability of the latent variables and separation of convection/advection from diffusion/scaling.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Directly answers our 'how do we learn the registration map itself accurately?' question, and does it with the RIGHT objective: it optimises the mapped-data n-width rather than fitting the warp in isolation. It also explicitly separates convection from SCALING - which is exactly the two degrees of freedom (position and width) our warp uses. Highest-value single reference for fixing our bottleneck.

papers.citation: Rambod Mojgani, Maciej Balajewicz, "Lagrangian basis method for dimensionality reduction of convection dominated nonlinear flows"
papers.what_it_shows: Approximates the flow in the Lagrangian frame, with global bases for BOTH the state and the position of the Lagrangian computational domain; certain wave-like solutions become low-rank in that frame.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The 'two bases, one for the state and one for the frame' structure is exactly our (shape basis, warp basis) split. Cite as the structural ancestor of our decomposition.

papers.citation: Nirmal J. Nair, Maciej Balajewicz, "Transported snapshot model order reduction approach for parametric, steady-state fluid flows containing parameter dependent shocks", Int. J. Numer. Methods Eng. (journal details from search)
papers.what_it_shows: Transports snapshots along a spatially and parametrically dependent transport field. Key observation: the transport fields are SMOOTH and continuous even when the solutions are not, so they can be accurately expressed with a LOW-ORDER POLYNOMIAL EXPANSION.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the published justification for our whole approach - and also a warning. They claim the transport field is easy because it is smooth and low-order. Our measurement says otherwise: our warp curves are smooth but only reach R^2 = 0.895/0.919 across NOVEL MATERIALS, which is a much harder extrapolation than their steady-flow parameter sweeps. That contrast (smooth is not the same as predictable across materials) is a genuinely publishable observation and directly contradicts a stated assumption in the literature. Frame it that way.

papers.citation: Philipp Krah, Arthur Marmin, Beata Zorawski, Julius Reiss, Kai Schneider, "A robust shifted proper orthogonal decomposition: Proximal methods for decomposing flows with multiple transports"
papers.what_it_shows: Extends sPOD to multiple transports by optimising co-moving fields directly with nuclear-norm penalties plus a robustness term for interpolation error and noise; three proximal algorithms; validated on synthetic benchmarks and 1-D/2-D incompressible and reactive flows. Code available.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The current best-in-class MULTI-transport decomposition with public code. This is the baseline a referee will most plausibly demand for a two-wave problem. Running it on our 988 fields is cheap relative to the credibility gain, and its failure or success would sharpen the additive-versus-compositional argument.

papers.citation: Beata Zorawski, Shubhaditya Burela, Philipp Krah, Arthur Marmin, Kai Schneider, "Automated transport separation using the neural shifted proper orthogonal decomposition"
papers.what_it_shows: Neural version of sPOD that automates the separation of multiple transports (id, title, authors and date confirmed via the arXiv API; I did not read the full abstract).
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Automated multi-transport separation is exactly the 'do we even need to hand-pick two levels?' question. Cite as the automated alternative to our hand-chosen (0.05, 0.95) level pair.

papers.citation: Shubhaditya Burela, Philipp Krah, Julius Reiss, "Parametric model order reduction for a wildland fire model via the shifted POD based deep learning method", Advances in Computational Mathematics (2025; journal DOI 10.1007/s10444-025-10220-4 from search)
papers.what_it_shows: Non-intrusive, data-driven pipeline: sPOD produces a low-dimensional model, then a deep-learning framework forecasts the dynamics across time AND parameter. (I fetched the abstract but the arXiv landing page did not expose the network architecture or the shift-prediction mechanism; those details need the full PDF.)
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The canonical 'predict both the shifts and the amplitudes from parameters with a network' paper - i.e. our exact pipeline, done neurally, for a reaction front. It is the direct methodological competitor for our warp_predict.py stage and must be cited there.

papers.citation: Davide Papapicco, Nicola Demo, Michele Girfoglio, Giovanni Stabile, Gianluigi Rozza, "The Neural Network shifted-Proper Orthogonal Decomposition: a Machine Learning Approach for Non-linear Reduction of Hyperbolic Equations" (CMAME, journal details from search)
papers.what_it_shows: Automatically DETECTS the correct pre-processing transformation with a deep-learning architecture, removing the requirement (present in earlier shifted methods) that the characteristic speeds be known in explicit functional form.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Establishes automatic shift detection as the state of the art. Important nuance for us: they treat not knowing the advection field as the hard case. We DO know it - equilibrium adsorption theory gives the wave velocities analytically from the isotherm. That asymmetry is our advantage and we should exploit it rather than imitate NNsPOD.

papers.citation: Harshith Gowrachari, Nicola Demo, Giovanni Stabile, Gianluigi Rozza, "Non-intrusive model reduction of advection-dominated hyperbolic problems using neural network shift augmented manifold transformation", Computers & Fluids (2025; journal from search)
papers.what_it_shows: Complete offline-online NNsPOD-ROM. I read the HTML: a ShiftNet MLP learns a FULL FIELD shift T_shift(x,t) trained with the reconstruction loss ||u_ref - u(x - T_shift(x,t_i), t_i)||^2, and at an unseen parameter the trained shift operator transports the predicted field back to the physical frame. Reported: 1 NNsPOD mode reaches 99.99% energy for 1-D advection; 4 modes vs 40 POD modes for a 2-D convective vortex.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Two direct lessons. (1) The loss is the RECONSTRUCTION loss, not a warp-fitting loss - i.e. they train the registration end-to-end against the quantity that actually matters. Our two-stage pipeline fits t_lo/t_hi in isolation and then pays for it; our own payoff curve shows the cost is severely nonlinear (R^2 1.0 -> 0.895 costs 0.0233 -> 0.0508). (2) The shift is a full field, not a scalar - as ours is (it varies with z). This is the most directly transferable fix available to us.

papers.citation: Philipp Krah, Steffen Buechholz, Matthias Haeringer, Julius Reiss, "Front Transport Reduction for Complex Moving Fronts", J. Sci. Comput. 96 (2023) (arXiv id and journal from search; abstract not fetched directly)
papers.what_it_shows: Decomposes the field as a front SHAPE function composed with a level-set function that parameterises the distance to the front, handling topological changes (splitting/merging fronts). Structurally similar to an autoencoder but interpretable. Public code (MOR-transport/FrontTransportReduction).
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Front Transport Reduction is the closest published relative to the IDEA of writing the field as shape(distance-to-front), and our sigma is a normalised distance-between-two-fronts coordinate. If the referee knows this line of work, they will see the resemblance immediately. Cite it and state the difference: FTR uses one level-set distance; we use a normalised INTERVAL between two fronts, which additionally factors out the width.

papers.citation: Victor Zucatti, Matthew J. Zahr, "Model reduction of convection-dominated viscous conservation laws using implicit feature tracking and landmark image registration"
papers.what_it_shows: Combines implicit feature tracking with LANDMARK image registration to build ROMs for convection-dominated viscous conservation laws, targeting the Kolmogorov barrier. (Title, authors, arXiv id and date confirmed from search results; I did not fetch the abstract.)
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Uses the word 'landmark' explicitly, in 2025, in ROM. Our two-wave warp is a two-landmark registration. This is the most recent paper that makes our object look standard, so it must be cited and distinguished. Recommend fetching the full abstract before writing the related-work paragraph.

papers.citation: Joshua Barnett, Charbel Farhat, "Quadratic approximation manifold for mitigating the Kolmogorov barrier in nonlinear projection-based model order reduction", J. Comput. Phys. (2022; journal from search)
papers.what_it_shows: A quadratic (rather than affine) approximation manifold; delivers the accuracy of a traditional PROM at dimension n2 ~ sqrt(n1), i.e. a quadratic square-root reduction in required dimension. Application-independent and linearization-free.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The cheapest possible non-neural way to beat our POD floor, and it needs no front tracking at all. If a quadratic manifold on our fixed-frame snapshots gets close to 0.02, the two-wave warp's advantage shrinks a lot. This is a cheap, high-information experiment and also a fair check on whether 'the frame' or merely 'nonlinearity of the decoder' is doing the work.

papers.citation: Shaowu Pan, Steven L. Brunton, J. Nathan Kutz, "Neural Implicit Flow: a mesh-agnostic dimensionality reduction paradigm of spatio-temporal data", JMLR 24(41), 1-60 (journal details from search)
papers.what_it_shows: Two MLPs: ShapeNet isolates spatial complexity, ParameterNet handles parametric dependence, time and sensors. Mesh-agnostic low-rank representation of large-scale parametric spatio-temporal data with improved generalisation.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: An architecture whose split (shape vs parameter) mirrors ours (shape basis vs warp) but with a nonlinear decoder, and which handles our exact data shape. A fair, well-cited neural baseline that is NOT a linear-reconstruction operator - so it is immune to the Lanthaler lower bound and a much stronger test of the 'do you need learning?' question than DeepONet was.

papers.citation: Anuj Srivastava, Wei Wu, Sebastian Kurtek, Eric Klassen, J. S. Marron, "Registration of Functional Data Using Fisher-Rao Metric"
papers.what_it_shows: A geometric framework separating PHASE and AMPLITUDE variability in functional data. Uses the Fisher-Rao Riemannian metric on the quotient by the time-warping group, with the square-root velocity function (SRVF) representation turning Fisher-Rao into the standard L2 metric. Yields a consistent estimator of a signal observed under random warping, scaling and vertical translation.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the mature statistics literature for exactly our object: warping functions of one variable. The SRVF representation gives a Hilbert-space coordinate in which EVERY point corresponds to a valid monotone warp - so regressing there makes monotonicity and positive span automatic. Our current safeguard (clamping hi_pred >= lo_pred + 1e-3) is an ad-hoc substitute that a statistically literate referee will flag. Adopting SRVF/log-span coordinates is a principled, citable upgrade to the warp predictor.

papers.citation: J. O. Ramsay, Xiaochun Li, "Curve Registration", J. Royal Statistical Society Series B 60, 351-363
papers.what_it_shows: The standard reference for continuous monotone curve registration (time warping) of functional data.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: Together with Kneip-Gasser, establishes that landmark-based monotone time warping is a 1990s idea. Cite it honestly at the point where we introduce sigma; doing so ourselves is far safer than being caught.

papers.citation: Alois Kneip, Theo Gasser, "Statistical Tools to Analyze Data Representing a Sample of Curves", Annals of Statistics 20
papers.what_it_shows: Landmark registration and the structural average: align a sample of curves by matching a set of identified landmarks (peaks, zeros of derivatives) and interpolating monotonically between them.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: The origin of landmark registration. TWO landmarks with linear interpolation between them - i.e. exactly our sigma - is the textbook two-landmark case from 1992. This is the strongest possible prior-art objection and we must own it.

papers.citation: Weibing Zhang, Yichu Shan, Andreas Seidel-Morgenstern, "Breakthrough curves and elution profiles of single solutes in case of adsorption isotherms with two inflection points", Journal of Chromatography A 1107, 216-225
papers.what_it_shows: Equilibrium theory for single-solute adsorption with isotherms possessing TWO INFLECTION POINTS: derives which portions of the concentration profile propagate as self-sharpening shocks and which as dispersive (simple) waves, and predicts the resulting composite breakthrough curves and elution profiles.
papers.why_it_matters_to_us: This is the exact physics of our Type V dual-term Do-Do isotherm, and it is the closed-form theory for our TWO WAVES. Three uses: (1) it converts 'we observed a two-wave breakthrough' from an empirical observation into a known, citable consequence of isotherm inflection structure - which strengthens the paper but removes any claim that the two-wave structure is our discovery; (2) it gives an ANALYTIC prior for t_lo(z) and t_hi(z) from the isotherm parameters alone, which is the single most promising route past our R^2 = 0.895 warp ceiling; (3) it is the domain reference our chemical-engineering referee will expect and whose absence would be conspicuous.

papers.citation: Robin Herkert, Patrick Buchfink, Tizian Wenzel, Bernard Haasdonk, Pavel Toktaliev, Oleg Iliev, "Greedy Kernel Methods for Approximating Breakthrough Curves for Reactive Flow from 3D Porous Geometry Data"
