findings.title: Every recorded L5 DeepONet number is stale: an extended learning-rate sweep in the repo beats them at every basis size, violating the project's own rule 4
findings.evidence: Recorded (RESULTS.md:157-163): p=8 0.0281, p=16 0.0293, p=32 0.0291, p=64 0.0296, p=128 0.0296, '59.0x floor'. From l5_fill1.log + l5_fill2.log at lr=3e-3 (above the old grid top of 1e-3), 3 seeds each, computed: p=8 0.0276, p=16 0.0280, p=32 0.0290, p=64 0.0284, p=128 0.02747. Every p improves; p=128 x-floor becomes 54.9x, not 59.0x; the best DeepONet anywhere becomes 0.0275, not 0.0281. CONTINUE_HERE.md:92 asserts 'DeepONet's optimum is lr = 1e-3' — that is now false. CONTINUE_HERE.md trap 3 says 'Compare against the STRONGEST competitor config, never the first one run. This has now happened FOUR times'; this is the fifth, and it is on the project's own headline arm.
findings.why_it_matters: A17 is the project's most important retraction and quotes '0.0281 -> 0.0296' as its evidence. That string is now wrong in four documents. Worse, the direction flips sign: at the true best learning rate DeepONet goes 0.0276 -> 0.0275, ratio 0.996. The CONCLUSION is unchanged and in fact strengthened (flat is flatter), so this is cheap to fix — but shipping numbers that the repo's own logs contradict, in the retraction that anchors the paper, is the one thing this project cannot afford. Note also that 3e-3 was the top of the extended grid and nothing above it was tried, so the optimum is still not bracketed.
findings.fix: Run one more lr rung (1e-2) at p=8 and p=128 to bracket the optimum, then regenerate the L5 table, A17, CONTINUE_HERE and every derived sentence from the merged l5_results + l5_fill1 + l5_fill2 arms. Restate as '0.0276 -> 0.0275 while the floor falls 28.7x; 54.9x above its own bound at p=128'. Also update RESULTS.md:288 'beats DeepONet's 0.0281' -> '0.0275'. Add a Part-B entry: the fifth instance of the strongest-config trap, caught pre-submission.

findings.title: FNO and WNO are named arms in the frozen protocol's L5 rung and were never run; the deviation is unrecorded
findings.evidence: Protocol line 62: `| L5 | Operator family | "you need an operator" | DeepONet, FNO, WNO, DeepOKAN, matched budget |`. run_l5.py:213-214: `ap.add_argument("--families", nargs="+", default=["deeponet", "deepokan"], choices=["deeponet", "deepokan"])` — FNO and WNO are not merely unused, they are not selectable. `grep -in "fno|wno|wavelet" run_l5.py` returns nothing. `grep -in fno RETRACTIONS.md` returns only B12 and B13, which are about a shared output head and a gate slicing bug; no entry drops FNO from L5. The protocol's own line 8 requires: 'Changes to this protocol after training begins must be recorded in RETRACTIONS.md with the date and the reason, not silently edited.'
findings.why_it_matters: Two compounding problems. (1) A frozen-protocol study that silently drops two of four pre-registered arms has broken its own guarantee, and the guarantee is the paper's methodological contribution. (2) Scientifically, 'you need an operator is eliminated' rests on DeepONet plus a KAN variant of DeepONet — one operator architecture family. FNO is the most-cited neural operator and has a genuinely different inductive bias (spectral convolution, not branch/trunk separability); the L5 bottleneck argument (the params->coefficient map binds) is a statement about branch-net regression that does not automatically transfer to FNO, whose lifting is not a coefficient regression at all. A referee will make this objection in one sentence.
findings.fix: Either (a) run FNO2d at matched ~200k params and 8000 steps — the model already exists in fno_model_adsorption.py and validate.py already gates it — which makes the elimination genuinely about operators; or (b) record a dated Part-A/Part-B entry withdrawing FNO and WNO from L5 with the reason, narrow the rung's claim in every document to 'branch-trunk operators', and say so in the abstract. Option (a) is strongly preferred: a one-family operator rung is the weakest link in an otherwise very strong ladder. WNO should be dropped explicitly by pointing at A9 (the implementation is a dilated CNN).

findings.title: 01_INTRODUCTION.md: paragraph-by-paragraph, nine claims are retracted, refuted, or unimplemented
findings.evidence: L5: 'typically executed via Finite Element Method (FEM) solvers like COMSOL Multiphysics, are notoriously computationally prohibitive. A single device-scale simulation can require hours to converge' -> RETRACTED A6; protocol:181 measures 4.2 s (MOF-303 config) / 73.1 s (generic) per condition at N_z=2000. L5: 'rendering high-throughput device optimization ... practically impossible' -> protocol:193 measures 10^4 conditions in 11.7 h single-core. L7: 'fail catastrophically -- often yielding non-physical hallucinations' -> RETRACTED A15 ('No arm diverges; the worst is a 9x degradation') and A8; best novel-material error is 0.0485 (verified from results/l1_results.json), a 4.9% error. L7: 'Because they are not strictly constrained by ... thermodynamics or mass conservation, their predictions cannot be trusted' -> refuted by L4b: bounded data-only 0.0124 vs bounded physics 0.0194; protocol:1093 'The best configuration on both axes uses no physics loss at all.' L9: 'This framework pioneers the integration of Physics-Informed Operator Learning' -> A12 (DeepOKAN published: Abueidda, Pantidis & Mobasher, CMAME 436:117699). L9/L11: 'synergizes Fourier Neural Operators (FNO) and DeepONets' -> FNO never run. L11: 'accelerating computation by orders of magnitude ... without sacrificing physical fidelity' -> L5: DeepONet sits 54.9x above its own POD lower bound and performs like a 4-mode reconstruction at any p. L11: 'resolution-invariant simulations' -> no resolution-transfer experiment exists anywhere in the repo. L11: 'PIKAN serves as a transparent, explainable engine for discovering the intrinsic kinetics' + 'coupled with SINDy, facilitates the extraction of closed-form, symbolic kinetic equations' -> refuted by L3 (MLP beats RBF-KAN at every budget, 8/9 significant) and RETRACTED A7 (SINDy returns dq/dt = 0); protocol open item 6 notes the SINDy library contains q*, i.e. regression onto the answer. L13: 'we present the first unified architecture' and 'our Foundation Digital Twin overcomes the extrapolation limits of conventional ML' -> the transfer gap was not closed by any of six interventions.
findings.why_it_matters: Every sentence in the Introduction that states a fact about this study is false as of today. If any of it survives into a submission the paper is not merely wrong, it is wrong in ways the authors' own repository documents — which converts an ordinary rejection into an integrity problem.
findings.fix: Do not edit this file. Retire it and write the Introduction from the evidence (see summary for the proposed structure). The only two sentences worth salvaging are the physical motivation for a Type V step isotherm and the framing of AWH under low RH — and both need citations they currently do not have.

findings.title: 02_METHODOLOGY_JUSTIFICATION.md: the 'strawman baseline' framing inverts the study's actual finding, and the section contains an unresolved literal placeholder
findings.evidence: Line 6: 'In our benchmarking (see Section X), these architectures achieved near-zero error on training regimes (memorization) but suffered catastrophic error explosions ... Consequently, we include these strictly as "strawman" baselines'. Three separate defects. (i) '(see Section X)' is a literal unedited placeholder. (ii) 'near-zero error on training regimes' is false — computed from results/l1_results.json: train nRMSE ridge 0.0677, mlp 0.0480, rf 0.0196, xgb 0.0126. (iii) 'strawman' inverts the result: XGBoost at 0.0485 is the BEST arm in L1, beats the MLP, and beats every KAN in L3 (best KAN anywhere 0.0633) and every DeepOKAN in L5 (best 0.0357). It also contradicts the project's own standing rule 4 ('Comparisons are against the strongest configuration of the competitor') and retraction B14, which withdrew a result precisely because an MLP baseline had been accidentally handicapped.
findings.why_it_matters: Declaring the winning arm a strawman is the most damaging single sentence in the drafts, because it is not just wrong — it is the specific intellectual vice (deciding the answer before the experiment) that the falsification ladder exists to prevent. A referee who sees it will not believe the ladder was run in good faith, regardless of how good the protocol is.
findings.fix: Retire the file. In the new Methods, gradient-boosted trees must be introduced as the strongest data-driven arm and the reference point every later rung is measured against, with their train/novel numbers stated (0.0126 / 0.0485, 33x the POD floor). Never use the word 'strawman' for an arm that won.

findings.title: Both draft files contain zero citations while asserting a dozen literature facts; §2.2-2.3 reads as a stripped-down neural-operator review
findings.evidence: `grep -c "\[.*\]|(20[0-9][0-9])|et al" 01_INTRODUCTION.md 02_METHODOLOGY_JUSTIFICATION.md` returns 0 and 0 — no bracketed reference, no parenthetical year, no 'et al.' in either file. Yet the following are asserted as established: 'atomistic simulations (e.g., Density Functional Theory and Grand Canonical Monte Carlo)'; 'FNO ... discretization-invariant and exceptionally computationally efficient (O(n log n) via the FFT)'; 'FNOs are notoriously susceptible to the Gibbs phenomenon (ringing artifacts)'; 'recent literature has proposed the Wavelet Neural Operator (WNO), which utilizes localized multi-scale wavelets rather than global Fourier modes'; 'they remain purely data-driven operators that drift from true mass conservation over long cyclic integrations'. The last one is measured nowhere in this project — there is no cyclic integration anywhere in the repo, and no mass-conservation drift was ever computed for any surrogate.
findings.why_it_matters: This is an originality/plagiarism exposure, not just a completeness gap. The §2.2-2.3 sequence (FNO is O(n log n) and discretization-invariant -> but Gibbs ringing at discontinuities -> therefore WNO with localized wavelets -> but WNO drifts) is the standard narrative arc of neural-operator review articles, rendered in review-article register with the citations removed. Similarity checkers flag exactly this pattern, and a referee in the operator-learning community will recognise the paragraph shape. The 'drift from mass conservation over long cyclic integrations' clause is additionally a fabricated-support risk: an unsupported empirical claim about competitor methods, in the authors' own voice.
findings.fix: Retire the file. In the new Methods, cite specifically: Li et al. (FNO, ICLR 2021); Lu et al. (DeepONet, Nat. Mach. Intell. 2021); Tripura & Chakraborty (WNO, CMAME 2023); Wang, Wang & Perdikaris (physics-informed DeepONet, Sci. Adv. 2021); Liu et al. (KAN, 2024); Shukla et al. (CMAME 2024, KAN-vs-MLP for PDE/operator learning — already cited correctly in the protocol at line 22 and RESULTS.md:145); Abueidda, Pantidis & Mobasher (DeepOKAN, CMAME 436:117699 — already correctly recorded in A12). Delete every empirical claim about a method not run here, or replace it with a measurement. Add citations for AWH/MOF water sorption (Kim et al. Science 2017; Hanikel/Yaghi MOF-303 work) before any MOF-303 parameter is named — currently blocked by A4 anyway.

findings.title: Hype register throughout: unearned superlatives, priority claims, and 'definitively prove'
findings.evidence: Verbatim: 'a profoundly promising paradigm' (01:3); 'notoriously computationally prohibitive' (01:5); 'fail catastrophically' (01:7); 'This framework pioneers' (01:9); 'a newly developed Physics-Informed Kolmogorov-Arnold Network' (01:9); 'we present the first unified architecture that bridges ultra-fast, operator-driven digital twins with highly interpretable physical discovery' (01:13); 'to accelerate the global deployment' (01:13); 'to definitively prove that localized, physics-informed operator networks are the optimal mathematical architecture' (02:23). Plus 'The Magic:' as a literal subheading in 00_MASTER_PLAN_DYNAMICS.md:26 and 'the "Special Sauce"' at 00:33.
findings.why_it_matters: Two of these are hard priority claims ('pioneers', 'the first unified architecture') that A12 already falsifies, and one ('definitively prove ... optimal') is an epistemic claim no benchmark can support and that L3 refutes on this project's own data. The rest is register: at npj Comput. Mater. / JCP / CMAME, 'profoundly promising', 'The Magic', and 'Special Sauce' cost reviewer goodwill before the science is read. The contrast is stark and instructive — RESULTS.md, RETRACTIONS.md and 03_LADDER_PROTOCOL.md are written in exactly the register a top journal rewards ('Flat to four decimals', 'the number was arithmetically impossible for the model', 'reported rather than dropped silently'). The problem is confined to the three legacy documents.
findings.fix: Write the paper in the voice of RESULTS.md, not the voice of 01/02. Concrete substitutions: 'profoundly promising' -> delete; 'fail catastrophically' -> 'transfer to held-out materials at 33x the achievable floor'; 'pioneers'/'first unified architecture' -> state the contribution as a measurement, not a precedence; 'definitively prove ... optimal' -> 'at matched parameter count, in this system'. Ban list for the draft: pioneer, novel (as self-description), catastrophic, profound, seamless, definitively, optimal architecture, first-ever, revolutionize, paradigm. A useful test the project already passes elsewhere: every sentence should name either a number or an experiment.

findings.title: The one number the whole value proposition rests on — reference solver cost — is quoted as three different values in three governing documents
findings.evidence: RETRACTIONS.md:27 (A6): 'Our own reference solves one condition in ~150 s (2.16 s in the original under-resolved setup)'. RESULTS.md:451: 'our own solver runs one condition in 4.2 s (MOF-303 config, N_z = 2000)'. 03_LADDER_PROTOCOL.md:1495: 'Our own solver runs one condition in ~150 s.' The protocol's own grid table (line 181) shows why all three are defensible and none is complete: at N_z=2000 the generic config costs 73.1 s and the MOF-303-like config costs 4.2 s — a 17x spread that protocol:187 attributes to k_LDF = 0.01 vs 0.05 changing the stiffness.
findings.why_it_matters: Speed is the only reason a surrogate exists, and A6 already retracted one speed claim. Quoting a scalar cost for a solver whose cost varies 17x with the material parameter that is being swept is not a typo — it invites a referee to ask what the cost distribution over the 988-run dataset actually is, and the answer is not in any document. Since the study's honest framing is 'accuracy per unit inference cost' (protocol:668), the cost side of that ratio has to be a distribution.
findings.fix: Replace every scalar speed claim with a measured distribution over the actual dataset: report median and 5th/95th percentile wall time per solve across the 988 runs (the data exists — manifest.json records elapsed_s and per-sample horizon_extensions), alongside the N_z=2000 grid-convergence error. Then state the surrogate's amortised throughput against that distribution, per A6's own recommended framing. Reconcile A6, RESULTS.md:451 and protocol:1495 to one sentence.

findings.title: The novel-condition split has only 2 held-out conditions, both mid-RH — no operating-condition generalisation claim is statistically supportable
findings.evidence: manifest: `'novel_conditions': [4, 9]` — 2 of 17. The 96 novel-condition samples are 2 conditions x 48 training materials. From the condition list, condition 4 is rh_feed 0.4295 and condition 9 is rh_feed 0.3390 — both mid-range; the extremes (cond 11 at rh 0.1649, cond 10 at 0.7952) are in the training set. Protocol:211 says '15 % of conditions held out'; 2/17 = 11.8%. metrics.py resamples clusters, and the calibration note (metrics.py:156-161) reports over-rejection already at 12 clusters — with 2 there is no usable cluster bootstrap at all. L1 nevertheless reports a novel-condition column (protocol:349-354: xgb 0.0513, rf 0.0455, mlp 0.0492, ridge 0.0650).
findings.why_it_matters: The Introduction's motivating scenario is a device tracking a changing weather profile — i.e. generalisation across operating conditions. The study can say essentially nothing about that axis: two clusters, both interior, no valid interval estimate. Any sentence in the paper implying condition-generalisation was tested is unsupported, and a referee who opens the manifest will find this in thirty seconds.
findings.fix: State explicitly in Methods that the novel-condition split has n_clusters = 2 and is reported as a descriptive diagnostic only, with no interval estimate and no verdict. Remove the novel-condition column from any table that carries CIs elsewhere, or mark it 'no CI (2 clusters)'. Scope every generalisation claim in the abstract to the material axis. If condition generalisation matters to the story, it needs a new split design (e.g. leave-one-condition-out over all 17, giving 17 folds) — cheap, since no retraining of the solver is required.

findings.title: L6's reported effect size and its table disagree: two different estimators are presented as one, and CONTINUE_HERE.md garbles both
findings.evidence: The table gives joint 0.0566 and separate 0.0721; a reader subtracts and gets +0.0155. The code block four lines later says 'observed mean diff: +0.0147'. I reproduced both from results/l6_results.json: the per-sample mean difference is +0.01554 (and the seed-mean difference is identically +0.0155), while the unweighted mean of the 12 per-material differences is +0.0147. Both are legitimate estimators; nothing in RESULTS.md says which is which. My reproduction via metrics.compare gives `diff +0.01554 CI [-0.01532, +0.04363]` against the reported `CI: [-0.0155, +0.0450]`. Separately, CONTINUE_HERE.md:62 reads 'H1, joint vs separate (L6) | diff -0.0155, CI [-0.045, +0.014]' — it has taken the point estimate from one convention and mirrored the CI from the other, so its stated point estimate is numerically equal to the other convention's CI bound. There is no analyze_l6.py in the repo; the block appears to have been written by hand.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the PRIMARY pre-registered hypothesis, and the failure condition was pre-declared to be reported 'in the abstract, in those words'. The verdict is safe under every convention (CI includes zero either way), so no conclusion changes — but a referee who subtracts the table and gets a different number from the box will check everything else in the paper by hand. RESULTS.md's own opening line promises 'Every number here is reproduced by a script in this repository'; this block is not.
findings.fix: Write analyze_l6.py so the block is generated, not typed; state the estimator explicitly ('per-sample mean difference, cluster-bootstrapped by material'); pick ONE convention and use it in every rung; pin the bootstrap seed and n_boot so the CI reproduces bit-for-bit. Fix CONTINUE_HERE.md:62. Also report the sd convention: the +/- values in the L6 table are population sd (ddof=0) on n=3 — I confirmed joint sd(ddof=0)=0.0039 vs sd(ddof=1)=0.0047 — which understates spread by ~22% at n=3 and should either be ddof=1 or be labelled.

findings.title: The learning-curve result being treated as live is from an incomplete run with no serialised output
findings.evidence: learning_curve.py:32 declares 'Output: results/learning_curve.json'. `ls results/` shows 27 files and learning_curve.json is not among them. learning_curve.log ends mid-run: the 'more conditions' axis stops at `0.75 508 48 0.05118 +0.822 +0.904` with no frac=1.00 row and no 'wrote results/...' line, unlike every completed log in the repo (e.g. warp_predict.log ends 'wrote results/warp_predict.json [370s]'). The same pattern applies to data/parametric_scale: generation died at roughly 1457 of 4080 files with no manifest.json.
findings.why_it_matters: The 1.82x material-axis result is the single most consequential open number in the project — it is what would force reopening L1 — and it currently exists only as terminal output in a truncated log. Under the project's own standing rules (no number from a failing category, every figure regenerates from an artifact) it is not yet a number. It should not be cited in RESULTS.md or a draft until the run completes and writes its JSON.
findings.fix: Re-run learning_curve.py to completion; confirm results/learning_curve.json exists and that analyze/figure code reads it rather than the log. Add the material-count axis in L1's own encoding and arm family for comparability. Then, and only then, open the L1 retraction. Separately, either finish data/parametric_scale (it is the instrument that answers this properly at 240 materials) or move it to data/_INCOMPLETE so a future session cannot mistake a partial directory for a dataset — the repo already has data/_RETRACTED and data/_probe_resume, so the convention exists.

findings.title: The frozen protocol still states 1020 runs and 720/96/204 splits; every result uses 988 and 691/96/201
findings.evidence: Protocol:208 '60 materials x 17 operating conditions = 1020 runs'; protocol:211-212 '20 % of materials and 15 % of conditions held out -> ~720 train / 96 novel-condition / 204 novel-material'. Every run log reports `splits {'train': 691, 'novel_condition': 96, 'novel_material': 201}` and 988 samples. The missing 32 ARE properly accounted for in data/parametric/manifest.json: `'n_rejected': 32`, with all 32 reasons of the form 'feed loads only 0.0XX of capacity' (the pre-declared <10%-of-capacity screen at protocol:243). So the data is clean; only the protocol text is stale.
findings.why_it_matters: Small, but it is the frozen document. A Methods section that says 1020 next to tables that say n=988 is the sort of arithmetic a careful referee checks first, and the project cannot afford to look sloppy in the one document whose value is that it was written first and not edited. The manifest's careful rejection accounting is exactly what should appear in the paper — it is currently invisible.
findings.fix: Add a dated amendment line under protocol §6b (not a silent edit) recording 1020 drawn, 32 rejected by the pre-declared capacity screen, 988 retained, 691/96/201. Put the rejection tally in the paper's Methods as a short table — a study that reports why 3.1% of draws were discarded, before anyone asks, buys a lot of credibility.

findings.title: Dataset screening removes only low-loading draws, which correlates with the low-RH regime the Introduction names as the motivation
findings.evidence: All 32 rejection reasons are 'feed loads only X of capacity' with X in [0.005, 0.100]; there are zero rejections for the other three declared screens (non-physical Henry constant, MTZ unresolvable, t_stoich out of range). Feed loading is driven by rh_feed x isotherm step position x q_max, so the screen preferentially removes low-RH / high-capacity / high-step-RH combinations. 01_INTRODUCTION.md:3 names 'even under arid conditions (relative humidity < 30%)' as the target regime. Of the 988 retained samples, 328 (33.2%) have rh_feed < 0.30, so coverage of that regime survives — the screen is not destroying it.
findings.why_it_matters: The effect is small (3.1% of draws) and coverage is preserved, so this is a transparency requirement rather than a bias problem. But it is a directional, non-random screen acting on exactly the corner the motivation highlights, and if a referee reconstructs it unaided it looks worse than it is. Stating it first costs one sentence and removes the objection entirely.
findings.fix: Report in Methods: the 32 rejections, the rule that produced them, the fact that all 32 were the loading screen, and the retained rh_feed distribution (33.2% below 0.30). Add one figure panel showing retained vs rejected draws in (rh_feed, q_max) space — Fig4_parametric_coverage already exists and is the natural home. State plainly that the screen is directional and why the alternative (fitting an isotherm to an unidentifiable near-zero-loading run) is worse.

findings.title: The 'white-box explainability' pillar of §2.4 has no implementation anywhere in the repository
findings.evidence: Line 21 claims 'the localized KAN edges can be extracted. When coupled with the Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy), this allows us to symbolically extract the exact, non-linear kinetic rate equations governing flexible "breathing" MOFs directly from the network structure.' `grep -rin "extract.*edge|edge.*extract|symbolic" *.py` over the whole repo returns ZERO matches — no edge-extraction code was ever written. `grep -rin "breath|MIL-53" *.py` returns exactly one hit, a docstring line in sindy_discovery.py, the script retracted by A7. Protocol open item 6 confirms: 'no breathing/flexible-framework physics exists anywhere in the data, so no breathing kinetics can be recovered from it.' The replacement identifiability study measured k_LDF R^2 = -0.61 on held-out materials.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the claim with the widest gap between assertion and artifact in the whole project: a named contribution pillar with no code, no data supporting the phenomenon it claims to explain, and a retracted predecessor. It is also the claim most likely to attract a reproducibility request, since 'symbolic extraction of kinetic laws' is the kind of result reviewers ask to see run.
findings.fix: Retire the file. The interpretability story in the new paper should be the one the project actually earned and which is genuinely better: the identifiability result. 'The equilibrium object is recoverable from an observable isotherm fingerprint (R^2 0.93-0.96 on shape parameters, 0.75 on delta_H via the van't Hoff slope across three temperatures) and the kinetic object is not (R^2 = -0.61)' is a real, measured, useful statement about what a surrogate can and cannot identify. That is a contribution; symbolic edge extraction is a promise.

findings.title: §2.2's single-shock premise is the exact assumption the project's own co-moving experiment refuted
findings.evidence: Line 11: 'In MOF adsorption, the mass-transfer zone (MTZ) propagates as a highly localized, sharp "shock front."' Protocol §6c and RESULTS.md:50-57 measure the opposite: a Type V isotherm gives a fast spreading Henry wave followed by a slow self-sharpening cooperative shock, with exit times c/c_in = 0.05 at 0.09 h and 0.99 at 18.90 h. RESULTS.md:236-238 measures the separation t(0.9)-t(0.1) spanning [0.025, 0.992] normalised time, a 40x range, and RESULTS.md:246 shows that single-front alignment triples the required rank (31 -> 102 modes for 99.9%).
findings.why_it_matters: The single-shock picture is not merely outdated prose — it is the specific physical misconception whose falsification is the intellectual pivot of the new paper. One front is why the textbook co-moving fix fails; two fronts is why the two-wave warp works and collapses the n-width from 31 to 13 modes. Leaving the old sentence anywhere in the repo obscures the one thing the paper most needs the reader to understand.
findings.fix: The two-wave measurement should be promoted from a physics aside to an early, figure-led result in the new paper — it is what makes the coordinate change non-obvious and non-generic. Show the 40x separation range and the mode-count table (31 / 102 / 17 / 13) as the argument for the frame, before any surrogate is trained.

what_is_excellent: RETRACTIONS.md as an institution. 17 Part-A withdrawals and 23 Part-B pre-contamination catches, with 14 of Part B explicitly labelled 'our own error' — in the analysis, the gates, and the frozen protocol itself. A17 in particular (withdrawing the explanatory role of the result the protocol had called 'the load-bearing result of the ladder') is the rarest kind of scientific writing. Do not soften, compress, or move this to supplementary material. It should be a numbered section of the paper.

The measured-not-inferred discipline, and the fact that it is stated as a rule (CONTINUE_HERE.md trap 7: 'Stop hypothesising, measure the term'), earned from B10 and B21, and then applied positively in l5_bottleneck.py. Splitting a linear reconstruction's error into basis error and coefficient-map error IN THE OPTIMAL BASIS, so the answer cannot depend on what basis DeepONet happened to learn, is the single best methodological move in the project.

The L5 mechanism result itself. 'The floor falls 28.7x, DeepONet moves 1.05x, train error is flat too, and at any p it performs like a 4-mode oracle reconstruction' is a genuinely publishable diagnosis, not a benchmark table. The oracle-rank calibration (mapping each method to an equivalent number of exactly-known modes) is an elegant device other people will borrow.

The bootstrap calibration work. Measuring that the percentile cluster bootstrap over-rejects at these cluster counts (8.5% at nominal 5% with 12 materials) and then adopting alpha = 0.005 to get a true 5% test — and withdrawing the one positive verdict that did not survive (A13) while noting that null verdicts were always conservative — is more statistical care than most papers in this literature show. metrics.py:1-35 documenting the 7.0% vs 32.5% clustered-vs-naive false-positive measurement is exactly right.

Forbidding pooled MSE in code rather than in prose. `pooled_mse()` exists only to raise NotImplementedError with the reason (var(T)/var(c) ~ 4.5e6). Enforcing a methodological rule at the API boundary, where it cannot be forgotten, is a pattern worth describing in the paper.

The L0 verification chain: four independent closed-form references (van Genuchten third-type, retarded front, thermal wave, Anzelius-Schumann), the B10 story of chasing the Ogata-Banks vs van Genuchten discrepancy to a 3.5% reflection term rather than 'fixing' a correct solver, and the stamped grid-convergence table with clean first-order behaviour in both configs. This is a properly verified reference and the paper should lead Methods with it.

The two design degeneracies caught before running (B18, B19). Recognising that 'LDF + fitted isotherm' as an L7 control is the model that generated the data, and that handing every L6 arm the eleven generative parameters leaves a separate-identification arm nothing to identify, are both non-obvious and both would have produced vacuous rungs. The re-specification of L6 over observable descriptors with a verified substitution table (R^2 per withheld parameter) is a better experiment than the original.

The L7 framing sentence: 'a classical model wins exactly when the physics it assumes is the physics that is there', supported by naming which assumption each closed form violates. This is a transferable statement earned from a measurement, and it is the register the whole paper should be written in.
The pre-declared failure condition for H1, written into the frozen protocol with the exact words to be used if it failed, and then honoured. Very few papers can show this.

The two-wave warp result as a piece of reasoning: measure the 40x separation range FIRST, use it to predict that one shift cannot work, refute the single-front frame including under an oracle, and let the failed measurement name its own successor. The exclusion of the 0.20-0.80 window because its interpolation floor reaches 29% of the signal — reported rather than dropped silently — is the right instinct.

The writing register of RESULTS.md, RETRACTIONS.md and 03_LADDER_PROTOCOL.md. Terse, numerate, every claim attached to an artifact, and willing to say 'and it turned out not to matter'. The hype problem is confined entirely to the three legacy documents (00, 01, 02); the good voice already exists and just needs to be the only voice.
summary:
VERDICT ON THE DRAFTS: 01_INTRODUCTION.md and 02_METHODOLOGY_JUSTIFICATION.md cannot be edited into shape. Every sentence in them that states a fact about this study is now false, and the two files are contamination hazards sitting unmarked in the repo root outside the validate.py perimeter. Retire both (rename with the _WITHDRAWN_ prefix the repo already uses), and add a prose gate. 00_MASTER_PLAN_DYNAMICS.md is superseded but harmless once labelled — keep it as a dated historical artifact, since "here is the plan we froze and here is how the evidence dismantled it" is genuinely valuable material for the paper's Discussion.

WRITING ASSESSMENT: two registers coexist in this repository. The legacy documents are venture-pitch prose — "profoundly promising", "pioneers", "fail catastrophically", "the first unified architecture", "definitively prove ... the optimal mathematical architecture", plus "The Magic:" and "the Special Sauce" as literal subheadings in the master plan. Referees at npj Comput. Mater. / JCP / CMAME punish all of it, and two of these are hard priority claims that A12 already falsifies. The governing documents, by contrast, are written exactly as a top journal wants: "Flat to four decimals"; "the number was arithmetically impossible for the model"; "the guard caught it; it is reported rather than dropped silently"; "a classical model wins exactly when the physics it assumes is the physics that is there". Nothing needs to be invented — the good voice already exists. The rule for the draft: every sentence names a number or an experiment, and no sentence describes the work as novel, first, or optimal.

ONE PAPER OR TWO — one paper, and this is not a close call, but for a reason that should shape the structure. The coordinate change is not currently a standalone positive result: predicted-warp 0.0508 versus fixed-frame 0.0510 is a 1.00x tie (warp_predict.log, verdict block), and the 2.17x that remains is oracle headroom, not delivered accuracy. Submitted alone it is "we found a better parameterisation that ties the baseline, and here is why we think it could be 2x better." Rejected. Conversely the six eliminations alone are a negative-results paper, and negative-results papers get read at top venues only when they carry a mechanism. Together they are one argument with a spine: the eliminations establish that nothing inside the linear-reconstruction family moves the error; the bottleneck measurement says why (the parameter-to-coefficient map carries ~4-5 usable modes out of 128, and three independent function classes are flat in rank against a floor that falls 28.7x); the coordinate change is the falsifiable consequence of that diagnosis, and it works in the sense that matters (n-width 31 -> 13, oracle 0.0203 beating the best trained arm anywhere) while relocating the obstruction to two smooth monotone 1-D curves. The eliminations are what make the coordinate change non-obvious; the coordinate change is what makes the eliminations more than a list. Split them and both halves lose their load-bearing member. Revisit this only if predicted-warp error drops materially below 0.040 — at that point the coordinate change becomes a strong standalone paper and the ladder becomes its companion.

TITLE OPTIONS (pick 1 for a methods venue, 2 for a physics-of-learning venue, 3 for a domain venue):
1. "Coordinates, not capacity: a pre-registered falsification ladder for surrogates of two-wave adsorption transport"
2. "What binds a parametric transport surrogate: the parameter-to-coefficient map, not the basis"
3. "Six eliminations and a change of variables: locating the transfer bottleneck in stiff adsorption-column surrogates"

ABSTRACT (198 words):
"Surrogate models for parametric transport are usually improved by adding data, capacity, a richer basis, a physics penalty, or an operator architecture. We tested all five, pre-registered, on a verified finite-difference reference for 1-D adsorption columns with a Type V isotherm, which produces a two-wave breakthrough whose wave separation varies 40-fold across 988 simulations. Under matched parameter count, encoding, training budget and three seeds, with cluster-robust intervals calibrated to a measured false-positive rate, none of the five closed the transfer gap to held-out materials. We then measured the binding constraint rather than inferring it. Decomposing a linear reconstruction in the optimal basis shows the basis error falls 28.7-fold while the coefficient-map error stays flat at 0.051; the parameters-to-coefficients map attains R^2 = 0.946 on mode 1, 0.39-0.58 on modes 2-5, and a median of -0.014 beyond mode 24. A DeepONet given 128 basis functions performs like a 4-mode oracle reconstruction. This is a coordinate problem, not a capacity problem: writing each field in a two-wave frame that removes both front positions collapses the required rank from 31 to 13 and the oracle error to 0.0203, below every trained arm. Our primary hypothesis, that separate equilibrium/kinetic identification beats joint fitting, is not supported."
(The last sentence is mandatory: protocol §1 pre-declared that H1's failure be reported "in the abstract, in those words.")

CENTRAL CLAIM, exact wording for the Introduction's final paragraph:
"We show that the transfer gap in a stiff two-wave transport surrogate is not a deficiency of data, capacity, basis richness, physics penalties, operator architecture, or structural decomposition — each of which we eliminate under matched conditions — but a property of the coordinates in which the solution field is represented. In a fixed frame the map from parameters to expansion coefficients carries roughly four to five modes of generalisable information regardless of how many are available, which bounds every method whose output is a linear combination of a learned basis. Writing the field in a frame that removes the two front positions collapses the required rank from 31 to 13 modes and the achievable error below that of any architecture we tested, relocating the obstruction from an unlearnable high-dimensional coefficient map to the estimation of two smooth monotone one-dimensional curves. We quantify the remaining prize at 2.2x and state the target a front-locating model must hit to claim it."

SECTION STRUCTURE:
1. Introduction. The transfer gap for parametric PDE surrogates, stated as a measurement not a lament. Why adsorption columns are a good testbed (stiff, nonlinear, industrially motivated, cheap enough for a full factorial). The falsification-ladder design and why pre-registration matters here specifically. Contribution in three bullets: six eliminations under information parity; a measured mechanism; a coordinate change that acts on that mechanism. No precedence claims.
2. The reference and its verification. Governing equations, Danckwerts BCs, Type V dual-term Do-Do isotherm with Henry's law intact and q_st = -dH + RT reproduced to 0.004%, LDF kinetics. Four closed-form verifications, grid convergence, mass closure 0.050%. Include the B10 anecdote in two sentences — it demonstrates the reference is trusted for a reason.
3. The physics that shapes the problem. The two-wave breakthrough, the 40x separation range, and the n-width measurement (algebraic, d_n ~ n^-1.23). Figure-led. This section must land before any surrogate appears, because it is what makes §7 non-generic.
4. Experimental design. Information parity (the six non-negotiables), splits and their cluster counts stated honestly including the 2-cluster condition axis, the calibrated alpha and the calibration that produced it, the dataset with its 32 pre-declared rejections.
5. The ladder. One compact subsection per rung with its verdict and its CI: data, capacity, basis family, physics-as-loss (including the bounds-vs-penalty interaction and the 11.5x, which is the study's largest single effect and is currently missing from RESULTS.md), operator family, classical control.
6. The mechanism. The basis/coefficient decomposition, per-mode R^2, the oracle-rank calibration, and the demonstration that three independent function classes are flat in rank against a floor that falls 28.7x. This is the intellectual centre of the paper and should be its longest section and its best figure.
7. Coordinates. Single-front alignment tested and refuted, including under an oracle — with the 40x measurement given first, as prediction rather than post-hoc explanation. Then the two-wave frame: rank 31 -> 13, oracle 0.0203, predicted 0.0508, the payoff curve mapping warp accuracy to field accuracy, and the honest statement that the gain is currently consumed by front-location error.
8. Identification (H1). The observable-descriptor re-specification, the verified substitution table, the result, and the measured reason (k_LDF R^2 = -0.61; Duhamel error amplification). Report NOT SUPPORTED in the pre-declared words. Include the pre-declared low-Damkohler re-test as a named, falsifiable follow-up.
9. Corrections and retractions. Numbered, in the body, not supplementary. Lead with A17.
10. Limitations. No experimental validation; no COF; all material parameters are literature-range placeholders and no result is named after a real framework; Da 155-3885 under-samples the informative Da ~ 1-50 regime; the condition axis has 2 clusters; solver cost is a distribution not a scalar.
11. Discussion. "The value of physical knowledge lies in how it is imposed, not whether it is present" (earned from L4b). "A classical model wins exactly when the physics it assumes is the physics that is there" (earned from L7). Both are transferable and both are measured.

THE FIVE THINGS THAT MUST HAPPEN BEFORE A WORD IS DRAFTED: (1) retire 01/02 and gate prose; (2) resolve L1 — either finish the learning curve and retract the elimination, or scope the rung to a fixed material pool and say so; (3) add the missing L4/L4b section to RESULTS.md; (4) refresh every L5 DeepONet number to the lr=3e-3 sweep already in the repo, and bracket the optimum with one more rung; (5) run FNO or formally withdraw it from the frozen protocol. Items 2 and 5 are the two a referee finds unaided.

area: Figures, tables and visual communication quality

findings.title: Fig4: not one plotted point has the colour its own legend assigns to it; the 'train' split is 100% invisible
findings.evidence:
The loop iterates over SAMPLES but plots MATERIAL descriptors:
```
for split, col in colours.items():
    xs = [mats[s["mat"]][xk] for s in S if s["split"] == split]
    ...
    ax.scatter(xs, ys, s=9, alpha=0.55, c=col, label=split, edgecolors="none")
```
manifest.json: 988 samples, 60 materials. Counter of samples: train 691, novel_material 201, novel_condition 96. Per-material split sets: 48 materials are frozenset({'train','novel_condition'}), 12 are frozenset({'novel_material'}).
So each train material is drawn 14.4x, then 2 orange points land on the EXACT same (x,y). Pixel census of figures/Fig4_parametric_coverage.png:
  train legend colour (147,175,206) -> 234 px, bbox y 214-232 x 570-589 (the legend swatch, 19x19 px, nothing else)
  novel_condition legend colour (238,191,147) -> 235 px, bbox y 257-275 x 570-589 (legend swatch only)
Dominant colour in the panel-1 data area is rgb(190,132,79), 3118 px. Predicted composite for 'opaque blue then 2x orange at alpha 0.55' = (191,133,80). Exact match. The novel_material dots render as fully opaque (181,66,63) = #b5423f, not the alpha-0.55 (214,151,149) shown in its legend swatch either.
findings.why_it_matters: The figure's legend is a false statement about the figure. A reader looking for the 48 training materials sees zero blue markers; the brown dots correspond to no legend entry at all. This is the same class of defect as retraction A1 (a plotted series that does not mean what it is labelled) and it survives every gate in validate.py because the data are real - only the rendering lies. It is also the figure that establishes dataset coverage and the train/test protocol, i.e. the figure a referee uses to decide whether the splits are honest.
findings.fix: Plot in material space, not sample space. Deduplicate to the 60 unique materials, assign each material exactly one split label (train-material vs held-out-material - the novel_condition split is a condition-axis property and does not belong on material-descriptor axes at all), and draw with alpha=1.0, distinct markers (filled circle vs open square), and edgecolors='k', lw=0.3. Put the condition-axis split in a separate small panel showing the 17 operating conditions in (T_in, RH_in, u) space with the held-out conditions marked. Add a rug/marginal histogram per axis so the reader can see the sampling density, and a fourth panel showing the derived Damkohler number distribution against the informative Da ~ 1-50 band (open item 6).

findings.title: Fig2_ground_truth.pdf is a 39.2 MB unrasterised QuadMesh - 1.7 million vector fill operations; journals will reject or mangle it
findings.evidence:
`im = ax.pcolormesh(t / 3600, z * 1e3, q, shading="auto", cmap="viridis")` with no `rasterized=`. The mesh is 2000 x 500 = 1,000,000 cells per panel, two panels.
Inflating the PDF's single content stream: 39,206,560 bytes on disk -> 232,685,770 bytes uncompressed, containing 1,698,291 path-fill (`f`) operators and 557,671 colour-set operators. First bytes of the stream confirm plain vector paths (`0 0 m / 657.4 0 l / ... / h / f`), not an image XObject.
Measured fix on the same array, figsize (4.6, 3.0):
  rasterized=True, dpi=300 ->    50,879 bytes (0.051 MB)
  rasterized=True, dpi=600 ->   118,383 bytes (0.118 MB)   <- 331x smaller than the current per-panel share
  imshow(interpolation='nearest'), dpi=600 -> 118,164 bytes
findings.why_it_matters: Elsevier/ACS/Wiley/AIP preflight and every commercial RIP either time out on a 232 MB content stream or silently flatten it at low resolution. Acrobat and most referees' PDF viewers will hang on this page. This alone will bounce the submission at the production stage before a referee sees it, and it is the figure that shows the ground truth the whole paper rests on.
findings.fix: Add `rasterized=True` to the pcolormesh and save at `dpi=600`; keep all axes, ticks, labels and the colorbar outline as vector (matplotlib rasterises only the artist you flag). Also downsample the mesh before plotting - 2000 z-cells across a ~2.4 in tall panel is >4x oversampled even at 600 dpi; `q[::4]` costs nothing visually. Belt and braces: set `matplotlib.rcParams['agg.path.chunksize']` and add a size assertion to validate.py, e.g. fail the gate if any figures/*.pdf exceeds 5 MB.

findings.title: Every figure PDF embeds Type 3 fonts, which IEEE/Elsevier/ACS artwork preflight rejects outright
findings.evidence: The rcParams block sets figure.dpi, savefig.dpi, font.size, grid and spine options but never touches `pdf.fonttype`. matplotlib 3.10.9 default is `pdf.fonttype = 3`, `ps.fonttype = 3`. Confirmed in the shipped files: `strings figures/Fig1_isotherm_form.pdf | grep -o /Type3` -> 1 occurrence; Fig7 -> 2 occurrences. No /TrueType or /Type1 font objects are present in any figure PDF.
findings.why_it_matters: Type 3 fonts are bitmap/charproc glyphs. IEEE PDF eXpress fails submissions containing them; Elsevier's artwork guidelines require Type 1 or TrueType; ACS Paragon Plus flags them. They also render badly on screen at zoom and break text search/accessibility in the published PDF. This is a two-line fix that currently blocks production for all seven figures.
findings.fix: Add `"pdf.fonttype": 42, "ps.fonttype": 42` to the rcParams update at line 36 and regenerate. While there, set `"svg.fonttype": "none"`. Add a validate.py gate that greps each produced PDF for `/Type3` and fails.

findings.title: Fig6 and Fig7 text falls to 4.4-6.1 pt at journal column width; no figure is authored to a column width
findings.evidence:
`fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13.2, 3.5))` for Fig6; Fig7 uses (10.5, 7.2); Fig4 (11, 3.2). Measured /MediaBox of the shipped PDFs and the scale factor to a 7.09 in (180 mm) double-column width:
  Fig6 11.28 x 3.51 in -> s=0.629: body 9pt becomes 5.7 pt, `fontsize=7` legends become 4.4 pt, panel height 2.21 in
  Fig7 10.43 x 7.13 in -> s=0.680: body 6.1 pt, legends 4.8 pt
  Fig4  9.08 x 3.60 in -> body 7.0 pt, legends 5.5 pt
  Fig2  9.13 x 6.13 in -> body 7.0 pt, legends 5.4 pt
At single-column (3.50 in) every figure lands between 2.2 and 3.5 pt.
findings.why_it_matters: Nature's guide sets a 5 pt absolute floor and 7 pt as the working minimum; Elsevier and ACS require >=7 pt at final size. Fig6 and Fig7 are below the floor for their legends and annotations, and Fig6's 3.77:1 aspect ratio leaves 1.09 in tall panels if forced into a single column. Every one of these figures will come back from production marked 'text too small'. Fig6's panel B additionally shows only one x tick (10^5) for three budgets, so the x axis is unreadable even before shrinking.
findings.fix: Author at final print size and never scale: define two constants, `W1 = 3.46` in (88 mm) and `W2 = 7.09` in (180 mm), and set every figsize to one of them. Set `font.size = 7`, `axes.labelsize = 7`, `xtick/ytick.labelsize = 6`, `legend.fontsize = 6`, `axes.titlesize = 7, titleweight='bold'`, `lines.linewidth = 1.2`, `axes.linewidth = 0.6`. Replace `bbox_inches='tight'` in `_save` (line 46) with `constrained_layout=True` at figure creation so the saved size equals the requested size exactly - `tight` is why the MediaBox widths (11.28, 10.43) differ from the requested figsizes (13.2, 10.5) and makes exact column-width authoring impossible. Fig6's three panels should become a 2x2 or a single-column stack.

findings.title: No figure in the paper shows a model prediction against ground truth - and the anti-fabrication gate that was supposed to force this is satisfied by a docstring
findings.evidence:
validate.py:158-177 `gate_plot_loads_model` flags any plotting script whose source matches `label\s*=\s*["'][^"']*(PIKAN|MLP|DeepONet|FNO|WNO|DeepOKAN)` unless the source also contains the substring `load_state_dict`. make_figures.py matches the first test (line 293, `label="MLP (1 param/edge)"`; line 331, `label="DeepOKAN"`). It passes the second only because of line 6 of its own module docstring:
`  * anything labelling a model curve must call \`load_state_dict\``
`grep -n load_state_dict make_figures.py` returns exactly one hit: line 6. There is no `load_state_dict(` call and no torch import anywhere in the file. Consequently all seven figures plot only aggregate scalars from JSON; not one panel shows c(z,t) or an exit curve predicted by any trained model.
findings.why_it_matters: Two problems. (1) The gate written in response to retraction A1 - a fabricated MLP-failure curve - is vacuous: any future plotting script can satisfy it by mentioning the gate's own name in a comment, which is precisely the failure mode it was built to prevent. (2) Substantively, a surrogate-modelling paper with no prediction-vs-truth overlay will be rejected on that ground alone. A referee cannot judge whether nRMSE 0.0485 means 'visually indistinguishable' or 'the second wave is missing'. Given that the whole physical story is the two-wave structure, showing which wave the best model gets wrong is the single most persuasive panel the paper could contain.
findings.fix: Tighten the gate to require a call, e.g. `re.search(r'load_state_dict\s*\(', src)`, and strip comments/docstrings before scanning (use `ast` and inspect only string literals passed to `label=`, not the module docstring). Then add the missing science: a figure with (a) the exit curve for the best, median and worst novel material - truth, best learned arm, best closed form; (b) the c(z,t) residual field for the median novel material with the two wave loci overlaid; (c) an error-vs-material scatter identifying which material is the worst case. These must be produced from a loaded checkpoint, which is exactly what the repaired gate would then enforce.

findings.title: Fig7 plots a superseded learning-rate grid: DeepONet's own better result (0.0275) exists in l5_fill2.json and is not shown
findings.evidence:
results/l5_results.json contains lrs {1e-4, 3e-4, 1e-3} for both families (15 arms each). Fig7A therefore plots deeponet best-per-p = [0.02812, 0.02925, 0.02908, 0.02962, 0.02960] and annotates 'moves 1.05x' and a '59x' gap at p=128.
l5_fill2.log records lr=3e-3 (above the top of that grid): p=128 novel = 0.0254 / 0.0263 / 0.0307 (mean 0.0275); l5_fill1.log records p=8 at lr=3e-3 = 0.0274 / 0.0261 / 0.0292 (mean 0.0276). The recomputed gap at p=128 is 0.0275/0.00050 = 55x, and the flatness becomes 1.00x rather than 1.05x.
make_figures.py:316 calls `analyze_l5.assert_wellformed(raw, need[0])` - a guard against a STALE file - but there is no guard against a NEWER, better arm living in a different file.
findings.why_it_matters: The panel's headline numbers ('59x', 'moves 1.05x') are computed from a grid that the project itself has established does not bracket DeepONet's optimum. A referee who notices l5_fill1/l5_fill2 in the repository - or who simply reruns with a wider lr - will conclude the operator baseline was under-tuned, which is the standard and fatal criticism of operator-learning comparisons. Ironically the corrected numbers strengthen the paper: flatness becomes exact (1.00x) and the level improves, so the refutation is more convincing with the fill data than without it.
findings.fix: Merge l5_fill1.json and l5_fill2.json into the L5 record, regenerate Fig7A/B with the full lr grid {1e-4, 2e-4, 3e-4, 1e-3, 3e-3}, and add an inset or a fourth series showing best-per-lr at p=128 so the reader can see the optimum is interior to the grid - that inset is the cheapest possible defence against 'you did not tune the baseline'. Extend assert_wellformed to also assert that no sibling results file contains an arm of the same family with a better score.

findings.title: Fig7 panel B: the crimson and green series are the same colour under deuteranopia, in the panel carrying the second-strongest result
findings.evidence:
Panel B draws `color="crimson"` (#DC143C, 'basis error (true coefficients)') and `color="#2ca02c"` ('coefficient-map error (predicted)') in the same axes. Brettel/Vienot CVD simulation followed by CIE76 dE in Lab:
  crimson vs #2ca02c: dE = 126.4 normal, 33.5 protan, **3.2 deutan**
A dE of 3.2 is at the just-noticeable-difference threshold - for a deuteranope these two lines are the same colour.
The custom palette has a second collision: #b5423f ('T' in Fig5B, cheby_kan in Fig6B/C) vs crimson (the POD-floor line used in Fig5A/6A/7A) gives dE = 3.1 protan, 12.7 deutan, so the same hue denotes 'a data series' in one panel and 'the theoretical floor' in another.
findings.why_it_matters: ~8% of male readers. The panel is mitigated by marker shape (o vs D) and dash pattern, so it is not unreadable, but the mitigation is accidental rather than designed, and the greyscale print version has the same problem. More broadly there is no single palette: Fig1 uses matplotlib tab10 defaults, Fig3-Fig6 use a custom {#3b6ea5, #e08b3a, #b5423f}, Fig7 reverts to tab10 {#1f77b4, #ff7f0e, #2ca02c}. #3b6ea5 means 'MLP' in Fig6 and the near-identical #1f77b4 means 'DeepONet' in Fig7 - a reader flipping between figures will conflate them.
findings.fix: Adopt one CVD-safe palette across the whole set and encode meaning, not arbitrary index. Okabe-Ito is the standard choice and every pair in it clears dE > 20 under protan and deutan: #0072B2 blue, #E69F00 orange, #009E73 green, #CC79A7 pink, #56B4E9 sky, #D55E00 vermillion, #F0E442 yellow, #000000. Reserve two semantic roles globally: BLACK dashed = a theoretical bound (POD floor / n-width), #999999 = a baseline. Assign one fixed colour per method for the entire paper (MLP, XGB, RF, ridge, DeepONet, DeepOKAN, RBF-KAN, Cheby-KAN, classical) and define it once in a module-level dict. Always double-encode with marker and line style so the figures survive greyscale printing. Ship a `figures/palette_check.png` in the SI showing the set under normal/protan/deutan/tritan simulation.

findings.title: Fig7 panel D asserts causation ('driven by stack width') from a design where width is perfectly collinear with p
findings.evidence:
The bars are plotted against `range(len(ps))` - i.e. the basis size p - and only the tick LABELS mention width: `ax.set_xticklabels([f"p={p}\nwidth {width[p]}" for p in ps])`. From l5_results.json the widths are p=8/w92, 16/88, 32/78, 64/62, 128/42 - a strictly decreasing function of p because the arms are parameter-matched. Collapse counts are {8:0, 16:0, 32:1, 64:4, 128:5} out of 9 runs per p. The title reads 'D. DeepOKAN collapse is driven by stack width'.
The experiment contains exactly one width per p, so width and p are perfectly confounded by construction; nothing in this panel can separate them. The plotted independent variable is p, not width.
findings.why_it_matters: The claim as titled is not testable from the data shown, and it is the counter-intuitive direction (NARROWER stacks collapse MORE), which is exactly the sort of assertion a referee will interrogate. Stating it as a title rather than a hypothesis is an unforced error in a paper whose entire credibility argument is that it does not overclaim.
findings.fix: Retitle to what the panel shows: 'DeepOKAN training collapses at large p (9 runs per p)'. Add the confound explicitly in the caption: 'width is set by parameter matching and falls monotonically with p, so this design cannot separate the two'. If the causal claim matters, run the disambiguating experiment - hold width fixed at 92 across all p (letting the parameter count vary) and re-measure the collapse rate; that is a cheap 45-run addition and it would convert an over-claim into a result. Also note `tot = len(raw['seeds']) * len({a['lr'] for a in raw['arms']})` at line 382 takes the lr set over ALL arms of both families; it is correct today only because both families happen to share {1e-4, 3e-4, 1e-3}, and will silently produce a wrong denominator the moment the fill runs are merged.

findings.title: Fig7 panel B's 'binding constraint' curve sits ABOVE DeepONet, so it does not bound what the title says it binds
findings.evidence: From results/l5_bottleneck.json: coef_pred_novel = 0.05150, 0.05108, 0.05094, 0.05101, 0.05105 across p = 8..128. From results/l5_analysis.json, DeepONet best-per-p = 0.02812 ... 0.02960. The green 'coefficient-map error (predicted)' line is therefore 1.73x WORSE than the blue DeepONet line it is drawn alongside, at every p. The panel title is 'B. The coefficient map is what binds' and the visual grammar (a dashed red floor below, a flat ceiling above, DeepONet in between) invites the reader to read green as an upper bound on blue.
findings.why_it_matters: If the explicit POD-plus-regressor coefficient map were the binding constraint on DeepONet, DeepONet could not beat it - yet it does, by 1.7x. The honest statement is weaker and different: 'an explicit coefficient map is flat in p for the same reason, and its per-mode R2 diagnoses why', i.e. shared mechanism, not a bound. A sharp referee will spot the ordering immediately and will then distrust the whole L5 mechanism argument, which is one of the paper's two best results. The flatness argument is genuinely strong; the bound framing is what is vulnerable.
findings.fix: Retitle 'B. An explicit coefficient map is flat for the same reason' and add one sentence to the caption stating that the explicit map is 1.7x worse than DeepONet, so it diagnoses the mechanism rather than bounding it. Better: add the missing series that WOULD make it a bound - reconstruct with the true coefficients on the first k modes and the predicted coefficients beyond, sweeping k, so the reader sees the error curve pass through DeepONet's level at the k where the coefficient map stops being informative. Panel C already reports that k is about 4-5 (r2[:6] = [0.946, 0.388, 0.579, 0.571, 0.460, 0.200]); showing it as a curve turns a plausibility argument into a measurement.

findings.title: Fig2's panel title reads 'MOF-303-like' and Fig1's entire q* axis is built from uncited placeholder constants (retraction A4)
findings.evidence:
make_figures.py:93 `("data/mof303_breakthrough.npz", "MOF-303-like, Type V")`, rendered as the panel title in Fig2_ground_truth.png. Fig1 calls `get_mof303_physics()` at line 54 and plots q* on an absolute axis reaching ~24 mol/kg.
fetch_real_mof_data.py:20 documents the source of those numbers: 'q_max 25 mol/kg (~0.45 g/g) representative MOF-303 saturation uptake'; lines 62-67 set `phys.q_max = 25.0`, `phys.isotherm_n = 4.0  # step sharpness`, `phys.henry_fraction = 0.06`.
RETRACTIONS.md:25 A4 withdraws 'Parameterized with the exact real-world thermodynamic constants of MOF-303' - 'Generic placeholders. Now explicitly labelled literature-range values pending citation'. CONTINUE_HERE.md:245 lists 'Replace the MOF-303 parameters with cited values; re-run affected figures' as an open item.
findings.why_it_matters: The prose has been retracted but the figures have not. A figure title is the highest-visibility claim surface in a paper - reviewers, and later the citing literature, will read 'MOF-303-like' as a material identity claim and will cite the absolute uptake values off Fig1's y axis. Fig1 in particular presents ~24 mol/kg with no indication that the number is a placeholder. This re-creates in the figures the exact claim that RETRACTIONS.md A4 withdrew from the text.
findings.fix: Until citations exist: retitle to 'representative Type V sorbent (parameters in Table 1, literature-range placeholders)' and add a footnote marker on every axis whose absolute scale depends on q_max. Better - and this also fixes the interpretability problem - non-dimensionalise the figures: plot q/q_max, c/c_in, and dimensionless time t/t_stoich. Then the figure makes a form claim (Type V vs Type I shape) that is robust to the parameter values, and the placeholder issue disappears from the figure entirely, confined to one clearly-flagged table row.

findings.title: Fig6A's annotation 'novel gets worse' is contradicted by the data it is drawn on
findings.evidence:
`ax.annotate("train falls 41x,\nnovel gets worse", ...)`. Recomputed from results/l2_results.json, xgb_depth family, mean over seeds:
  depth  2: train 0.04495  novel 0.05696
  depth  5: train 0.01264  novel 0.04848   <- novel MINIMUM
  depth 10: train 0.00110  novel 0.05453
Train falls 40.8x (the '41x' is correct). Novel goes 0.05696 -> 0.05453 across the plotted range, i.e. it ends 4.3% BETTER than it started; it is U-shaped with a minimum at depth 5 and rises only over depths 5-10.
findings.why_it_matters: The panel is titled 'capacity buys fit, not generalisation', which the data support beautifully - novel error is flat to within 15% while train collapses 41x. But the annotation states a monotone worsening that the plotted line visibly does not show, and a referee checking the endpoints finds a claim overshooting its evidence in a paper whose selling point is that it does not do that. The panel also plots seed means with no error bars while the neighbouring panel B has them, so a reader cannot tell whether the depth 5 -> 10 rise (0.04848 -> 0.05453) exceeds seed noise.
findings.fix: Change the annotation to 'train falls 41x; novel is flat to 15% and never approaches the floor', which is stronger and true. Add the seed spread as a shaded band on both series so the U-shape can be judged against noise, and mark the depth-5 minimum. Applying the same fix to Fig5A: `sds` there is `np.std` (population SD, ddof=0, n=3) plotted as a bare `yerr` with no definition anywhere - state in every caption whether the interval is SD, SEM or a bootstrap CI, and use the same convention in all figures.

findings.title: Fig5B's power-law overlays are anchored to a single point instead of the fit, making an excellent fit look like a bad one
findings.evidence: `anchor = np.sqrt(tail[15]) / (16.0 ** a)` forces the dotted line through the measured curve at n=16 rather than using the least-squares intercept. Recomputed from results/nwidth.json: the plotted exponents are essentially exact - channel c, plotted a = -1.2271 vs actual log-log slope over n=8..64 of -1.2268 (q: -1.1088 vs -1.1088; T: -1.1972 vs -1.1975). But the point-anchoring makes the dotted line deviate by up to +23.2% at n=8 (c), +17.2% (q), +24.0% (T), which is exactly what is visible in the rendered PNG - the dotted overlays float above the solid curves at the left of the fit band.
findings.why_it_matters: The fit is genuinely excellent and the figure makes it look sloppy. Panel B is the evidential basis for 'the n-width is algebraic', which is the pre-registered prediction that L5 goes on to refute - the reader must be able to see that the measurement was right and only the inference from it was wrong. Separately, the panel asserts 'algebraic' without showing the alternative: nwidth.json reports algebraic_r2 = 0.9910 vs exponential_r2 = 0.9737 for c, which is a comparison of R2 across two different transforms (log-log vs log-linear) and is not a valid model-selection statistic.
findings.fix: Two lines: fit `np.polyfit(log n, log d_n, 1)` over n = 8..64 and plot `exp(intercept) * n**slope`, and print the fitted exponent with a bootstrap CI in the legend. To settle 'algebraic vs exponential' properly, either plot both fits and their residuals in a small sub-axis, or report a like-for-like criterion computed on the same response (e.g. AIC/BIC on log d_n for the model log d_n = a log n + b versus log d_n = c n + d, which are directly comparable because the response is identical). Given that L5 refutes the prediction built on this spectrum anyway, the honest and stronger move is to state the exponent with its CI and its scope and drop the algebraic/exponential dichotomy from the main text.

findings.title: Fig3 and Fig5A are bar charts on logarithmic axes with arbitrary truncated baselines
findings.evidence: Fig3: `ax.bar(names, vals, ...)` then `ax.set_yscale("log")`. Fig5A: `ax1.bar(arms, means, yerr=sds, ...)`, `ax1.set_yscale("log")`, `ax1.set_ylim(floor * 0.5, max(means) * 3.0)`. In the rendered Fig5A the bars are clipped at the bottom of the axes (1e-3) and the POD-floor annotation text overlaps them; in Fig3 the y axis carries a single labelled tick (10^-3).
findings.why_it_matters: A bar encodes a quantity by its length from zero. On a log axis there is no zero, so the baseline is whatever the ylim happens to be, and the bar lengths encode nothing - in Fig5A the ratio of the tallest to the shortest bar as drawn is set by `floor*0.5`, not by the data. Cleveland/Tufte and every journal graphics guide treat this as a misencoding, and referees at top-tier venues do flag it. Both panels also carry the whole rung's headline number, so the misencoding is on the most-read graphic.
findings.fix: For Fig3, use a horizontal dot plot: one row per closed-form check, a filled dot at the measured error on a log x axis, the 5e-3 gate as a vertical rule, and the numeric value printed at the right margin. That reads correctly on a log axis, fits a single column, and is compact enough to move to the SI. For Fig5A, plot the ratio-to-floor on a linear axis (values 33.3, 33.5, 40.3, 46.4 - bars are legitimate there because the floor is a true zero for that quantity) with the absolute nRMSE printed on each bar; or keep absolute error but switch to a dot-and-CI plot with the floor as a rule.

findings.title: Fig7C's annotated statistic is computed over 128 modes but only 32 bars are shown, and undisclosed clipping is one run away from biting
findings.evidence: `k = min(32, len(r2))` limits the bars, but the annotation computes `np.median(r2[24:])` over the full array. From results/l5_bottleneck.json at p=128, len(r2) = 128; median of r2[24:] = -0.0138 (the annotated '-0.014'), while the median over the plotted subset r2[24:32] is -0.0369. Separately `np.clip(r2[:k], -0.5, 1.0)` silently truncates; the actual minimum in the first 32 is -0.3898, so no bar is clipped today, but nothing warns the reader or the author if a rerun produces a value below -0.5.
findings.why_it_matters: The reader cannot verify the annotated number from the bars in front of them - the eight visible bars past mode 24 have a median 2.7x more negative than the quoted figure. This is a small thing, but this paper's entire argument is that its numbers can be checked, and a caption number that does not match the panel is the kind of detail that costs credibility disproportionately.
findings.fix: Either plot all 128 modes (a bar chart of 128 thin bars on a log-x axis reads fine and shows the tail collapsing, which is a stronger picture), or state the annotation as 'median R2 over modes 25-128 = -0.014 (only the first 32 shown)'. Replace the silent clip with an explicit out-of-range marker (a caret at the axis limit) plus a printed count of clipped bars, and set the ylim from the data. Better still, add a cumulative curve on a twin axis: reconstruction error using only modes with R2 > threshold, which converts the panel from a diagnostic into the quantitative statement 'DeepONet at any p performs like a 4-mode oracle'.

findings.title: Fig2's two panel columns use unshared colour scales and the viridis map saturates over most of the domain
findings.evidence: Each `pcolormesh` gets its own autoscaled limits and its own colorbar; the rendered PNG shows 0-10 mol/kg on the left and 0-22 on the right. In both maps the saturated (q ~ q_max) region occupies more than half the panel and renders as flat yellow, so the only structure a reader can see is the front locus. The upper row already shows the two-wave exit curve, but the lower row - the field the surrogates actually predict - conveys almost nothing beyond 'a front moves'.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the figure that must make the reader believe the two-wave structure is a field-level phenomenon and not an artefact of the outlet trace, because the two-wave warp is the paper's terminal result. As drawn it does not do that: the second wave is invisible in the field maps, the two columns cannot be compared because their scales differ, and the panels are unlabelled (no A/B/C/D anywhere in Fig2, Fig3 or Fig4, while Fig1/5/6/7 put letters inside axes titles - three different labelling conventions across seven figures).
findings.fix: Plot q/q_max on a shared 0-1 scale with one colorbar for both columns. Overlay the two wave loci t_lo(z) and t_hi(z) as white lines - these are already computed by comoving2.py - so the reader sees the two fronts in the field, and add a third row showing dq/dt or the c field where the wave separation is far more visible. Use bold corner panel labels (a, b, c) placed with `ax.text(-0.15, 1.05, 'a', transform=ax.transAxes, fontweight='bold')` in every figure, one convention throughout. Add contour lines at c/c_in = 0.1 and 0.9 to tie the field panels directly to the warp definition sigma = (t - t_lo)/(t_hi - t_lo).

findings.title: The figure set covers five of eight rungs and none of the live research frontier; the paper's two strongest results have no figure
findings.evidence: `FIGS = {"fig1": fig_isotherm, "fig2": fig_ground_truth, "fig3": fig_verification, "fig4": fig_parametric_coverage, "fig5": fig_l1, "fig6": fig_l2_l3, "fig7": fig_l5}`. There is no fig_l4, no fig_l6, no fig_l7, no warp figure, no learning-curve figure and no ladder schematic - despite results/l4_results.json, l4b_bounded.json, l6_results.json, l7_results.json, comoving.json, comoving2.json and warp_predict.json all existing and being complete. The two results the project itself ranks highest - the two-wave warp (oracle 0.0203 at levels 0.10-0.90, beating DeepONet's 0.0281, n-width 31 -> 13 modes) and the coefficient-map bottleneck - are represented by zero figures and two panels of one figure respectively.
findings.why_it_matters: The seven existing figures were designed for the ORIGINAL framing (a PIKAN-beats-MLP demonstration). The paper is now a falsification ladder that terminates in a coordinate-change result. As it stands, four of seven figures are setup (isotherm, ground truth, verification, coverage), three are eliminations, and the constructive finding that the paper builds toward is absent. A referee reading only the figures would not learn that the paper has a positive result at all.
findings.fix: See the full proposed figure and table set in the summary field below.

findings.title: Fig1's 'matched' Langmuir control is matched in parameters but not in what the reader sees, and the callout arrow is ambiguous
findings.evidence: The docstring/comment says 'Type I comparison at MATCHED saturation capacity and matched dH', and the code does set `lang.isotherm_n = 1.0`, `lang.henry_fraction = 1.0`, and b0 so half-saturation falls at RH = 0.15. But in the rendered panel A the Type V curve plateaus near 24 mol/kg while the Langmuir reaches only ~21.5 at RH = 95% and is still climbing - the reader sees two curves with visibly different saturation. In panel B the annotation arrow runs from (25, 3) to (3, gradient[40]); over most of its length it lies along the Type V curve and only its tip touches the Type I curve it refers to.
findings.why_it_matters: The matched-parameter control is the correct and rigorous way to argue that isotherm FORM (not capacity) drives the mechanism - it is one of the best-designed things in the figure set - and the presentation partly undercuts it. The ambiguous arrow lets a hurried reader attach the 'no usable working capacity' verdict to the wrong curve.
findings.fix: State the matching explicitly in the panel (annotate 'both: q_max = 25 mol/kg, dH = -50 kJ/mol' inside the axes) so the reader knows the difference is form, not capacity. Shade the practical AWH operating window (roughly 10-40% RH) in both panels. Replace the long arrow with a short leader terminating on the Type I curve, or drop the arrow and colour the annotation text to match the curve it describes.

findings.title: _save writes PNG and PDF from one call with bbox_inches='tight' and no reproducibility metadata
findings.evidence:
```
def _save(fig, name):
    os.makedirs(OUT, exist_ok=True)
    for ext in ("png", "pdf"):
        fig.savefig(f"{OUT}/{name}.{ext}", bbox_inches="tight")
```
The PNG inherits `savefig.dpi = 300` from the rcParams; the PDF inherits it too, which is why the unrasterised Fig2 mesh is emitted as vector paths rather than a raster at a chosen resolution. `bbox_inches='tight'` is why every shipped MediaBox differs from the requested figsize (Fig6 requested 13.2 in, shipped 11.28 in). No `metadata=` argument is passed, so the PDFs carry a CreationDate that changes on every rebuild.
findings.why_it_matters: Non-deterministic output means a rebuilt figure never byte-matches the archived one, which weakens the reproducibility claim the repository otherwise takes very seriously. The unpredictable final width makes it impossible to guarantee a column fit, and the 300 dpi PNG is below the 600 dpi that most journals require for combination line-art/halftone figures.
findings.fix: Build every figure with `constrained_layout=True` and drop `bbox_inches='tight'`. Save PNG at dpi=600 and PDF at dpi=600 (which only affects rasterised artists). Pass `metadata={'CreationDate': None}` to make PDF output byte-deterministic. Add an assertion in `_save` that the figure width equals W1 or W2 to within 0.01 in, so a figure can never silently drift off the column grid.

what_is_excellent: The anti-fabrication discipline is real where it counts: every plotted series does trace to a measured result file. I recomputed the headline annotations independently and they are exact - Fig5A '33x floor' (xgb 0.04848 / floor 0.00145575 = 33.3), Fig6A 'train falls 41x' (40.8x), Fig7A 'falls 28.7x' (0.01440/0.00050), 'moves 1.05x' (0.02960/0.02812), '59x' (0.02960/0.00050), Fig7C 'median R2 beyond mode 24 = -0.014' (-0.0138). Not one number is decorative. Do not touch the computation paths.

make_figures.py:244-245 and 315-316 call `analyze_l3.assert_wellformed(l3)` and `analyze_l5.assert_wellformed(raw, need[0])` from inside the figure functions, with the comment 'A figure must never silently plot a stale results file (defect B15)'. Figures that refuse to render against a malformed or stale input file are better practice than essentially any published computational paper. Keep this and extend it, do not remove it.

Fig5B draws the fitted power law only over the range it was actually fitted on (n = 8-64), shades that range with axvspan, labels it 'fit range n = 8-64' inside the axes, and the source comment (lines 218-220) explains that the spectrum steepens beyond and that 691 samples cannot resolve the tail. Drawing the scope limit of a claim INTO the figure, rather than burying it in a caption, is exactly right and should become the template for the rest of the set.

Fig7A annotates the DeepONet-to-floor gap with a double-headed arrow spanning the two curves and places the '59x' label at their geometric mean, with the source comment 'Mark the gap itself rather than either curve, so the label is unambiguous' (line 337). That is a considered visual-reasoning decision and it works - the eye goes to the quantity being claimed. Reuse this device for the warp figure's oracle-to-predicted gap.

Fig7C's encoding is the best single panel in the set: bars coloured green above R2 = 0.5 and grey below, a solid zero rule, a dotted 0.5 threshold rule, and the whole mechanism readable in one glance. The design conveys 'only the first few coefficients are predictable' without the reader needing the caption. Keep the encoding; only fix the annotation/plot-range mismatch and the silent clip.

Fig1's Langmuir control is constructed at matched q_max and matched dH (lines 64-67) rather than at library-default parameters. Matching the confound before making a form argument is the methodologically correct construction and is what makes the Type V claim survive scrutiny. Preserve the construction; only fix the presentation.

Fig7D puts the cross-family comparison inside the panel ('DeepONet: 0 of 45 runs collapsed') and reports the degenerate-solution agreement ('all collapsed runs agree to 2.7e-7 across p, lr AND seed'). Reporting a training pathology quantitatively, in-panel, instead of dropping the failed runs, is precisely the behaviour the paper's credibility argument rests on.

Every figure function carries a one-line docstring stating the claim the figure must support, and main() prints it as the figure is built. This makes each figure auditable against a stated purpose - which is how I was able to check panel-by-panel whether the panels deliver what they promise. Keep it and extend it to the new figures.
summary:
## Verdict

The figures are scientifically honest and computationally traceable - I recomputed every headline annotation from the JSONs and all of them are exact. Nothing is synthesised. That is the hard part and it is done.

Everything else is not ready. There are three hard production blockers (a 39.2 MB rasterisation failure, Type 3 fonts in all seven PDFs, and a legend in Fig4 that describes no pixel in its own data area), two over-claims in figure titles/annotations, one stale panel, and a figure set that was designed for the abandoned narrative. The paper's two strongest results - the two-wave warp and the coefficient-map bottleneck - have zero and two panels respectively, and there is no figure anywhere showing a model prediction against ground truth.

## The three things to fix before anything else

1. `figures/Fig2_ground_truth.pdf`: 39,206,560 bytes, a 232.7 MB inflated content stream, 1,698,291 vector fill operations. `rasterized=True` at dpi=600 gives 118,383 bytes - measured, 331x smaller, no visual loss.
